chapters.title: The River Bank
paragraphs: The Mole had been working hard all morning, spring-cleaning his little home. First he used brooms, then dusters; then he climbed up ladders and steps and chairs with a brush and a bucket of whitewash, until his throat and eyes were full of dust, his black fur was spattered with whitewash, and his back ached and his arms were tired out. Spring was stirring in the air above him and in the earth below and all around, and it crept even into his dark, humble little house, bringing a restless, almost holy longing for something more. So it was hardly surprising that he suddenly threw his brush on the floor, said “Bother!” and “Oh, blow!” and then “To blazes with spring-cleaning!” and dashed out of the house without even stopping to grab his coat. Something above was calling him, and he would not be refused. He headed for the steep little tunnel that served him as the gravel driveway owned by animals whose homes are closer to the sun and air. So he scraped and scratched and scrabbled and scrooged, and then he scrooged again and scrabbled and scratched and scraped, working busily with his little paws and muttering to himself, “Up we go! Up we go!” until at last, pop! his snout came out into the sunlight, and he found himself rolling in the warm grass of a great meadow.

“This is wonderful!” he told himself. “This is much better than whitewashing!” The sun beat warm on his fur, soft breezes stroked his hot forehead, and after so long shut away in his cellar-like home, the songs of happy birds sounded almost like shouting to his dulled ears. He bounded along with all four legs off the ground at once, thrilled to be alive and to enjoy spring without any of its cleaning, and made his way across the meadow until he reached the hedge on the far side.

“Halt!” said an elderly rabbit at a gap in the hedge. “Sixpence to use this private road!” In an instant the impatient, scornful Mole had knocked him head over heels and trotted on along the hedge, teasing the other rabbits as they peeked out of their holes in a hurry to see what the commotion was. “Onion sauce! Onion sauce!” he called mockingly, and he was gone before they could think of a really satisfying reply. Then they all began to squabble with one another. “How _stupid_ you are! Why didn’t you tell him——” “Well, why didn’t _you_ say——” “You could have reminded him——” and so on, as usual; but of course by then it was far too late, as it always is.

It all seemed too good to be true. He wandered busily this way and that through the meadows, along the hedgerows and across the thickets, and everywhere he found birds building nests, flowers budding, and leaves pushing out—everything cheerful and active and hard at work. And instead of a guilty conscience nagging at him and whispering “whitewash!” he somehow could only feel how delightful it was to be the one lazy dog among all these busy citizens. After all, the best part of a holiday is perhaps not so much resting yourself as watching everyone else hard at work.

He thought his happiness could not be greater when, wandering along without any aim, he suddenly found himself standing at the edge of a brimming river. He had never seen a river before in his life—this sleek, winding, full-bodied creature, chasing and chuckling, grabbing things with a gurgle and letting them go with a laugh, only to fling itself on new playmates who shook themselves free and were caught and held again. Everything quivered and shimmered—glints and gleams and sparkles, rustle and swirl, chatter and bubble. The Mole was bewitched, entranced, fascinated. He trotted beside the river the way a very small child trots beside a man who holds him spellbound with exciting stories; and when he was tired at last, he sat down on the bank while the river kept chattering to him, a babbling parade of the best stories in the world, sent from the heart of the earth to be told at last to the hungry sea.

As he sat on the grass looking across the river, a dark hole in the opposite bank, just above the water’s edge, caught his eye, and he began dreamily to think what a cozy home it would make for an animal with few needs who liked a small, stylish riverside house, above the flood line and far from noise and dust. As he gazed, something bright and small seemed to twinkle in the depths of it, vanished, then twinkled again like a tiny star. But it could hardly be a star in such an unlikely place, and it was too bright and too small for a glow-worm. Then, as he watched, it winked at him, and so showed itself to be an eye; and a small face slowly began to form around it, like a frame around a picture.
A small brown face, with whiskers.
The face was round and solemn, and in its eyes was the very same twinkle that had drawn his attention at the start.
Small neat ears and thick silky fur.
It was the Water Rat!
Then the two animals stood there and eyed each other warily.
“Hello, Mole!” said the Water Rat.
“Hello, Rat!” said the Mole.
“Would you like to come across?” asked the Rat after a moment.
“Oh, it’s all very well to _talk_,” said the Mole, rather crossly, since he was new to rivers and riverside life and how things worked there.

The Rat said nothing, but bent down, untied a rope and pulled on it; then he stepped lightly into a little boat that the Mole had not noticed. It was painted blue on the outside and white on the inside, and it was just big enough for two animals; and the Mole’s whole heart went out to it at once, even though he did not yet fully understand what it was for.

The Rat rowed quickly across and tied up. Then he held out his forepaw as the Mole stepped carefully down. “Lean on that!” he said. “Now then, step lively!” and to his surprise and delight the Mole found himself actually sitting in the back of a real boat.
“What a wonderful day this has been!” he said, while the Rat pushed away from the bank and took up the oars once more. “Do you know, in my whole life I’ve never set foot in a boat before.”
“What?” cried the Rat, his jaw dropping. “Never set foot in a—you never—well, I—so what on earth have you been doing all this time?”

“Is it really that nice?” asked the Mole shyly, though he was quite ready to believe it as he leaned back in his seat and looked over the cushions, the oars, the oarlocks and all the fascinating fittings, and felt the boat rock gently beneath him.

“Nice? It’s the _only_ thing,” the Water Rat said gravely, leaning forward for his stroke. “Believe me, young friend, there is _nothing_—absolutely nothing—that’s half as worthwhile as simply messing about in boats. Just messing,” he went on in a dream: “messing—about—in—boats; messing——”
“Watch out, Rat!” the Mole cried suddenly.
Too late. The boat plowed straight into the bank, and the dreamer, the delighted oarsman, tumbled over backwards and ended up flat in the bottom of the boat with his feet sticking up in the air.

“—about in boats—or _with_ boats,” the Rat went on, quite unruffled, as he got to his feet with a good-natured laugh. “Whether you’re in them or out of them hardly matters. Nothing much matters at all, and that’s what is so delightful. You can get away or not get away; you can arrive where you were headed, or turn up somewhere else entirely, or go nowhere whatsoever, and either way you’re always busy and never doing anything in particular. Once you’ve finished, there’s always something else waiting, which you may do if you feel like it, though you’d be far better off leaving it alone. Listen! If you really have nothing else planned for this morning, why don’t we float off down the river together and spend a whole long day at it?”

Mole wriggled his toes for sheer joy, let out a deep sigh of perfect contentment that swelled his chest, and sank back blissfully into the soft cushions. “I’m having the most _marvelous_ day!” he said. “Come on, let’s get going right away!”

“Wait just a moment, then!” said the Rat. He slipped the rope through a ring on his landing-stage and scrambled up to his hole above. After a little while he came back into view, staggering beneath a plump wicker picnic basket.
“Stow that down by your feet,” he told Mole as he lowered it into the boat. Then he cast off the rope and picked up the oars again.
“What’s in it?” asked the Mole, wriggling with curiosity.
“There’s cold chicken in it,” replied the Rat shortly; “ coldtonguecoldhamcoldbeefpickledgherkinssaladfrenchrollscresssandwiches pottedme atgingerbeerlemonadesodawater——”
“Oh, stop, stop,” cried the Mole in ecstasy. “This is too much!”

“Do you honestly think so?” asked the Rat, in all seriousness. “It’s only what I always bring along on little outings like this. The other animals keep telling me I’m stingy, and that I _barely_ pack enough!”

The Mole never heard a word he said. Absorbed in the new life he was entering, drunk on the sparkle, the ripple, the scents and sounds and sunlight, he trailed a paw in the water and dreamed long daydreams. The Water Rat, good little fellow that he was, rowed steadily on and kindly left him alone.
“I do like your clothes, old chap,” he said, after some thirty minutes had gone by. “One of these days I mean to buy myself a black velvet smoking jacket, the moment I can afford one.”
“Oh, forgive me,” said the Mole, shaking himself awake with an effort. “You must think I’m dreadfully rude; it’s just that all of this is so new to me. And so—this—is—a—River!”
“_The_ River,” the Rat corrected him.
“And you really live by the river? What a lovely life!”

“By it, and with it, and on it, and in it,” said the Rat. “It’s my brother and my sister, my aunts, my company, my food and drink, and (naturally) my laundry. It’s my whole world, and I want no other. Whatever it lacks isn’t worth having, and whatever it doesn’t know isn’t worth knowing. Goodness, the times we’ve had together! Winter or summer, spring or autumn, it always has some fun and excitement to offer. In February, when the floods come up, my cellars and basement fill to the brim with drink I can’t use, and the brown water slides past my best bedroom window. Or else when it all drains away and leaves patches of mud that smell like plum-cake, with rushes and weeds choking the channels, and I can potter around with dry feet over most of the riverbed, finding fresh things to eat and all the odds and ends that careless people have let fall out of their boats!”
“But doesn’t it get dull sometimes?” the Mole dared to ask. “Only you and the river all day, with nobody else to chat with?”

“Nobody else to—well, I shouldn’t be hard on you,” said the Rat, holding back his temper. “You’re new here, and naturally you wouldn’t know. These days the riverbank is so crowded that plenty of folk are leaving altogether: oh no, it’s nothing like it used to be. Otters, kingfishers, dabchicks, moorhens, all of them underfoot from morning to night and forever wanting you to _do_ something—as though a fellow had no affairs of his own to look after!”
“What’s over _there?_” asked the Mole, waving a paw toward a backdrop of woodland that framed the water meadows darkly on one side of the river.
“That? Oh, that’s only the Wild Wood,” the Rat answered curtly. “We river-bankers don’t go in there much.”
“Aren’t they—aren’t they very _nice_ people in there?” asked the Mole, a little nervously.

“W-e-ll,” said the Rat, “let me think. The squirrels are fine. _And_ the rabbits—a few of them, though rabbits are a mixed bunch. And then of course there’s Badger. He lives right in the middle of it, and he wouldn’t live anywhere else, not for any money. Dear old Badger! Nobody meddles with _him_. They know better,” he added, with a look.
“Why, who _would_ interfere with him?” asked the Mole.
“Well, of course—there—are others,” the Rat explained, hesitating.

“Weasels—and stoats—and foxes—and the like. They’re decent enough in their way—I get on very well with them—we greet each other when we meet, and so on—but now and then they turn wild, there’s no getting around it, and then—well, you simply can’t trust them, and that’s the truth.”
The Mole knew very well that animal manners forbid dwelling on possible trouble ahead, or even hinting at it; so he dropped the subject.
“And beyond the Wild Wood?” he asked. “Where everything is blue and hazy, and you can see what might be hills or might not, and something like the smoke of towns, or is it only drifting cloud?”

“Beyond the Wild Wood comes the Wide World,” said the Rat. “And that’s something that doesn’t matter to either of us. I’ve never been there, and I’m never going, and neither are you, if you have any sense at all. Please don’t ever mention it again. Now then! Here at last is our backwater, where we’re going to have lunch.”

Leaving the main stream, they now glided into what looked at first like a little lake with land all around it. Green turf sloped down to either edge, and brown, snaky tree roots gleamed beneath the surface of the quiet water. Ahead of them the silvery shoulder and foamy tumble of a weir, arm in arm with a restless, dripping mill-wheel that in turn held up a gray-gabled mill house, filled the air with a soothing murmur, dull and muffled, yet with little clear voices speaking up cheerfully out of it now and then. It was so beautiful that the Mole could only hold up both forepaws and gasp, “Oh my! Oh my! Oh my!”

The Rat steered the boat in to the bank, tied her up, helped Mole, who was still unsteady on his feet, safely onto land, and swung out the lunch hamper. Mole begged, as a special favor, to be allowed to unpack everything on his own, and the Rat was delighted to humor him and stretch out full-length on the grass for a rest. Meanwhile his excited friend shook out the tablecloth and spread it, took the mysterious parcels out one at a time and laid out what was inside them in proper order, gasping “Oh my! Oh my!” at every new surprise. When everything was ready, the Rat said, “Now, dig in, old fellow!” And Mole was only too glad to obey. He had begun his spring-cleaning very early that morning, as people _will_ do, and hadn’t stopped for a bite or a sip since, and a great deal had happened to him since that faraway moment, which now felt like days ago.
“What are you looking at?” said the Rat after a while, when the edge of their hunger had been dulled and the Mole’s eyes could wander off the tablecloth a little.
“What I’m watching,” said Mole, “is a line of bubbles that I can see moving along the top of the water. It strikes me as rather funny.”
“Bubbles? Aha!” said the Rat, and he chirped cheerfully in an inviting sort of way.
A broad, shiny snout poked up over the lip of the bank, and then the Otter heaved himself out of the river and shook the water off his fur.
“Greedy rascals!” he said, heading for the food. “Why didn’t you invite me, Ratty?”
“This was a last-minute affair,” the Rat explained. “By the way—my friend Mr. Mole.”
“Pleased to meet you, I’m sure,” said the Otter, and the two animals were friends at once.

“Such a racket everywhere!” the Otter went on. “All the world seems to be out on the river today. I came up this backwater to try for a moment’s peace, and then I stumble on you fellows!—At least—I beg your pardon—I don’t quite mean that, you know.”
There was a rustle behind them, from a hedge where last year’s leaves still clung thick, and a striped head with high shoulders behind it peered out at them.
“Come on, old Badger!” shouted the Rat.
The Badger walked a pace or two toward them; then he grunted, “H’m! Company,” turned his back, and vanished.
“That’s _just_ the kind of fellow he is!” said the disappointed Rat. “Can’t stand Society! Well, that’s the last we’ll see of him today. Now, tell us, _who’s_ out on the river?”
“For one, Toad’s out on the water,” the Otter answered. “Racing boat brand-new, clothes brand-new, everything brand-new!”
The two animals looked at each other and laughed.

“First it was nothing but sailing,” said the Rat. “Then he got tired of that and took up punting. Nothing would do but he must punt all day, every day, and he made a fine mess of it. Last year it was living on a houseboat, and all of us had to go and stay with him on it and pretend we liked it. He was going to spend the rest of his life on a houseboat. It’s always the same, whatever he takes up: he gets tired of it and starts on something new.”
“A thoroughly decent fellow, though,” the Otter remarked thoughtfully. “But he’s no good at keeping steady—least of all in a boat!”

From where they sat they could catch a glimpse of the main stream across the island that lay between them, and just then a racing boat flashed into view. The rower—a short, stout figure—was splashing badly and rolling about a great deal, but working as hard as he could. The Rat stood up and called to him, but Toad—for it was he—only shook his head and settled grimly back to his rowing.
“If he keeps lurching around like that, he’ll be out of that boat in a minute,” said the Rat, settling back down.
“He certainly will,” the Otter chuckled. “Have I ever told you that good story about Toad and the lock-keeper? Here’s how it went. Toad....”

A wandering May-fly swerved unsteadily across the current, in the tipsy way that young blades among May-flies have when they’re seeing life. There was a swirl of water and a “cloop!” and the May-fly was not to be seen anymore.
Neither was the Otter.
The Mole looked down. The voice was still ringing in his ears, but the grass where the Otter had sprawled was plainly empty. There was not an Otter to be seen, all the way to the distant horizon.
But then there was a streak of bubbles on the surface of the river again.
The Rat hummed a little tune, and Mole remembered that animal manners forbid any comment whatever when a friend vanishes suddenly, whether for some reason or for none at all.
“Well, well,” said the Rat, “I suppose we ought to be getting along. I wonder which of us had better pack the lunch basket?” He did not sound as if he was terribly keen on the job.
“Oh, please let me,” said the Mole. So, of course, the Rat let him.

Packing the basket was not nearly as pleasant as unpacking it. It never is. But the Mole was determined to enjoy everything. Just when he had packed the basket and strapped it up tight, he spotted a plate staring up at him from the grass; and when that was fixed, the Rat pointed out a fork that anybody ought to have seen; and last of all, what do you know, there was the mustard pot, which he had been sitting on without realizing it. Still, somehow the job got finished at last, without much loss of temper.

The afternoon sun hung low as the Rat rowed gently homeward in a dreamy frame of mind, murmuring bits of poetry to himself and paying Mole little notice. But Mole was stuffed with lunch and brimming with satisfaction and pride, and he already felt perfectly at home in a boat (or so he believed). He was getting fidgety too, and before long he said, “Ratty! Please, _I_ want a turn at the oars now!”
The Rat shook his head, smiling. “Not yet, my young friend,” he said. “Wait until you’ve had a few lessons first. It’s not as easy as it looks.”

For a minute or two Mole kept quiet. But he grew more and more envious of the Rat, who rowed along so strongly and effortlessly, and his pride began whispering that he could do just as well. All at once he leaped to his feet and snatched the oars. The Rat, who was staring out over the water and reciting more poetry to himself, was so startled that he toppled backwards off his seat, heels in the air, for the second time that day. Mole, in triumph, took his place and gripped the oars, completely sure of himself.
“Stop that, you _silly_ ass!” the Rat shouted from the floor of the boat. “You can’t manage it! You’ll capsize us!”

Mole swung the oars back with a flourish and took an enormous stab at the water. He missed the surface completely, his legs shot up over his head, and he found himself sprawled on top of the Rat, who was lying flat. In a great fright he grabbed for the side of the boat, and in the next instant—Sploosh!
Over went the boat, and he found himself struggling in the river.

Oh my, how cold the water was, and oh, how _very_ wet it felt! How it sang in his ears as he sank down, down, down! How bright and welcoming the sun looked when he bobbed up to the surface, coughing and sputtering! How black his despair was when he felt himself going under again! Then a strong paw clamped onto the scruff of his neck. It was the Rat, and plainly he was laughing. Mole could _feel_ him laughing, all the way down his arm and through his paw and into Mole’s own neck.

The Rat took hold of an oar and shoved it under one of Mole’s arms, then did the same on the other side. Then, swimming behind, he pushed the helpless animal ashore, hauled him out, and plunked him down on the bank, a soggy, sodden heap of misery.

Once the Rat had given him a rubdown and wrung out some of the water, he said, “Now then, old fellow! Run up and down the towpath as fast as you can until you’re warm and dry again, and I’ll go diving for the lunch basket.”

So the miserable Mole, wet on the outside and ashamed on the inside, trotted about until he was fairly dry. Meanwhile the Rat plunged into the water again, recovered the boat, set her right side up and tied her fast, fetched his floating belongings ashore a few at a time, and finally dived successfully for the lunch basket and struggled to land with it.

When everything was ready for another start, Mole, limp and downcast, sat down in the back of the boat. As they pushed off, he said in a low voice, shaky with feeling, “Ratty, my generous friend! I’m truly sorry for the foolish and ungrateful way I behaved. I feel quite faint when I think that I might have lost that beautiful lunch basket. I’ve been a complete donkey, and I know it. Will you forgive me this once, and let us carry on as we were?”

“Don’t give it another thought, bless you!” the Rat replied cheerfully. “What’s a little wet to a Water Rat? Most days I’m in the water more than I’m out of it. Don’t think about it anymore. And listen, I truly believe you should come and stay with me for a while. It’s very plain and rough, mind you—nothing like Toad’s house, though you haven’t seen that yet—but I can make you comfortable. I’ll teach you to row and to swim, and before long you’ll be as handy on the water as any of us.”

Mole was so moved by this kind way of talking that he couldn’t find his voice to answer, and had to wipe away a tear or two with the back of his paw. The Rat, kindly, looked off in another direction, and soon Mole’s spirits lifted again. He even managed to talk right back to a pair of moorhens who were snickering together about how bedraggled he looked.

Back at the house, the Rat built a cheerful fire in the parlor and settled Mole in an armchair in front of it, after fetching him a dressing gown and slippers. Then he told him river stories until suppertime. They were thrilling stories indeed to a creature who lived underground, like Mole: stories of weirs and sudden floods and leaping pike, and of steamers that hurled hard bottles (at any rate bottles were certainly hurled, and _from_ steamers, so presumably _by_ them); of herons, and how choosy they were about whom they spoke to; of adventures down drains, and night fishing with Otter, or long trips far afield with Badger. Supper was a very merry meal, but soon afterward his thoughtful host had to lead a dreadfully sleepy Mole upstairs to the best bedroom. There he laid his head on the pillow in great peace and happiness, knowing that his newfound friend the River was lapping at his windowsill.

This day was only the first of many like it for the liberated Mole, each one longer and fuller of interest as the ripening summer moved on. He learned to swim and to row, and he entered into the joy of running water; and with his ear to the reed stems he caught, now and then, something of what the wind was forever whispering among them.

chapters.title: The Open Road
paragraphs: “Ratty,” said the Mole suddenly, one bright summer morning, “would you do me a favor, please? I have something to ask you.”

The Rat was sitting on the riverbank, singing a little song. He had just made it up himself, so he was far too wrapped up in it to give Mole, or anything else, proper attention. Since early morning he had been swimming in the river with his friends the ducks. Whenever the ducks suddenly stood on their heads, as ducks do, he would dive down and tickle their necks, just below where their chins would be if ducks had chins, until they had to bob up to the surface in a hurry, sputtering and furious and shaking their feathers at him, because it is impossible to say quite _all_ you feel when your head is underwater. In the end they begged him to go away, mind his own business and let them mind theirs. So the Rat left, sat down on the riverbank in the sunshine, and made up a song about them, which he called
“DUCKS’ DITTY.”

Along the quiet backwater,
By rushes tall and green,
Ducks go dabbling, dabbling,
Tails up, all unseen!
Ducks’ tails, drakes’ tails,
Yellow feet a-quiver,
Yellow bills below the surface,
Busy in the river!

Muddy green weeds below
Where the roach swim—
There we keep our pantry,
Cool and full and dim.

Each to his own delight!
_We_ love to be
Heads down, tails up,
Dabbling free!

High in the blue above
Swifts wheel and call—
_We_ are down dabbling,
Up tails all!
“I can’t say I think _all_ that much of that little song, Rat,” Mole remarked carefully. He was no poet himself and didn’t mind who knew it, and he was an honest sort of animal.

“Neither do the ducks,” the Rat answered cheerfully. “They say, ‘_Why_ can’t we do what we like, _when_ we like and _how_ we like, instead of other fellows sitting on banks watching us all the time, making remarks and poetry and things about us? What _nonsense_ it all is!’ That’s what the ducks say.”
“So it is, so it is,” said the Mole, very heartily.
“No, it isn’t!” cried the Rat, offended.
“Well, then, it isn’t, it isn’t,” said the Mole soothingly. “But what I wanted to ask was, would you take me to visit Mr. Toad? I’ve heard so much about him, and I’d love to meet him.”

“Why, of course,” said the good-natured Rat, leaping to his feet and putting poetry out of his head for the day. “Get the boat out, and we’ll paddle up there right now. There’s never a bad time to call on Toad. Early or late, he’s always the same fellow. Always cheerful, always glad to see you, always sorry when you leave!”
“He must be a very nice animal,” said Mole, climbing into the boat and taking the oars while the Rat made himself comfortable in the back.

“He’s truly the best of animals,” answered Rat. “So plain-hearted, so good-natured, and so loving. Maybe he isn’t very clever—we can’t all be geniuses—and he may well be both boastful and vain. But he has some fine qualities, has Toady.”
As they came around a bend in the river, a handsome, stately old house of weathered red brick came into view, its neat lawns stretching down to the water’s edge.

“That’s Toad Hall,” said the Rat. “See that creek on the left, where the sign says, ‘Private. No landing allowed’? It leads to his boathouse, and that’s where we’ll leave the boat. The stables are over there on the right. What you’re looking at now is the banqueting hall, which is very old. Toad is quite wealthy, you know, and this is honestly one of the nicest houses around here, though we never admit that to Toad.”

They glided up the creek, and the Mole pulled in his oars as they passed into the shadow of a large boathouse. Here they saw many handsome boats, hanging from the crossbeams or pulled up on a slipway, but none on the water; and the place felt unused and deserted.

The Rat looked around. “I see,” he said. “Boating is played out. He’s tired of it and done with it. I wonder what new craze he’s taken up now? Come along and let’s find him. We’ll hear all about it soon enough.”

They climbed out and strolled across the bright, flowery lawns looking for Toad. They soon found him resting in a wicker garden chair, with a preoccupied look on his face and a large map spread across his knees.

“Hooray!” he cried, jumping up when he saw them. “This is splendid!” He shook both their paws warmly, not waiting to be introduced to the Mole. “How _kind_ of you!” he went on, dancing around them. “I was just about to send a boat down the river for you, Ratty, with strict orders that you were to be brought up here at once, whatever you were doing. I need you badly—both of you. Now, what will you have? Come inside and have something! You don’t know how lucky it is that you turned up just now!”
“Let’s sit quietly for a bit, Toady!” said the Rat, dropping into an easy chair, while the Mole took another beside him and made a polite remark about Toad’s “delightful home.”
“The finest house on the whole river,” Toad bellowed. “Or anywhere else, for that matter,” he couldn’t resist adding.

At this the Rat gave Mole a nudge. Unluckily, Toad caught him at it, and his face turned bright red. For a moment there was an awkward silence. Then Toad burst out laughing. “All right, Ratty,” he said. “That’s just how I am, you know. And it isn’t such a bad house, is it? You like it yourself, you know you do. Now listen. Let’s be sensible. You’re exactly the animals I was hoping for. You’ve got to help me. It’s terribly important!”

“Something to do with your rowing, I’d guess,” said the Rat, looking perfectly innocent. “You’re coming along reasonably well, although you still throw up plenty of spray. Given loads of patience and heaps of coaching, you could——”

“Oh, pooh! Boating!” interrupted Toad, in great disgust. “A silly childish pastime. I gave that up _ages_ ago. A complete waste of time, that’s what it is. It honestly makes me sorry to see you fellows, who ought to know better, spending all your energy in such a pointless way. No, I’ve discovered the real thing, the only true occupation for a lifetime. I intend to devote the rest of mine to it, and I can only regret the wasted years behind me, squandered on trifles. Come with me, dear Ratty, and your agreeable friend too, if he’d be so good, just as far as the stable yard, and you’ll see what you’ll see!”

So he led the way to the stable yard, the Rat following with a deeply suspicious look; and there, pulled out of the coach house into the open, they saw a gypsy caravan, shining with newness, painted a canary yellow trimmed with green, and with red wheels.

“There you are!” cried Toad, planting his feet apart and puffing himself up. “Real life, right there, packed into that little cart! The open road, the dusty highway, the heath, the common, the hedgerows, the rolling downs! Camps, villages, towns, cities! Here today, up and away somewhere new tomorrow! Travel, change, interest, excitement! The whole world spread out in front of you, and a horizon that never stops changing! And mark my words, this is the finest cart of its kind ever built, with no exceptions whatever. Come inside and see how it’s all arranged. I planned every bit of it myself, I did!”
Mole was enormously interested and thrilled, and he hurried after Toad up the steps and into the caravan. The Rat merely snorted, jammed his hands deep in his pockets, and stayed right where he was.

It really was very compact and comfortable. There were little sleeping bunks, a small table that folded up against the wall, a cooking stove, lockers, bookshelves, a birdcage with a bird in it, and pots, pans, jugs and kettles of every size and kind.

“Everything’s here!” said Toad triumphantly, pulling open a locker. “You see—biscuits, potted lobster, sardines—everything you could possibly want. Soda water here—tobacco there—writing paper, bacon, jam, cards and dominoes—you’ll find,” he went on, as they came back down the steps, “you’ll find that absolutely nothing has been forgotten when we set off this afternoon.”
“Pardon me,” said the Rat slowly, chewing on a piece of straw, “but did I just hear you say something about ‘_we_,’ and ‘_set off_,’ and ‘_this afternoon?_’”

“Come now, Ratty, my dear, good old friend,” Toad begged, “please don’t get all stiff and sniffy about it, because you know perfectly well you’ve _got_ to come. I can’t possibly get along without you, so just call it settled and don’t argue, since that’s the one thing I can’t stand. You can’t really intend to spend your entire life stuck to that dull, musty old river of yours, living in a hole in the bank and only _boating?_ I’m here to show you the world! I’ll turn you into a proper _animal_, my boy!”

“I don’t care,” said the Rat stubbornly. “I’m not coming, and that’s final. I _am_ going to stay with my old river, _and_ live in a hole, _and_ go boating, just as I always have. What’s more, Mole is going to stay with me and do as I do, aren’t you, Mole?”

“Naturally I am,” Mole said loyally. “I’ll always side with you, Rat, and whatever you decide is how it has to be. Still, it does sound as if it might have been—oh, rather good fun, you know!” he added in a wistful voice. Poor Mole! The Life Adventurous was something so new and exciting to him, and this new side of it tempted him so much, and he had lost his heart at first glimpse to the canary-yellow cart and every one of its dear little fittings.

The Rat could see what was going through Mole’s mind, and he wavered. He hated letting people down, he was fond of Mole, and he would do nearly anything to please him. Toad was watching both of them closely.

“Come inside and have some lunch,” he said smoothly, “and we’ll talk it over. There’s no need to settle anything in a rush. Of course, _I_ don’t really care either way. All I want is to make you fellows happy. ‘Live for others!’ That’s my motto in life.”

During lunch—which was excellent, of course, as everything at Toad Hall always was—Toad simply let himself go. Ignoring the Rat, he proceeded to play on the inexperienced Mole as if he were a harp. Mole was naturally a talkative animal and always carried away by his imagination, and Toad painted the prospects of the trip, and the joys of the open life and the roadside, in such glowing colors that Mole could hardly stay in his chair for excitement. Somehow, it soon seemed to be taken for granted by all three that the trip was settled; and the Rat, though still not convinced in his own mind, let his good nature override his objections. He couldn’t bear to disappoint his two friends, who were already deep in schemes and expectations, planning each day’s separate activity for several weeks ahead.

Once everyone was ready, Toad, triumphant by now, marched his friends out to the paddock and put them to work catching the old gray horse. Nobody had asked the poor creature, and he was extremely put out: Toad had simply handed him the dustiest job of this whole dusty expedition. He frankly preferred the paddock, and he took a lot of catching. In the meantime Toad crammed the lockers even fuller of supplies, and hung nosebags, nets of onions, bundles of hay and baskets all along the underside of the cart. Finally the horse was caught and harnessed, and off they went, everybody talking at once, each animal either plodding along beside the cart or perched on the shaft, whichever suited his mood. The afternoon was golden. The dust their feet stirred up smelled rich and satisfying; birds called and whistled cheerily to them from the thick orchards on both sides of the road; friendly travelers passing by said “Good day,” or paused to say kind things about the handsome cart; and rabbits, sitting at their front doors in the hedgerows, threw up their front paws and cried, “Oh my! Oh my! Oh my!”

Late that evening, weary and happy and miles from home, they stopped on a lonely common far from any houses, let the horse loose to graze, and ate a plain supper on the grass beside the cart. Toad boasted at length about everything he meant to do in the days ahead, while the stars grew fuller and brighter around them, and a yellow moon, appearing suddenly and silently out of nowhere in particular, came to keep them company and listen to their talk. At last they went to their little bunks in the cart; and Toad, stretching out his legs, said drowsily, “Well, good night, you fellows! This is the real life for a gentleman! Talk about your old river!”
“I _don’t_ talk about my river,” said Rat, who was nothing if not patient. “You _know_ I don’t, Toad. But I _think_ about it,” he went on, sadly, dropping his voice, “I think about it—all the time!”

The Mole stretched an arm out from under his blanket, found the Rat’s paw in the dark, and squeezed it. “I’ll do whatever you want, Ratty,” he whispered. “Shall we slip away tomorrow morning, quite early—_very_ early—and go home to our dear old hole by the river?”

“No, no, we’ll see it through,” the Rat whispered back. “Thanks awfully, but I ought to stick by Toad until this trip is over. It wouldn’t be safe to leave him on his own. It won’t take long. His crazes never do. Good night!”
The end was indeed nearer than even the Rat suspected.

All that fresh air and excitement had left Toad sleeping like a log, and the next morning no amount of shaking would drag him out of bed. So Mole and Rat quietly and manfully got on with things themselves. Rat took charge of the horse, built the fire, scrubbed last night’s cups and plates and laid out everything for breakfast, while Mole set off on a long trudge to the nearest village for milk and eggs and the other supplies Toad had, naturally, forgotten to bring. By the time Toad finally strolled onto the scene, bright and merry, all the hard work had been done and the two of them were sitting about utterly worn out. He remarked what a pleasant, easy life they were all living now, compared with the cares and worries and wearisome chores of keeping house at home.

They had a pleasant ramble that day over grassy hills and along narrow side lanes, and camped as before on a common, only this time the two guests made sure that Toad did his fair share of the work. As a result, when it was time to start the next morning, Toad was by no means so enthusiastic about the simplicity of the primitive life, and in fact tried to climb back into his bunk, from which he was hauled out by force. Their way lay, as before, across country by narrow lanes, and it wasn’t until the afternoon that they came out onto the high road, their first high road; and there disaster, swift and unforeseen, leapt out at them—disaster that was momentous indeed for their expedition, but simply overwhelming in its effect on the later career of Toad.

They were strolling easily down the high road, with Mole at the horse’s head, chatting to him, because the horse had complained that he was being dreadfully left out and that nobody paid him the slightest attention. Toad and Water Rat walked behind the cart, talking together—or rather Toad was talking, while Rat said every so often, “Yes, exactly; and what did _you_ say to _him?_”—and thought all the while about something quite different. Then, far behind them, they heard a faint warning hum, like the drone of a distant bee. Glancing back, they saw a small cloud of dust with a dark, driving center, coming at them at an unbelievable speed, and out of the dust came a thin “Poop-poop!” that wailed like an animal in uneasy pain. They hardly noticed it and turned back to their conversation, when suddenly (or so it seemed) the peaceful scene was transformed, and in a blast of wind and a whirl of noise that sent them leaping for the nearest ditch, It was on them! The “Poop-poop” rang brassily in their ears. They caught one moment’s glimpse of an interior of glittering plate glass and rich leather, and the magnificent motor-car, huge, breathtaking, full of passion, with its driver tense and hugging his wheel, took possession of all the earth and air for a fraction of a second. It flung up a smothering cloud of dust that blinded them and wrapped them up completely, and then shrank to a speck in the far distance, turning back into a droning bee once more.

The old gray horse had been plodding along, dreaming of his quiet paddock, and in a raw, new situation like this he simply gave in to his natural feelings. Rearing, plunging and backing steadily, in spite of everything Mole did at his head and all the lively language Mole aimed at his better nature, he drove the cart backwards toward the deep ditch at the side of the road. It teetered for a moment—then there was a heartbreaking crash—and the canary-colored cart, their pride and joy, lay on its side in the ditch, a hopeless wreck.

Rat danced up and down in the road, simply beside himself with rage. “You villains!” he shouted, shaking both fists. “You scoundrels, you highwaymen, you—you—road-hogs!—I’ll have the law on you! I’ll report you! I’ll take you through every court in the land!” His homesickness had quite slipped away from him, and for the moment he was the captain of the canary-colored ship, run onto a sandbank by the reckless jostling of rival sailors. He was trying to remember all the fine, cutting things he used to say to the skippers of steam-launches when their wash, as they drove too near the bank, used to flood the parlor carpet at his home.

Toad sat straight down in the middle of the dusty road with his legs stretched out in front of him and stared fixedly after the vanishing motor-car. He was breathing in short gasps, his face wore a calm, satisfied look, and every now and then he faintly murmured “Poop-poop!”

Mole was busy trying to calm the horse, and after a while he managed it. Then he went to look at the cart lying on its side in the ditch. It was a sorry sight indeed. The panels and windows were smashed, the axles were hopelessly bent, one wheel was off, sardine tins were scattered all over the wide world, and the bird in the birdcage was sobbing pitifully and begging to be let out.
Rat came to help him, but even together they could not set the cart upright. “Hi! Toad!” they cried. “Come and lend a hand, can’t you!”

Toad never answered a word or moved from his seat in the road, so they went over to see what was the matter with him. They found him in a kind of trance, with a happy smile on his face and his eyes still fixed on the dusty trail left by their destroyer. Every now and then he could still be heard murmuring “Poop-poop!”
Rat grabbed him by the shoulder and shook him. “Well, Toad, are you going to give us a hand or not?” he demanded sternly.

“What a glorious, stirring sight!” murmured Toad, never offering to move. “The poetry of motion! The _real_ way to travel! The _only_ way to travel! Here today—in next week tomorrow! Villages skipped, towns and cities leapt over—always somebody else’s horizon! Oh, bliss! Oh, poop-poop! Oh my! Oh my!”
“O, _stop_ being an ass, Toad!” cried Mole in despair.

“And to think I never _knew!_” Toad went on in a dreamy drone. “All those wasted years behind me, and I never knew, never even _dreamed!_ But _now_—now that I know, now that I fully understand! O, what a flowery path lies spread before me from this day on! What clouds of dust shall rise behind me as I speed along my reckless way! What carts I shall fling carelessly into the ditch in the wake of my magnificent onrush! Horrid little carts—common carts—canary-colored carts!”
“What are we to do with him?” Mole asked Water Rat.

“Nothing at all,” Rat replied firmly. “There’s really nothing to be done. You see, I’ve known him for ages. He’s possessed now. He’s got a new craze, and it always takes him this way at first. He’ll go on like this for days, like an animal walking in a happy dream, quite useless for any practical purpose. Never mind him. Let’s go and see what can be done about the cart.”

A careful look showed them that even if they managed to set it upright by themselves, the cart would never travel again. The axles were in a hopeless state, and the missing wheel was smashed to pieces.

Rat looped the horse’s reins over its back and took it by the head, holding the birdcage, with its hysterical passenger, in his free hand. “Come on!” he told Mole grimly. “The nearest town is five or six miles off, and walking is all we can do. The sooner we get going, the better.”

“But what about Toad?” Mole asked anxiously as the two of them started out. “We can’t abandon him here, sitting in the middle of the road all by himself, in the state he’s in! It’s not safe. What if another Thing comes along?”
“O, _bother_ Toad,” said Rat savagely. “I’m done with him!”

They had not gone very far, however, when they heard a pattering of feet behind them, and Toad caught up with them and thrust a paw through the elbow of each, still breathing in short gasps and staring into empty space.

“Now listen, Toad!” Rat said sharply. “The minute we reach town, you’re going straight to the police station to ask whether they know anything about that motor-car and its owner, and to file a complaint about it. After that you need to find a blacksmith or a wheelwright and arrange to have the cart collected, repaired and set right again. That will take a while, but the wreck isn’t entirely hopeless. Meanwhile Mole and I will find an inn with comfortable rooms, and we’ll stay there until the cart is ready and your nerves have got over the shock.”

“Police station! Complaint!” Toad murmured dreamily. “Me, _complain_ about that beautiful, that heavenly vision I have been blessed with! _Mend_ the _cart!_ I’m finished with carts for all time. I never want to set eyes on that cart or hear it mentioned again. Oh, Ratty! You can’t imagine how much I owe you for agreeing to come along on this trip! I wouldn’t have set out without you, and then I might never have seen that—that swan, that sunbeam, that thunderbolt! I might never have heard that entrancing sound, or breathed in that bewitching smell! It’s all thanks to you, my dearest of friends!”

Rat turned his back on Toad in despair. “Do you see what we’re up against?” he asked Mole, talking over Toad’s head. “He’s completely hopeless. I give up. Once we’re in town we’ll head for the railway station, and with any luck we’ll find a train to take us back to the river bank tonight. And if you ever catch me going off on a pleasure trip with this maddening animal again!”—He snorted, and for the remainder of that weary trudge he spoke to nobody but Mole.

As soon as they reached the town, they marched to the station and parked Toad in the second-class waiting room, paying a porter twopence to watch him like a hawk. Next they left the horse in an inn’s stable and explained as best they could what was to be done about the cart and everything in it. Some time later a slow train set them down at a station not far from Toad Hall, and they led the spellbound, sleepwalking Toad to his front door, pushed him inside, and told his housekeeper to give him something to eat, get him out of his clothes and tuck him into bed. After that they fetched their boat from the boat-house and sculled home down the river, and very late indeed they sat down to supper in their own cozy riverside parlor, to Rat’s enormous joy and contentment.

The next evening Mole, who had got up late and spent the day taking it easy, was sitting on the bank with his fishing line when Rat, who had been out calling on friends and swapping gossip, wandered over to look for him. “Have you heard?” he said. “It’s all anybody is talking about, up and down the river bank. Toad took an early train up to Town this morning. And he has ordered a big, very expensive motor-car.”

chapters.title: The Wild Wood
paragraphs: For a long time, Mole had wanted to get to know Badger. By every account Badger was a very important person, and though hardly anyone ever saw him, everyone around the place felt his unseen influence. But whenever Mole brought up his wish with Water Rat, he was always put off. “It’s all right,” Rat would say. “Badger will turn up one of these days—he’s always turning up—and then I’ll introduce you. The best of fellows! But you have to take him not only _as_ you find him, but _when_ you find him.”
“Couldn’t you invite him here for dinner or something?” said Mole.
“He wouldn’t come,” Rat said plainly. “Badger can’t stand Society, or invitations, or dinners, or anything of that kind.”
“Well, then, what if we go and call on _him?_” suggested Mole.

“Oh, I’m sure he wouldn’t care for that at _all_,” Rat said, looking quite alarmed. “He’s terribly shy and would be certain to take offense. I’ve never once dared to knock on his door myself, and I know him very well. Anyway, we can’t. It’s completely out of the question, because his home is right in the heart of the Wild Wood.”
“Well, so what if he does?” said Mole. “You told me yourself the Wild Wood was all right.”

“Oh, I know, I know, it is,” Rat said, sidestepping the question. “But I don’t think we’ll go there just now. Not _just_ yet. It’s a long way off, and he wouldn’t be at home at this time of year anyway. If you’ll only be patient, he’ll turn up one of these days.”

Mole had to be satisfied with that. But Badger never did come along, and every day brought its own pleasures, and it wasn’t until summer was long over, and the cold and the frost and the muddy roads kept them mostly indoors, and the swollen river raced past their windows too fast for any kind of boating, that Mole found his thoughts returning, again and again, to the solitary gray Badger, who lived his own life by himself in his hole in the middle of the Wild Wood.

In winter Rat slept a great deal, going to bed early and getting up late. During his short day he sometimes scribbled poetry or did other small chores around the house; and of course there were always animals dropping in for a chat, so there was plenty of storytelling and comparing notes about the summer just past and everything that had happened in it.

What a rich chapter it had been, looking back on it all! And its illustrations so many, and so brightly colored! The pageant of the river bank had marched steadily along, unfolding in scene after scene that followed one another in stately procession. Purple loosestrife came early, shaking its lush, tangled locks along the edge of the mirror where its own face laughed back at it. Willow-herb, tender and wistful, like a pink cloud at sunset, was quick to follow. Comfrey, the purple one holding hands with the white, crept out to take its place in the line; and at last, one morning, the shy and lingering dog-rose stepped delicately onto the stage, and you knew, as if string music had announced it in stately chords that wandered into a gavotte, that June had finally come. One member of the company was still awaited: the shepherd-boy for the nymphs to woo, the knight the ladies waited for at the window, the prince who would kiss the sleeping summer back to life and love. But when meadow-sweet, charming and fragrant in his amber jerkin, moved graciously to his place in the group, then the play was ready to begin.

And what a show it had been! The drowsy animals, snug in their holes while wind and rain pounded on their doors, thought back to crisp mornings an hour before sunrise, when the white mist still hung close over the water; to the shock of the early dive, the scamper along the bank, and the glorious change that swept over earth, air and water when the sun suddenly rejoined them, so that gray turned to gold and color was born again and sprang up out of the ground. They thought back to the drowsy siesta of a hot noon, deep in the green undergrowth with the sun slanting through in little golden shafts and spots; to afternoons of boating and bathing, rambles down dusty lanes and through yellow cornfields; and finally to the long, cool evening, when so many threads were drawn together, so many friendships rounded off and so many adventures planned for the next day. On those short winter days, with the animals gathered around the fire, there was plenty to talk about. Even so, Mole had a good deal of time on his hands. So one afternoon, while Rat sat in his armchair before the blaze, now dozing, now fiddling with rhymes that refused to fit, Mole decided to go out on his own, explore the Wild Wood, and perhaps get to know Mr. Badger.

The afternoon was cold and still, under a hard, steely sky, when he slipped out of the warm parlor into the open. The countryside around him lay bare and completely leafless, and it seemed to him that he had never seen so far, or so deeply, into the insides of things as on this winter day, when Nature was sunk in her yearly sleep and looked as though she had kicked off the blankets. Copses, dells, quarries and every hidden corner, which in leafy summer had been mysterious mines to explore, now lay open with all their secrets showing, pitifully, and seemed to beg him to overlook their shabby poverty for a while, until they could once more revel in rich costume and trick and lure him with the same old deceptions. In a way it was sad, and yet it was cheering—even exhilarating. He was glad he liked the country plain, harsh and stripped of its finery. Now he had reached the bare bones of it, and they were fine and strong and simple. He had no wish for warm clover or the play of seeding grasses; the screens of hedge and the billowing draperies of beech and elm seemed better out of the way. And with a very cheerful heart he pressed on toward the Wild Wood, which lay ahead of him, low and menacing, like a black reef in some still southern sea.

There was nothing to alarm him at first. Twigs crackled under his feet, logs tripped him, and fungus on the stumps looked like caricatures, startling him for a moment with their likeness to something familiar and far away; but that was all fun, and exciting. It led him on, and he pushed in to where the light was dimmer, and the trees crouched closer and closer, and the holes on either side made ugly mouths at him.
By now everything was hushed. Dusk crept up on him, steady and swift, closing in from ahead and from behind, and the light seemed to be draining away like floodwater.
Then the faces began.

At first it was only over his shoulder, and blurry, that he thought he glimpsed a face: a small, nasty, wedge-shaped face peering out at him from a hole. But when he spun around to look straight at it, the thing was gone.

He walked faster, telling himself in a cheerful voice not to start imagining things, or he would never hear the end of it. He passed one hole, then another, then another; and then—yes!—no!—yes! Beyond doubt a narrow little face with hard eyes had popped up from a hole for a moment, and vanished. He faltered—steeled himself for the effort and strode on. Then all at once, as though it had been like this from the start, every hole, near and far (and there were hundreds), seemed to have a face of its own, appearing and disappearing in a flash, each one fixing him with a stare of malice and hatred: all hard-eyed and wicked and sharp.
Once he got away from those holes in the banks, he told himself, the faces would stop. So he veered off the path and plunged into the parts of the wood where nobody ever walked.
Then the whistling began.

At first it was faint and shrill and a long way behind him; yet somehow it made him hurry on. Then, just as faint and shrill, it sounded far in front of him, and he slowed, longing to turn back. While he stood there undecided, it rose up on both sides at once, and seemed to be taken up and handed on along the entire length of the wood, right to its farthest limit. They were awake and watchful and ready, obviously, whoever they were! And he—he was alone and unarmed, miles from any help, and night was coming on.
Then the pattering began.

To begin with he took it for nothing more than falling leaves, the sound was so light and delicate. But as it swelled it settled into a steady beat, and he knew it could only be the pat-pat-pat of little feet, still a very long way off. Was it ahead or behind? First it seemed to be one, then the other, then both. It swelled and multiplied, and however he listened, anxiously, leaning one way and then another, it seemed to be tightening around him from every side. While he stood motionless, listening, a rabbit came tearing through the trees straight at him. He waited for it to slow down, or to veer away on some other path. Instead it nearly brushed against him as it shot past, its face set and hard, its eyes staring. “Get out of here, you fool, get out!” Mole heard it mutter, as it swung around a stump and vanished down a welcoming burrow.

The pattering swelled until it sounded like a sudden hailstorm on the dry carpet of leaves around him. The whole wood seemed to be running now, running hard, hunting, chasing, closing in on something or—somebody? Panic took hold of him and he began to run as well, without aim, with no idea where. He ran into things, tripped over things and tumbled into things, ducked under things and swerved around things. In the end he hid himself in the deep dark hollow of an old beech tree, which promised shelter, cover—perhaps even safety, though who could say? In any case he was too worn out to run another step, and all he could do was burrow into the dry leaves that had blown into the hollow and hope he was safe for the time being. And lying there, panting and shaking, listening to the whistling and pattering outside, he finally understood it, in its full horror, that dreadful thing which other small dwellers of field and hedgerow had met here and remembered as their blackest hour—that thing which Rat had tried, without success, to spare him from—the Terror of the Wild Wood!

Back at home, Rat sat warm and comfortable, dozing by his fire. The paper with his half-finished verses slid off his knee, his head tipped back, his mouth dropped open, and he drifted along the green banks of dream-rivers. Then a coal settled, the fire crackled and threw up a tongue of flame, and he jerked awake. He remembered what he had been busy with, reached down to the floor for his verses and frowned over them for a minute, then glanced around for Mole, meaning to ask whether he knew a good rhyme for this or that.
But Mole wasn’t there.
He listened for a while. The house seemed very quiet.
Then he called out “Moly!” a few times, and when nobody answered he stood up and walked out to the hall.
Mole’s cap was missing from its usual peg. His galoshes, which always lay by the umbrella stand, were gone too.

Rat went out of the house and studied the muddy ground by the door, hoping to spot Mole’s tracks. And there they were, plain as anything. The galoshes were brand new, bought just for the winter, and the studs on their soles were still fresh and sharp. He could see their prints in the mud, running along straight and full of purpose, heading directly for the Wild Wood.

Rat’s face turned very grave, and for a minute or two he stood lost in thought. Then he went back inside, buckled a belt around his middle, pushed a pair of pistols into it, snatched up a stout club that was standing in a corner of the hall, and set off for the Wild Wood at a brisk walk.

Dusk was already settling in by the time he came to the first scattering of trees, and he marched straight into the wood without a second thought, glancing anxiously left and right for some trace of his friend. Wicked little faces poked out of holes here and there, only to duck back out of sight when they saw the brave fellow with his pistols and the big ugly club in his fist. The whistling and pattering he had heard so clearly when he first stepped in faded away and stopped, and everything went very quiet. Boldly he pushed along the whole length of the wood until he reached its far edge. Then he left the paths behind altogether and began crossing the wood back and forth, working his way patiently over every bit of ground, calling out cheerfully the whole time, “Moly, Moly, Moly! Where are you? It’s me—it’s old Rat!”

After an hour or more of patient searching through the wood, he finally heard, to his great joy, a small voice calling back. Following the sound through the thickening dark, he came to the base of an old beech tree with a hollow in its trunk, and from inside the hollow a weak voice said, “Ratty! Is it really you?”
Rat crawled into the hollow and found Mole there, worn out and still shaking. “Oh, Rat!” he cried. “You can’t imagine how scared I’ve been!”

“Oh, I understand perfectly,” Rat said, in a soothing tone. “You really shouldn’t have done it, Mole. I tried my best to stop you. Those of us who live on the river bank almost never come here alone. When we must, we go at least in twos; then we’re usually fine. And besides, there are a hundred things you need to know, things we understand and you don’t yet. Passwords, I mean, and signs, and sayings that carry power, and plants you keep in your pocket, and verses you recite, and little tricks and dodges you practice; all easy enough once you know them, but a small animal has to know them, or he’ll land in trouble. Of course, if you were Badger or Otter, that would be a different matter altogether.”
“But surely brave Mr. Toad wouldn’t be afraid to come here on his own, would he?” Mole asked.
“Old Toad?” Rat said, with a hearty laugh. “Not on your life would he show his face here alone, not for a whole hat full of gold guineas, that Toad.”
Rat’s easy laughter did Mole a world of good, and so did the sight of that stick and those shiny pistols. His shivering stopped, and he began to feel braver and more like his old self.

“Well now,” Rat said after a moment, “we really have to pull ourselves together and start for home while a little light is left. We can’t possibly spend the night here, you see. It’s too cold, for one thing.”

“Dear Ratty,” said poor Mole, “I’m terribly sorry, but I’m completely done in, and that’s the honest truth. If I’m ever going to make it home, you _have_ to let me rest here a little longer and win back my strength.”
“Oh, fine,” said good-natured Rat. “Rest all you like. It’s nearly black as pitch out there anyway, and a bit of moon should turn up later on.”

So Mole snuggled deep into the dry leaves and stretched out, and before long he drifted off—though his sleep was restless and full of bad dreams. Rat, meanwhile, wrapped himself up as warmly as he could and lay there patiently keeping watch, a pistol held ready in his paw.
At last Mole woke up, much refreshed and feeling like himself. Rat said, “Right! I’ll just step outside and make sure all is quiet, and then we really must get going.”
He walked to the mouth of their hiding place and stuck his head outside. Then Mole heard him murmuring to himself, “Well, well! Here’s—a—pretty—how-do-you-do!”
“What’s up, Ratty?” asked Mole.
“_Snow_ is up,” Rat replied briefly; “or rather, _down_. It’s snowing hard.”

The Mole came over and crouched beside him. Looking out, he saw that the wood that had frightened him so much looked completely different now. The holes, hollows, pools, pitfalls and other black dangers for travelers were disappearing fast, and a shining carpet of fairy-work was spreading everywhere, so delicate it seemed a shame to tread on it with rough feet. A fine powder hung in the air and tingled against the cheek, and the black trunks of the trees stood out in a light that seemed to come from below.

“Ah, well, there’s no help for it,” said Rat after a little thought. “I suppose we have to set off and trust to luck. The trouble is, I’m not at all sure where we are. And with the snow, everything looks completely changed.”

It certainly did. The Mole would never have guessed it was the same wood. Still, they set off bravely along the way that looked most hopeful, holding on to each other and pretending, with unbeatable cheerfulness, that they recognized an old friend in every new tree that stared grimly and silently back at them, or that they spotted openings, gaps and paths with a familiar bend to them, in a dull stretch of white ground and black tree trunks that never changed.

An hour or two later—they had lost all track of time—they stopped, discouraged, worn out and hopelessly lost, and sat down on a fallen tree trunk to catch their breath and decide what to do. They ached with tiredness and were bruised from tumbling; they had fallen into several holes and were soaked through; the snow was getting so deep that they could barely drag their little legs through it, and the trees were thicker and more alike than ever. There seemed to be no end to this wood, and no beginning, and no variety in it, and, worst of all, no way out.

“We can’t sit here very long,” said the Rat. “We’ll have to make another push and do something. The cold is terrible, and soon the snow will be too deep for us to wade through.” He peered around and thought. “Listen,” he went on, “here’s what I’m thinking. There’s a sort of dip just ahead of us, where the ground looks all hilly and lumpy and bumpy. Let’s make our way down into that and look for some kind of shelter, a cave or a hole with a dry floor, out of the snow and the wind, and we’ll have a good rest there before we try again, since we’re both pretty well worn out. Besides, the snow may stop, or something may turn up.”

So once more they got to their feet and struggled down into the dip, where they searched about for a cave or some dry corner that would shelter them from the biting wind and the whirling snow. They were poking around one of the lumpy spots the Rat had mentioned when suddenly the Mole tripped and fell flat on his face with a squeal.
“Ow! My leg!” he yelped. “My poor, poor shin!” And he sat up in the snow and clutched the injured leg against him with both front paws.
“Poor old Mole!” said the Rat kindly.

“Not your lucky day, is it? Here, let me see that leg. Yes,” he continued, kneeling down to inspect it, “you’ve certainly cut your shin. Hold on while I dig out my handkerchief, and I’ll bandage it for you.”
“I must have caught my foot on some buried branch or stump,” Mole said glumly. “Oh dear! Oh dear!”

“It’s a very clean cut,” said the Rat, studying it closely again. “A branch or a stump never did that. It looks as if it was made by the sharp edge of something metal. Strange!” He thought for a while and looked over the humps and slopes around them.
“Well, never mind what done it,” said Mole, so pained he forgot his grammar. “It hurts just as much, whatever done it.”

Meanwhile Rat had finished bandaging the leg with his handkerchief, left Mole sitting there, and gone off to dig busily in the snow. He scratched, he shoveled, he poked about, all four paws hard at it, while Mole waited with growing impatience and called out every so often, “Oh, _come_ on, Rat!”
All at once Rat shouted “Hooray!” and then “Hooray-oo-ray-oo-ray-oo-ray!” and started dancing a wobbly little jig on the snow.
“What _have_ you found, Ratty?” asked the Mole, still nursing his leg.
“Come and see!” said the delighted Rat, still jigging.
The Mole limped over to the spot and took a good look.

“Well,” he said at last, in a slow voice, “I SEE it, sure enough. I’ve run into plenty of these before. Nothing out of the ordinary, if you ask me. A door-scraper! So what? Why are you jigging around over a door-scraper?”
“But can’t you see what it _means_, you—you dim-witted creature?” cried the Rat impatiently.

“Of course I understand what it means,” answered Mole. “It means that some VERY careless, absent-minded person has dropped his door-scraper in the middle of the Wild Wood, _right_ where it’s _certain_ to trip up _everyone_ who passes. Awfully inconsiderate of him, if you ask me. Once I’m home, I’m going to lodge a complaint with—with somebody or other, you just wait and see!”
“Oh, dear, oh, dear!” cried Rat, hopeless at how thick Mole was being. “Stop arguing and come help me dig!” Back he went to his shoveling, and the snow flew up around him in every direction.
After a bit more hard work his efforts paid off, and a very shabby doormat lay uncovered.
“There, what did I tell you?” exclaimed the Rat in great triumph.

“Absolutely nothing at all,” replied the Mole, with perfect truthfulness. “Now then,” he went on, “you seem to have found another bit of household rubbish, worn out and thrown away, and I suppose you’re perfectly happy. Go ahead and dance your jig around that if you must, and get it over with, and then maybe we can move on and not waste any more time on rubbish heaps. Can we EAT a doormat? Or sleep under a doormat? Or sit on a doormat and sled home over the snow on it, you maddening rodent?”
“Are—you—telling—me,” cried the excited Rat, “that this doormat doesn’t _tell_ you anything?”

“Honestly, Rat,” said Mole, rather peevishly, “I think this silliness has gone on long enough. Whoever heard of a doormat _telling_ somebody something? They don’t. They’re not the type. A doormat knows its place.”

“Now listen here, you—you blockhead,” replied the Rat, really angry, “this has to stop. Not another word, just scrape—scrape and scratch and dig and search around, especially on the sides of the lumps, if you want to sleep warm and dry tonight, because it’s our last chance!”

The Rat attacked a snowbank beside them with enthusiasm, probing everywhere with his stick and then digging furiously; and the Mole scraped busily too, more to please the Rat than for any other reason, since he thought his friend was getting light-headed.

After some ten minutes of hard work, the tip of the Rat’s stick struck something that sounded hollow. He kept working until he could get a paw through and feel around; then he called the Mole to come and help. The two animals went at it hard, until at last the result of their labor stood in full view of the astonished and, until now, doubting Mole.

In the side of what had looked like a snowbank stood a solid little door, painted dark green. An iron bell-pull hung beside it, and below that, on a small brass plate, neatly engraved in square capital letters, they could read by the light of the moon
MR. BADGER.

Mole was so astonished and delighted that he toppled backward into the snow. “Rat!” he cried, quite ashamed of himself. “You’re a marvel! A genuine marvel, that’s what you are. Now I see the whole thing! Right from the moment I fell and cut my shin, you reasoned it out one step at a time inside that wise head of yours. You looked at the cut, and straight away your magnificent mind told you, ‘Door-scraper!’ Then you went and tracked down the very door-scraper that did the damage! And did you stop there? No. Plenty of people would have been content, but not you. Your brain kept right on going. ‘If I can only turn up a doormat,’ you said to yourself, ‘my theory will be proven!’ And naturally you found your doormat. You’re so clever I believe you could find anything you pleased. ‘Now,’ you say, ‘that door is as good as standing in front of me. All that’s left is to find it!’ I’ve read about this sort of thing in books, but I never saw it happen in real life. You belong somewhere you’ll be properly admired. You’re wasted here among ordinary folks like us. If I only had your brains, Ratty——”

“Since you haven’t,” snapped the Rat, rather unkindly, “I suppose you plan to sit in the snow all night and _talk?_ Up you get, this minute! Hang on to that bell-pull over there and ring it hard, as hard as you can, while I pound on the door!”

Rat set about pounding on the door with his stick, while Mole leaped up and caught hold of the bell-pull. He hung there swinging with both feet dangling in the air, and from somewhere far inside they could just make out the faint answer of a deep-voiced bell.

chapters.title: Mr. Badger
paragraphs: They waited patiently for what felt like a very long time, stamping their feet in the snow to keep them warm. At last they heard slow, shuffling footsteps coming toward the door from the inside. The Mole remarked to the Rat that it sounded like someone walking in carpet slippers that were too big and worn down at the heel. That was clever of Mole, because it was exactly what it was.
A bolt scraped back, and the door opened a few inches, just far enough to show a long snout and a pair of sleepy, blinking eyes.
“Listen,” said a gruff, suspicious voice, “if this happens _one_ more time, I’ll be absolutely furious. Who is it _now_, bothering people on a night like this? Out with it!”
“Oh, Badger,” cried Rat, “please open up. It’s Rat, with my friend Mole. We got lost in the snow.”

“What, Ratty, my dear little fellow!” exclaimed the Badger, in a completely different voice. “Come in, both of you, right away. Why, you must be half frozen. Well, I never! Lost in the snow! And in the Wild Wood, too, and at this hour of the night! Come on, now, in you come.”
In their eagerness to get inside, the two animals stumbled over each other, and with great joy and relief they heard the door close behind them.

The Badger wore a long dressing gown, and his slippers really were worn down at the heel. He held a flat candlestick in his paw and had probably been on his way to bed when their knocking began. He looked down at them kindly and patted both their heads. “This is no night for small animals to be out,” he said, like a father. “I’m afraid you’ve been up to one of your pranks again, Ratty. But come along; come into the kitchen. There’s a first-rate fire there, and supper and everything.”

He shuffled ahead of them, carrying the light, and they followed, nudging each other eagerly, down a long, gloomy and, to tell the truth, rather shabby passage. It led into a sort of central hall, and from it they could dimly make out other long, tunnel-like passages branching away, mysterious and seemingly endless. But the hall had doors in it as well, sturdy oak doors that looked comfortable. The Badger flung one of these open, and at once they found themselves in all the glow and warmth of a large kitchen lit by the fire.

The floor was worn red brick, and a log fire burned on the wide hearth, between two inviting chimney corners tucked into the wall, well away from any hint of a draft. A couple of high-backed benches, facing each other on either side of the fire, gave extra seating to anyone who liked company. In the middle of the room stood a long table of plain boards set on trestles, with a bench down each side. At one end, where an armchair had been pushed back, lay the remains of the Badger’s plain but generous supper. Rows of spotless plates gleamed from the shelves of the dresser at the far end of the room, and from the rafters overhead hung hams, bundles of dried herbs, nets of onions and baskets of eggs. It seemed a place where heroes could fittingly feast after a victory, where tired harvesters could line up by the dozen along the table and hold their Harvest Home with laughter and song, or where two or three friends with simple tastes could sit as they pleased, eating and smoking and talking in comfort and contentment. The ruddy brick floor smiled up at the smoky ceiling; the oak benches, shiny from long wear, traded cheerful glances; the plates on the dresser grinned at the pots on the shelf, and the merry firelight flickered and played over everything alike.

The kind-hearted Badger pushed them onto a high-backed bench in front of the fire and told them to peel off their wet coats and boots. He brought them dressing gowns and slippers, then washed Mole’s shin himself in warm water and patched the cut up with sticking plaster, until it looked better than new. At last they were warm and dry, enfolded in firelight and cozy heat, tired legs stretched out before them, while behind them came the promising clatter of plates being set on the table. To these storm-battered animals, safe in port at last, the cold, pathless Wild Wood they had only just left outside seemed miles and miles off, and everything they had gone through there felt like a half-forgotten dream.

When they were thoroughly toasted, the Badger called them to the table, where he had been busy setting out a meal. They had felt pretty hungry before, but now that they actually saw the supper spread out for them, it seemed only a question of what to attack first, since everything looked so tempting, and whether the other dishes would be kind enough to wait until they had time to give them attention. For a long while no one could talk; and when conversation slowly started up again, it was the regrettable kind that comes from talking with your mouth full. The Badger did not mind that sort of thing at all, and he took no notice of elbows on the table, or of everybody speaking at once. Since he never went into Society himself, he had come to think that these things were among the things that didn’t really matter. (We know, of course, that he was wrong, and took too narrow a view; they matter very much, though it would take too long to explain why.) He sat in his armchair at the head of the table and nodded gravely now and then as the animals told their story. He didn’t seem surprised or shocked at anything, and he never said, “I told you so,” or, “Just what I always said,” or remarked that they ought to have done this, or ought not to have done that. The Mole began to feel very friendly toward him.

Supper was over at long last. Each animal felt stuffed as snugly into his skin as was reasonably safe, and by now none of them cared a fig for anyone or anything. They drew up around the glowing embers of the big log fire, delighted to be up _so_ late, and _so_ free to please themselves, and _so_ well fed. When they had chatted a while about this and that, Badger said warmly, “Well now! What’s the news where you live? How is old Toad getting along?”

“Oh, from bad to worse,” said the Rat gravely, while the Mole, perched on a bench and basking in the firelight with his heels higher than his head, tried to look suitably sad. “Another smash-up only last week, and a bad one. You see, he insists on driving himself, and he’s hopelessly bad at it. If he would only hire a decent, steady, well-trained animal, pay him good wages and leave everything to him, he’d be fine. But no; he’s convinced he’s a born driver, and that nobody can teach him anything; and everything else follows from that.”
“How many has he had?” asked the Badger gloomily.

“Crashes, or cars?” asked Rat. “Ah, well, with Toad it comes to the same thing. This is number seven. As for the rest—you know that coach-house of his? It’s stacked—truly stacked right up to the rafters—with bits of motorcars, not one of them larger than your hat! That’s where the other six went, as far as anyone can tell.”
“Three trips to the hospital so far,” put in the Mole; “and the fines he’s had to pay—it’s simply awful to even think about.”

“Yes, and that’s only part of the problem,” Rat went on. “Toad has money, as we all know, but he isn’t a millionaire. He’s a hopeless driver, too, and he has no respect for the law whatsoever. Sooner or later he’ll end up killed or ruined, one or the other. Badger! We’re his friends. Shouldn’t we be doing something?”
The Badger thought hard for a moment. “Now look here!” he said at last, rather sternly. “Of course you know I can’t do anything _now?_”

His two friends nodded, understanding his point perfectly. According to the rules of animal etiquette, no animal is ever expected to do anything strenuous, or heroic, or even moderately active during the winter off-season. All are sleepy, and some are actually asleep. All are more or less shut in by the weather; and all are resting after hard days and nights, during which every muscle was severely tested and every ounce of energy stretched to the limit.

“Very well, then!” the Badger continued. “_But_ once the year has really turned, and the nights are shorter, and halfway through them you wake up and feel restless and want to be up and doing by sunrise, if not before—_you_ know!——”
Both animals nodded gravely. _They_ knew!
