“Right, _then_,” Badger continued, “the three of us—you, me and our friend Mole here—will take Toad in hand, and no mistake. We won’t put up with any nonsense. We’ll talk some sense into him, and use force if it comes to that. We’ll _make_ him into a sensible Toad. We’ll—you’re asleep, Rat!”
“Not me!” said the Rat, waking up with a jerk.

“He’s been asleep two or three times since supper,” said the Mole, laughing. He himself felt wide awake and even lively, though he didn’t know why. The reason, of course, was that he was an underground animal by birth and upbringing, so the setting of Badger’s house suited him exactly and made him feel at home. The Rat, on the other hand, slept every night in a bedroom whose windows opened onto a breezy river, and so naturally found the air here still and stuffy.

“Well, it’s high time we were all in bed,” said the Badger, getting to his feet and fetching more flat candlesticks. “Follow me, you two, and I’ll show you where you’ll sleep. And no hurry tomorrow morning—breakfast whenever you like!”

He led the two animals to a long room that seemed half bedroom and half loft. The Badger’s winter stores, which really were visible everywhere, took up half the room—piles of apples, turnips and potatoes, baskets full of nuts, and jars of honey. But the two little white beds on the rest of the floor looked soft and inviting, and the sheets on them, though coarse, were clean and smelled wonderfully of lavender. The Mole and the Water Rat shook off their clothes in some thirty seconds and tumbled in between the sheets, happy and content.

Just as the kindly Badger had ordered, the two weary animals slept in and came down to breakfast very late the next morning. In the kitchen a cheerful fire was blazing, and two young hedgehogs were perched on a bench at the table, spooning oatmeal porridge out of wooden bowls. When the two friends walked in, the hedgehogs let their spoons clatter down, scrambled to their feet, and bowed their heads politely.
“No, no, stay seated,” said the Rat pleasantly, “and finish your porridge. Where did you youngsters come from? Got lost in the snow, I expect?”

“Yes, please, sir,” the older hedgehog answered politely. “Me and little Billy here, we was trying to get to school—mother _would_ send us, whatever the weather—and naturally we got ourselves lost, sir, and Billy went and got scared and started crying, him being young and timid. And finally we came across Mr. Badger’s back door by luck, and took the liberty of knocking, sir, because Mr. Badger’s a good-hearted gentleman, as everybody knows——”

“I see,” said Rat, slicing himself a few strips of bacon off a big slab, while Mole cracked some eggs into a saucepan. “And how’s the weather out there? And you don’t have to call me ‘sir’ every other word,” he added.
“Oh, it’s awful, sir, the snow’s terrible deep,” said the hedgehog. “Gentlemen like you can’t go out at all today.”
“Where’s Mr. Badger?” asked the Mole, as he warmed the coffeepot in front of the fire.
“The master’s gone off to his study, sir,” the hedgehog answered, “and he said as how he’d be especially busy this morning, and nobody was to disturb him, not for anything.”

Everyone there understood this explanation perfectly. The fact is, as already explained, that when you live a life of intense activity for six months of the year, and of comparative or actual drowsiness for the other six, you can’t keep pleading sleepiness during the second half whenever there are people about or things to be done. The excuse gets tiresome. The animals knew very well that Badger, having eaten a hearty breakfast, had retired to his study, settled himself in an armchair with his legs up on another and a red cotton handkerchief over his face, and was being “busy” in the usual way at this time of year.

The front-door bell rang out with a loud clang. Rat, whose paws were slick with buttered toast, sent the smaller hedgehog, Billy, to find out who it was. A good deal of stomping echoed from the hall, and before long Billy came back with the Otter walking in ahead of him. The Otter flung himself at Rat, hugging him and bellowing a fond hello.
“Get off!” spluttered the Rat, with his mouth full.

“Figured you’d be here,” said Otter happily. “When I got to the River Bank this morning, everyone was in a terrible state. Rat hadn’t come home all night, and neither had Mole—something awful must have happened, they said, and of course the snow had buried all your tracks. But I knew that when folks get into trouble they usually head for Badger, or else Badger hears about it somehow, so I came straight here, through the Wild Wood and the snow! My, it was gorgeous, making my way through it while the red sun climbed and showed against the black tree trunks! It was so still, and every now and again a heap of snow would slide off a branch with a sudden flop! that made you jump and dive for cover. In the night, snow castles and snow caverns had popped up out of nowhere—and snow bridges, terraces, ramparts too—I could have stayed there playing with them for hours. In places the weight of the snow had ripped off great limbs, and robins were perching and hopping on them, all cocky and self-satisfied, as though they had done it themselves. A straggling line of wild geese flew over, high against the gray sky, and a few rooks swooped about above the trees, took a look, and flapped away home looking disgusted. But I didn’t meet a single sensible soul to ask for news. About halfway through, I found a rabbit sitting on a stump, scrubbing his silly face with his paws. He was thoroughly frightened when I sneaked up behind him and laid a heavy paw on his shoulder. I had to cuff him on the head once or twice before I could get any sense out of him. Finally I got it out of him that one of them had seen Mole in the Wild Wood last night. All the burrows were talking about it, he said: how Mole, Mr. Rat’s special friend, was in a bad way, having lost his path, and how ‘They’ were out hunting and had been driving him around in circles. ‘Then why didn’t one of you _do_ something?’ I asked. ‘Maybe you haven’t got brains, but there are hundreds and hundreds of you, great plump fellows, fat as butter, with tunnels running everywhere, and you could have taken him in and kept him safe and comfortable, or at least given it a try.’ ‘What, _us?_’ was all he said. ‘_Do_ something? Us rabbits?’ So I cuffed him again and left him. There was nothing more to be done. Anyway, I’d learned something, and if I’d been lucky enough to run into any of ‘Them,’ I’d have learned more—or _they_ would have.”
“Didn’t you feel at all—er—scared?” asked the Mole, a little of yesterday’s terror creeping back at the mention of the Wild Wood.

“Nervous?” The Otter laughed, flashing a gleaming set of strong white teeth. “I’d give them something to be nervous about if any of them tried their tricks on me. Here, Mole, be a good little fellow and fry me some slices of ham. I’m terribly hungry, and I’ve got a mountain of things to tell Ratty here. I haven’t seen him in ages.”

So good-natured Mole cut several slices of ham, set the hedgehogs to frying them, and went back to his own breakfast. Meanwhile the Otter and the Rat put their heads together and happily talked river-shop, which is long, never-ending talk that rambles on like the babbling river itself.

One plate of fried ham had just been emptied and sent back for a refill when the Badger came in, yawning and rubbing his eyes. He greeted everyone in his quiet, plain way, asking kindly after each of them. “It must be nearly lunchtime,” he said to the Otter. “You’d better stay and eat with us. You must be hungry on a cold morning like this.”
“I certainly am!” replied the Otter, winking at Mole. “Watching these greedy young hedgehogs stuff themselves with fried ham has made me absolutely famished.”
The hedgehogs were just starting to feel hungry again after their porridge and all their hard work at the frying pan. They looked up timidly at Mr. Badger, but they were too shy to say a word.
“Here, you two youngsters, run along home to your mother,” the Badger said kindly. “I’ll send someone with you to show you the way. I’m sure you won’t want any dinner today.”
He gave them sixpence each and a pat on the head, and off they went, bowing and tugging at their caps and forelocks respectfully as they left.

Soon they all sat down to lunch together. Mole found himself seated beside Mr. Badger. The other two were still deep in river gossip, and nothing could pull them out of it, so he took the chance to tell Badger how comfortable and homelike he found everything. “Once you’re well underground,” he said, “you know exactly where you are. Nothing can happen to you, and nothing can get at you. You’re completely your own master, with no need to ask anyone’s opinion or care what they say. Life goes on overhead just the same, and you let it, and you don’t trouble yourself about it. When you feel like it, up you go, and there everything is, waiting for you.”

The Badger simply beamed at him. “That’s exactly what I say,” he answered. “There’s no safety, no peace and quiet, anywhere except underground. And then, if your ideas grow bigger and you want more room—why, a bit of digging and scraping, and there you are! If you decide your house is a little too big, you block up a hole or two, and there you are again! No builders, no tradesmen, no remarks from fellows peering over your wall, and best of all, no _weather_. Look at Rat, now. A couple of feet of floodwater, and he has to move into rented rooms: uncomfortable, badly located, and horribly expensive. Or take Toad. I’ll say nothing against Toad Hall; it’s easily the best house in these parts, _as_ a house. But suppose a fire breaks out—where’s Toad? Suppose roof tiles blow off, or walls sink or crack, or windows get smashed—where’s Toad? Suppose the rooms are drafty—and I _hate_ a draft myself—where’s Toad? No, being up and out of doors is good enough for roaming around and earning your living; but a place underground to come back to at the end of it—that’s my idea of _home!_”

Mole agreed wholeheartedly, and as a result the Badger grew very fond of him. “When lunch is over,” he said, “I’ll show you all around this little place of mine. I can tell you’ll appreciate it. You understand what a home ought to be, you do.”

So after lunch, once the other two had settled into the chimney-corner and begun a heated argument about _eels_, the Badger lit a lantern and told Mole to follow him. They crossed the hall and went down one of the main tunnels. The flickering lantern light showed glimpses on either side of rooms large and small, some hardly more than cupboards, others almost as wide and grand as Toad’s dining hall. A narrow passage turned off at a right angle and led them into another corridor, where it was all the same again. Mole was stunned by the size of it, the sheer extent and branching of the place: the length of the dim passages, the solid vaulted ceilings of the crammed storerooms, the stonework everywhere, the pillars, the arches, the paved floors. “How on earth, Badger,” he said at last, “did you ever find the time and strength to do all this? It’s astonishing!”

“It _would_ be astonishing indeed,” said the Badger plainly, “if I _had_ done it. But the fact is, I did none of it. I only cleaned out the passages and rooms I had a use for. There’s a great deal more of it all around. I can see you don’t understand, so I’ll have to explain. Well, a very long time ago, on the spot where the Wild Wood stands waving now, before it had ever planted itself and grown into what it is today, there was a city—a city of people, you know. Right here, where we’re standing, they lived, and walked, and talked, and slept, and went about their business. Here they stabled their horses and held their feasts; from here they rode out to fight or drove out to trade. They were a powerful people, and rich, and great builders. They built to last, because they believed their city would last forever.”
“But what became of them all?” asked Mole.

“Who knows?” said Badger. “Folks arrive, settle for a time, thrive and build—and then they leave. That is how it goes with them. We, though, stay on. I’ve heard there were badgers living here long before that city ever existed. And now there are badgers living here again. Our kind lasts. We might go away for a spell, but we wait, we’re patient, and in the end we return. It will always be so.”
“Well, and when they finally left, those people?” said Mole.

“When they left,” the Badger went on, “the strong winds and steady rains took over the job, patiently and ceaselessly, year after year. Perhaps we badgers helped a little too, in our small way—who knows? It was all down, down, down, bit by bit—ruin and leveling and vanishing. Then it was all up, up, up, bit by bit, as seeds grew into saplings and saplings into forest trees, and bramble and fern crept in to help. Fallen leaves piled up and buried everything, and streams in their winter floods carried sand and soil to clog and cover it. In time our home was ready for us again, and we moved in. Up above us, on the surface, the same thing happened. Animals arrived, liked the look of the place, took up quarters, settled down, spread out, and flourished. They didn’t trouble themselves about the past—they never do; they’re too busy. The place was a bit lumpy and hilly, naturally, and full of holes; but that was rather an advantage. And they don’t trouble themselves about the future either—the future when perhaps the people will move in again, for a while, as may very well happen. The Wild Wood is pretty well populated by now, with all the usual crowd, good, bad, and in between—I name no names. It takes all sorts to make a world. But I think you know something about them yourself by this time.”
“I certainly do,” said Mole, with a slight shiver.

“There, there,” said Badger, giving him a pat on the shoulder, “you see, this was the first time you’d met them. They really aren’t so bad, and we all have to live and let live. Still, I’ll put the word out tomorrow, and I expect you won’t be bothered again. Any friend of _mine_ goes wherever he pleases in this country, or I’ll want to know why!”

When they got back to the kitchen, they found Rat pacing up and down, very restless. The underground air was weighing on him and fraying his nerves, and he seemed truly afraid that the river would run off if he wasn’t there to keep an eye on it. So he had his overcoat on and his pistols stuck in his belt again. “Come along, Mole,” he said anxiously as soon as he saw them. “We have to get going while it’s still daylight. I don’t want to spend another night in the Wild Wood.”
“It’ll be fine, my good fellow,” said the Otter. “I’m coming with you, and I know every path blindfolded. And if there’s a head that needs punching, you can safely count on me to punch it.”

“You really needn’t worry, Ratty,” the Badger added calmly. “My passages go farther than you think, and I have escape tunnels to the edge of the wood in several directions, though I’d rather not have everybody know about them. When you really do have to go, you’ll leave by one of my short cuts. In the meantime, relax and sit down again.”

Rat was still eager to be off and look after his river, though. So the Badger picked up his lantern again and led the way along a damp, airless tunnel that twisted and dipped, partly vaulted and partly cut through solid rock, for a weary stretch that felt like miles. At last daylight began to show dimly through tangled growth hanging over the mouth of the passage. The Badger said a hasty good-bye, pushed them quickly through the opening, made everything look as natural as possible again with creepers, brushwood, and dead leaves, and withdrew.

They found themselves standing right at the edge of the Wild Wood. Behind them were rocks and brambles and tree roots, heaped and tangled in confusion. In front lay a great stretch of quiet fields, bordered by lines of hedges black against the snow, and far ahead a glint of the familiar old river, while the wintry sun hung red and low on the horizon. The Otter, who knew all the paths, took charge of the party, and they straggled out in a straight line toward a distant stile. They paused there a moment and looked back. They saw the whole mass of the Wild Wood, dense, menacing, and compact, grimly set in the vast white landscape. Then, both at once, they turned and hurried toward home: toward firelight and the familiar things it shone on, and toward the voice of the river, sounding cheerfully outside their window, the river they knew and trusted in all its moods, which never frightened them with any surprise.

As he hurried along, eagerly looking forward to being at home again among the things he knew and liked, Mole saw clearly that he was an animal of plowed field and hedgerow, tied to the furrowed earth, the well-used pasture, the lane for evening strolls, the tended garden plot. The harshness, the stubborn endurance, and the clash of real struggle that came with Nature in the rough were for others. He must be wise and keep to the pleasant places where his lot had been cast, which held adventure enough, in their way, to last a lifetime.

chapters.title: Dulce Domum
paragraphs: The sheep ran huddling together against the fences of the pen, blowing out of their narrow nostrils and stamping with their dainty front feet, their heads thrown back, while a light steam rose from the crowded pen into the frosty air. The two animals hurried past in high spirits, chattering and laughing a great deal. They were on their way back across country after a long day out with Otter, hunting and exploring on the wide uplands where some of the streams that feed their own River first trickle out of the ground. The dusk of the short winter day was closing in around them, and they still had some way to go. They had been trudging aimlessly across the plowed fields when they heard the sheep and headed toward them. Now, leading away from the sheep-pen, they found a well-trodden track that made walking easier. It also answered that small questioning something that every animal carries inside, and which said, unmistakably, “Yes, that’s right; _this_ leads home!”

“It looks as if we’re coming to a village,” said Mole, rather doubtfully, slowing his pace. The track had in time become a path, and then a lane, and now it handed them over to the care of a proper, well-graveled road. The animals did not think much of villages, and their own highways, busy as they were, went their own independent way, paying no attention to church, post office, or pub.

“Oh, never mind!” said Rat. “At this time of year they’re all safely indoors by now, sitting around the fire: men, women, and children, dogs and cats and all. We’ll slip through without any trouble or unpleasantness, and if you like we can peek at them through their windows and see what they’re up to.”

The early nightfall of mid-December had settled over the little village by the time they approached it, treading softly on a first thin layer of powdery snow. There was little to see except squares of dusky orange-red on either side of the street, where the firelight or lamplight of each cottage spilled through the windows into the dark world outside. Most of the low, latticed windows had no blinds, and to those looking in from outside, the people within had a happy grace. They were gathered around the tea-table, busy with handiwork, or talking with laughter and gestures, and they had the very quality a skilled actor finds hardest to capture: the natural grace of people who have no idea they are being watched. Moving at will from one little theater to the next, the two onlookers, so far from home themselves, had a wistful look in their eyes as they watched a cat being stroked, a sleepy child picked up and bundled off to bed, or a tired man stretching and knocking out his pipe on the end of a smoldering log.

But it was one little window, with its blind drawn down, a plain blank glow against the night, that most strongly gave off the feeling of home, of a small curtained world inside walls, with the harsher world of outside Nature shut out and forgotten. Close against the white blind hung a bird-cage, sharply outlined, every wire, perch, and fitting distinct and recognizable, down to yesterday’s dull-edged lump of sugar. On the middle perch the fluffy occupant, his head tucked well into his feathers, looked so near that they could easily have stroked him if they had tried; even the delicate tips of his puffed-out plumage were drawn clearly on the lighted screen. As they watched, the sleepy little fellow stirred uneasily, woke, shook himself, and lifted his head. They could see the gape of his tiny beak as he yawned in a bored sort of way and looked around, and then tucked his head into his back again while the ruffled feathers slowly settled into perfect stillness. Then a gust of bitter wind caught them on the back of the neck, and a small sting of frozen sleet on their skin woke them as from a dream. They knew that their toes were cold, their legs were tired, and their own home was a weary way off.

Once past the village, where the cottages ended abruptly, they could smell the friendly fields again on either side of the road through the darkness. They braced themselves for the last long stretch, the home stretch, the stretch that we know is bound to end sometime in the rattle of the door-latch, the sudden firelight, and the sight of familiar things welcoming us like long-lost travelers from far across the sea. They plodded along steadily and silently, each thinking his own thoughts. Mole’s ran a good deal on supper, since it was pitch-dark and, as far as he knew, a strange country to him, and he was following obediently in Rat’s footsteps and leaving the guiding entirely to him. As for Rat, he was walking a little ahead, as was his habit, with his shoulders hunched and his eyes fixed on the straight gray road in front of him. So he did not notice poor Mole when the summons suddenly reached him and struck him like an electric shock.

We others, who have long since lost the subtler of the physical senses, do not even have proper words for an animal’s communication with the world around him, living or otherwise. We have only the word “smell,” for instance, to cover the whole range of delicate thrills that murmur in an animal’s nose night and day, summoning, warning, inciting, repelling. It was one of these mysterious fairy calls out of the void that suddenly reached Mole in the darkness. It made him tingle all through with its very familiar appeal, even though he could not yet clearly remember what it was. He stopped dead in his tracks, his nose searching this way and that in its effort to catch again the fine thread, the telegraph current, that had so strongly moved him. A moment later he had caught it once more, and this time recollection came with it in a full flood.

Home! So that was what it all meant: the coaxing, the soft touches drifting through the air, the invisible little hands tugging at him, every one of them in the same direction! It had to be very near him right now, the old home he had rushed away from and never looked for again, on the day he first discovered the river! And now it had sent out scouts and messengers to catch him and fetch him back. Ever since that bright morning when he got away, he had scarcely spared it a thought, he had been so wrapped up in his new life, with its pleasures and surprises and fresh, enchanting experiences. Now, as old memories came flooding in, how sharply it rose before him in the dark! Shabby, yes, and small, and sparsely furnished, but it was his, the home he had made with his own paws, the one he had been so happy to return to after a day’s work. And the home, plainly, had been happy with him too, and missed him, and wanted him back, and was telling him so through his nose, sadly and with a hint of reproach, yet without any bitterness or anger; it only wished to remind him, plaintively, that it was there, and that it wanted him.
The call was unmistakable, the summons perfectly clear. He had to answer it this very moment and go. “Ratty!” he shouted, bursting with joyful excitement. “Wait! Come back! I need you, quickly!”
“Oh, _come_ along, Mole, do!” Rat answered cheerfully, still plodding on.

“Stop, _please_, Ratty!” begged poor Mole, his heart aching. “You don’t understand! It’s home, my old home! I just caught a whiff of it, and it’s near here, truly very near. And I _must_ go there, I have to, I have to! Oh, turn around, Ratty! Please, please turn around!”

By this time Rat was very far ahead, too far to hear clearly what Mole was calling, too far to catch the sharp note of painful pleading in his voice. And he was very busy thinking about the weather, because he could smell something too, something suspiciously like approaching snow.

“We really can’t stop now, Mole!” came the answer. “We’ll come back for it tomorrow, whatever you’ve found. But I don’t dare linger now—it’s late, more snow is on the way, and I’m not certain which way to go! I need your nose, Mole, so hurry up, there’s a good fellow!” And Rat kept hurrying along without waiting to hear a reply.

Poor Mole stood alone in the road, his heart torn in two, with a big sob gathering and gathering somewhere low down inside him, ready to leap up to the surface before long in a passionate burst, he knew. But even under a test like this his loyalty to his friend stood firm. Not for a moment did he dream of abandoning him. Meanwhile, the wafts from his old home pleaded, whispered, and cast their spell, and at last claimed him commandingly. He did not dare stay any longer inside their magic circle. With a wrench that tore at his very heartstrings, he turned his face down the road and followed meekly after Rat, while faint, thin little smells, still chasing his retreating nose, scolded him for his new friendship and his heartless forgetfulness.

Making an effort, he drew level with Rat, who suspected nothing and was chatting happily about what they’d do once they got home, how cheerful a blazing log fire in the sitting room would be, and what a big supper he planned to eat. He never noticed how quiet his friend was, or how miserable he felt. But some distance later, beside a few tree stumps where a little wood ran along the edge of the road, he halted and said gently, “Listen, Mole, old chap, you look worn out. Not a word out of you, and you’re dragging your feet as if they were made of lead. Let’s sit down here and rest a minute. The snow has kept off so far, and we’ve done the hardest part of the trip.”

Mole dropped miserably onto a tree-stump and tried to hold himself together, for he could feel it coming. The sob he had fought off for so long would not be beaten. It pushed its way up and out into the air, and then came another, and another, and more of them, thick and fast, until poor Mole finally stopped struggling and wept freely, helplessly, and openly. Now he knew it was all over, and that he had lost something he could hardly say he had ever found.

Rat was astonished and dismayed by how violently Mole was overcome with grief, and for a while he did not dare say a word. At last he asked, very softly and with great sympathy, “What is it, old fellow? What on earth can be wrong? Tell us what’s troubling you, and I’ll see what I can do.”

Poor Mole could hardly manage a word, because sobs kept heaving up out of his chest, one right after another, and stopped his speech and choked it as it came. “I know it’s a—shabby, dingy little place,” he finally gasped out in pieces. “Nothing like—your snug home—or Toad’s lovely hall—or Badger’s huge house—but it was my very own little home—and I loved it—and then I went off and forgot all about it—and then suddenly I caught its scent—there on the road, when I called out and you wouldn’t listen, Rat—and it all came flooding back—and I _wanted_ it!—Oh dear, oh dear!—and when you _wouldn’t_ turn around, Ratty—and I had to walk away from it, with its smell still in my nose—I thought my heart would break.—We could have just popped over and had one look, Ratty—only one look—it was so near—but you wouldn’t turn around, Ratty, you wouldn’t turn around! Oh dear, oh dear!”
The memory brought fresh waves of sorrow, and sobs took full charge of him again, keeping him from saying any more.

Rat kept his eyes fixed on the road ahead and said nothing, merely giving Mole’s shoulder a gentle pat. Then, after a bit, he mumbled in a dark mood, “Now I understand the whole thing! What an absolute _pig_ I’ve been! A pig—that’s what I am! Nothing but a pig—a plain, ordinary pig!”

He waited until Mole’s sobs gradually became less stormy and more rhythmic; he waited until at last there were plenty of sniffs and only an occasional sob. Then he got up from his seat and, remarking casually, “Well, now we’d really better be getting on, old chap!” he set off up the road again, back over the weary way they had come.
“Where on earth are you (hic) off to (hic), Ratty?” the tearful Mole cried, looking up in alarm.
“We are going to find that home of yours, old fellow,” Rat told him cheerfully. “So you’d better come along. It’s going to take some searching, and we’ll be depending on your nose.”

“Oh, please come back, Ratty!” cried Mole, scrambling up and hurrying after him. “It’s no use, I tell you! It’s too late, and too dark, and the place is much too far, and snow is coming! And—and I never meant you to find out how I felt about it—it was all an accident and a mistake! Think of the River Bank, and your supper!”

“Bother the River Bank, and supper too!” said Rat warmly. “I tell you, I’m going to find this place tonight, even if I have to stay out all night. So cheer up, old chap, take my arm, and we’ll be back there again before you know it.”

Mole was still sniffling and pleading and holding back, but his bossy friend towed him back down the road all the same, keeping up a steady run of cheerful chatter and stories to lift his spirits and make the tiring walk feel shorter. When Rat finally guessed they were getting close to the stretch of road where Mole had been “held up,” he said, “Now, stop talking. This is business! Put that nose to work, and concentrate.”

For a short way they walked on without speaking. Then all at once Rat felt something through the arm he had hooked into Mole’s, a faint, electric sort of shiver running down his friend’s body. In an instant he let go, stepped back, and stood waiting, every sense alert.
The signals were coming through!
Mole stood rigid for a moment, while his raised nose, quivering slightly, felt the air.
Then a quick dash ahead—a slip—a pause—a doubling back; and after that a slow, steady, confident advance.

Rat, wildly excited, stuck close behind Mole, who moved like a sleepwalker as he stepped over a dry ditch, wriggled through a hedge, and followed his nose across a wide field, bare and open and without a path in the dim starlight.
All at once, with no warning at all, he dived. But Rat was on his guard and followed right after him, down into the tunnel that Mole’s faithful, unerring nose had led him to.

The air was close and stale, with a strong smell of earth, and to Rat it seemed a long time before the passage ended and he could stand up straight, stretch, and shake himself. Mole struck a match, and by its light Rat saw that they stood in an open space, neatly swept and sanded underfoot. Right in front of them was Mole’s little front door, and over the bell-pull beside it, painted in Gothic lettering, were the words “Mole End.”

Mole lifted a lantern off a hook on the wall and lit it... and when Rat looked about, he found they were standing in a kind of entrance yard. On one side of the door sat a garden bench, and on the other a roller; for Mole, being a neat animal at home, couldn’t bear to see other animals scuff up his ground into little tracks ending in piles of dirt. Wire baskets of ferns hung along the walls, taking turns with brackets that held plaster figures—Garibaldi, and the child Samuel, and Queen Victoria, and other heroes of modern Italy. Along one side of the yard stretched a skittle alley, with benches beside it and small wooden tables printed with circles that suggested where beer mugs had stood. A little round pond with goldfish in it lay in the middle, ringed by a border of cockle shells. From its center rose a fanciful tower, also decked in cockle shells, and crowned with a big silvered glass ball that showed everything all wrong, which was very pleasing to look at.

Mole’s face lit up at the sight of all these things he loved so much. He hurried Rat through the door, lit a lamp in the hall, and took one look around his old home. He saw the dust lying thick over everything, saw the bleak, empty look of a house left alone for so long, and its small, skimpy size, and its worn and shabby furnishings—and he collapsed again onto a hall chair, with his nose in his paws. “Oh, Ratty!” he cried miserably, “why on earth did I do it? Why did I bring you to this poor, cold little place, on a night like this, when by now you could have been back at the River Bank, toasting your toes in front of a blazing fire, with all your own nice things around you!”

Rat paid no attention to his gloomy self-blame. He was dashing here and there, opening doors, looking into rooms and cupboards, and lighting lamps and candles and setting them up everywhere. “What a splendid little house this is!” he called out cheerfully. “So snug! So well planned! Everything here, and everything in its place! We’ll have a jolly night of it. The first thing we need is a good fire, and I’ll take care of that—I always know where to find things. So this is the parlor? Wonderful! Was it your own idea, those little sleeping bunks in the wall? Excellent! Now, I’ll fetch the wood and the coal, and you get a duster, Mole—you’ll find one in the drawer of the kitchen table—and try to tidy things up a bit. Look lively, old fellow!”

Cheered on by his lively friend, Mole pulled himself together and dusted and polished with energy and good will, while Rat ran back and forth with armfuls of fuel and soon had a cheerful blaze roaring up the chimney. He called to Mole to come and warm himself, but Mole promptly fell into another fit of the blues, dropping onto a couch in dark despair and burying his face in his duster. “Rat,” he moaned, “what about your supper, you poor, cold, hungry, worn-out animal? I have nothing to give you—nothing—not a crumb!”

“What a fellow you are for giving up!” said Rat, reproachfully. “Why, just a minute ago I saw a sardine opener on the kitchen dresser, as plain as anything, and everybody knows that means there are sardines somewhere nearby. Get up! Pull yourself together, and come along with me to hunt for food.”

So off they went to hunt, searching through every cupboard and turning out every drawer. The result wasn’t so very discouraging after all, though of course it could have been better: a tin of sardines—a box of captain’s biscuits, nearly full—and a German sausage wrapped in silver paper.
“Now there’s a real banquet!” remarked Rat, laying out the table. “Plenty of animals I know would pay dearly for a seat at our supper tonight!”
“No bread!” groaned Mole sorrowfully. “No butter, no——”

“No _pâté de foie gras_, and no champagne either!” Rat went on with a grin. “Which reminds me—what’s that little door at the far end of the passage? Your cellar, naturally! This house has every luxury! Hang on a moment.”

He headed for the cellar door and soon came back, a little dusty, with a bottle of beer in each paw and another tucked under each arm. “You seem to be a self-indulgent rascal, Mole,” he said. “Deny yourself nothing. This is truly the jolliest little place I’ve ever been in. Now, wherever did you find those prints? They make the place feel so homey. No wonder you’re so fond of it, Mole. Tell us all about it, and how you came to make it what it is.”

Then, while Rat busied himself fetching plates, and knives and forks, and mustard that he stirred up in an egg cup, Mole—his chest still heaving from the strain of his earlier feelings—began to tell the story. He was a bit shy at first, but he grew freer as he warmed to his subject: how this had been planned, and how that had been worked out, and how this one was paid for with a windfall from an aunt, and that one was a wonderful find and a bargain, and this other thing was bought with hard-earned savings and a good deal of “going without.” His spirits were finally quite restored, and he simply had to go and pet his belongings, and take a lamp and show off their good points to his guest and go on and on about them, quite forgetting the supper they both needed so badly. Rat, who was desperately hungry but tried to hide it, nodded gravely, examined each thing with a wrinkled brow, and said “wonderful” and “most remarkable” every now and then, whenever he got a chance to put in a remark.

At long last Rat coaxed him over to the table and was just settling down to business with the sardine opener when noises floated in from the yard outside—the shuffle of tiny feet on the gravel, a jumble of small voices, and scraps of talk that reached their ears—“Right, everyone in a row—raise the lantern a little, Tommy—clear your throats first—and no coughing once I’ve counted one, two, three.—Where’s young Bill?—Come on, hurry up, we’re all waiting——”
“What’s going on?” asked Rat, pausing in his work.

“That must be the field mice,” said Mole, looking a little proud. “Every year around now they go from door to door singing carols. They’re practically a tradition around here. And they never leave me out—Mole End is their final stop—and in the old days I’d give them something hot to drink, and a bite of supper too sometimes, whenever I could afford it. It will feel like the old days to hear them again.”
“Let’s go and see them!” shouted Rat, springing to his feet and dashing for the door.

It was a pretty sight, and a fitting one for the season, that met their eyes when they flung the door open. In the front yard, lit by the dim glow of a horn lantern, eight or ten little field mice stood in a half circle, with red wool scarves around their necks, their front paws pushed deep into their pockets, and their feet jigging to keep warm. With bright, beady eyes they glanced shyly at one another, giggling a little, sniffling, and wiping their noses on their coat sleeves a good deal. As the door opened, one of the older ones, who was carrying the lantern, was just saying, “Now then, one, two, three!” and right away their shrill little voices rose on the air, singing one of the old carols that their forefathers made up in fields that lay fallow and frozen, or while snowed in beside chimney corners, and handed down to be sung in the muddy street to lamp-lit windows at Christmastime.
CAROL

People of the village, on this frosty night,
Swing your doors open, wide and bright,
Wind may follow, and snow in flight,
Yet bring us in by your fire’s warm light;
Joy shall be yours in the morning!

Here we stand in the cold and the sleet,
Blowing on fingers, stamping our feet,
Come from far away, you to greet—
You by the fire and we in the street—
Wishing you joy in the morning!

For before half the night was gone,
Suddenly a star has led us on,
Raining down blessings, one by one—
Blessings tomorrow, and more anon,
Joy for every morning!

Good Joseph trudged through the snow—
Saw the star above a stable low;
Mary could not farther go—
Welcome thatch, and straw below!
Joy was hers in the morning!

And then they heard the angels tell
“Who were the first to cry _Noel?_
Animals all, as it befell,
In the stable where they did dwell!
Joy shall be theirs in the morning!”

The voices stopped. The singers, bashful but smiling, exchanged sideways glances, and silence followed—but only for a moment. Then, from high above and far away, down the tunnel they had so recently traveled, there came to their ears, in a faint musical hum, the sound of distant bells ringing a joyful, clanging peal.
“Beautifully sung, boys!” Rat called out warmly. “Now step inside, every one of you, and get warm by the fire, and have something hot to drink!”

“Yes, come in, field mice,” cried Mole eagerly. “This is just like old times! Shut the door behind you. Pull that bench up to the fire. Now, you just wait a minute, while we—Oh, Ratty!” he cried in despair, flopping down on a seat, with tears about to fall. “What are we doing? We have nothing to give them!”
“Leave all that to me,” said the bossy Rat. “Here, you with the lantern! Step over here. I need a word with you. Tell me, are any shops open at this time of night?”
“Why, certainly, sir,” the field mouse answered respectfully. “At this time of year our shops stay open at all sorts of hours.”
“Then listen,” said Rat. “Off you go right now, you and your lantern, and fetch me——”

A long murmured discussion followed, of which Mole caught only fragments, like—“Fresh, mind you!—no, a pound of that is plenty—be sure it’s Buggins’s, I’ll accept nobody else’s—no, only the very best—if they’re out of it there, try another shop—yes, of course it has to be homemade, nothing from a tin—oh well, do what you can!” In the end coins chinked as they passed from paw to paw, the field mouse was handed a big basket to carry his purchases home in, and away he scurried with his lantern.

The rest of the field mice sat in a row on the bench, their small legs swinging, and gave themselves up to enjoying the fire, toasting their chilblains until they tingled. Meanwhile Mole, failing to draw them into easy conversation, plunged into family history and made each of them recite the names of his many brothers, who were too young, it seemed, to be allowed out caroling this year, but who hoped very soon to win their parents’ permission.

Rat, meanwhile, was busy studying the label on one of the beer bottles. “I see this is Old Burton,” he said approvingly. “_Sensible_ Mole! Just the thing! Now we’ll be able to mull some ale! Get the things ready, Mole, while I pull the corks.”

It took no time at all to mix the drink and shove the tin warmer far into the glowing center of the fire; and before long every field mouse was sipping and spluttering and choking (a little hot spiced ale goes a very long way), wiping streaming eyes, laughing, and forgetting that he had ever been cold in his life.

“These fellows put on plays too,” Mole explained to Rat. “They make them up all by themselves, and act them out afterward. And they do it very well, too! They gave us a splendid one last year, about a field mouse who was captured at sea by a Barbary pirate and made to row in a galley. When he escaped and got home again, his sweetheart had gone into a convent. Here, _you!_ You were in it, I remember. Get up and recite a bit.”

The field mouse he spoke to got up on his feet, giggled shyly, looked around the room, and stayed completely tongue-tied. His friends cheered him on, Mole coaxed and encouraged him, and Rat even went so far as to take him by the shoulders and shake him, but nothing could overcome his stage fright. They were all hard at work on him, like lifeguards applying the Royal Humane Society’s rules to someone who had been underwater a long time, when the latch clicked, the door opened, and the field mouse with the lantern came back, staggering under the weight of his basket.

Nobody mentioned acting any more once the solid, genuine contents of the basket had been spilled across the table. Rat took command, and every guest was given a job to do or an errand to run. Within minutes supper was ready. Mole, sitting down at the head of the table as if in a dream, found that the table which had been so empty a short while ago was now heaped with delicious, hearty things. He watched his small friends’ faces light up and glow as they tucked in at once; then, being truly ravenous, he gave in himself and dived into the food that had appeared so wonderfully, thinking that this was turning out to be a lovely homecoming after all. While they ate they reminisced, and the field mice brought him up to date on all the local news and answered, as best they could, the hundred questions he kept asking. Rat said hardly a word, simply watching that every guest got what he liked and more than enough of it, and that Mole had nothing to fret or fuss over.

Finally the mice trooped out, thanking him warmly and calling out their seasonal greetings, with their jacket pockets crammed with treats for the little brothers and sisters waiting at home. Once the door had shut behind the last of them and the jingle of lanterns had faded into the distance, Mole and Rat poked up the fire, pulled their chairs close, made one more nightcap of hot ale, and went over everything that had happened during that long day. At last Rat gave a huge yawn and said, “Mole, old chap, I’m ready to collapse. Tired doesn’t begin to describe it. Is that your bunk over there? All right, then, I’ll sleep in this one. What a splendid little house! It’s all so convenient!”
He climbed into his bunk and rolled himself up snugly in the blankets, and sleep gathered him up at once, the way a swath of barley is folded into the arms of the reaping machine.

Mole, worn out too, was happy to go to bed straight away, and he soon lay with his head on the pillow, feeling very glad and peaceful. Before shutting his eyes, though, he let them roam around his old room, softly lit by the firelight, which fell across familiar, friendly objects that had been part of him for ages without his ever noticing, and which now greeted him with a smile and no hard feelings. His mind was exactly where tactful Rat had been quietly steering it. He saw plainly how simple and humble—even how cramped—it all was; yet he also saw plainly how much it meant to him, and what a precious thing it is to have somewhere like that to be tied to in life. He had no wish to give up his new life with its glorious wide-open spaces, or to turn away from the sunshine and fresh air and all they gave him, and slink home to stay. The world above ground was far too powerful for that; it still called to him, even down here, and he knew he would have to go back out to the bigger stage. But it was wonderful to know that he had this to return to: a place that belonged to him alone, with belongings that were delighted to see him again and could always be trusted to give the same plain, warm welcome.

chapters.title: Mr. Toad
paragraphs: It was a bright morning in early summer. The river was back inside its usual banks and flowing at its usual pace, and a hot sun seemed to be tugging everything green and bushy and spiky up out of the ground toward it, as if on strings. Mole and Water Rat had been up since dawn, busy with all the jobs that come with boats and the start of the boating season: painting and varnishing, mending paddles, fixing cushions, searching for lost boat-hooks, and so on. They were finishing breakfast in their little parlor and eagerly talking over their plans for the day when a heavy knock came at the door.
“Bother!” said Rat, with egg all over him. “See who it is, Mole, there’s a good fellow, since you’ve finished eating.”
Mole went to answer the knock, and Rat heard him cry out in surprise. Then Mole threw the parlor door wide open and announced, with great importance, “Mr. Badger!”

This was truly remarkable, that Badger should pay a formal visit to them, or to anybody. If you wanted him badly, you generally had to catch him as he slipped quietly along a hedgerow in the early morning or the late evening, or else track him down at his own house in the middle of the Wood, which was a serious undertaking.
Badger tramped heavily into the room and stood looking at the two animals with a very grave expression. Rat let his egg-spoon drop onto the tablecloth and sat there with his mouth hanging open.
“The hour has come!” Badger said at last, with great solemnity.
“What hour?” asked Rat uneasily, glancing at the clock on the mantelpiece.

“You ought rather to ask _whose_ hour,” answered Badger. “Why, Toad’s hour! The hour of Toad! I said I would take him in hand as soon as winter was well over, and I am going to take him in hand today!”
“Toad’s hour, of course!” cried Mole with delight. “Hooray! It’s all coming back to me! _We’ll_ teach him how to be a sensible Toad!”

“This very morning,” Badger went on, settling into an armchair, “as I heard last night from a reliable source, another new and exceptionally powerful motor-car will arrive at Toad Hall, to be kept if he likes it or sent back if he doesn’t. At this very moment, perhaps, Toad is busy dressing himself in those uniquely hideous clothes he is so fond of, which turn him from a (fairly) good-looking Toad into a Thing that sends any decent-minded animal who meets it into a violent fit. We must get moving before it is too late. You two will come with me to Toad Hall at once, and the rescue will be carried out.”
“Right you are!” cried Rat, jumping up. “We’ll rescue the poor unhappy creature! We’ll convert him! By the time we’re through with him, he’ll be the most converted Toad there ever was!”

They set off up the road on their mission of mercy, with Badger in the lead. Animals who go about in company walk in a proper, sensible way, in single file, rather than sprawling across the whole road and being no use or help to each other if sudden trouble or danger comes.

They reached the carriage-drive of Toad Hall and found, just as Badger had expected, a shiny new motor-car of enormous size, painted bright red (Toad’s favorite color), standing in front of the house. As they came near the door, it was thrown open, and Mr. Toad, dressed in goggles, cap, leggings and an enormous overcoat, came swaggering down the steps, pulling on his long leather gloves.
“Well, hello! Come on, you fellows!” he called out merrily as soon as he spotted them. “You’ve arrived just in time to join me for a jolly—to go for a jolly—for a—er—jolly——”
His hearty voice faltered and died away as he saw the stern, unyielding looks on the faces of his silent friends, and his invitation was left unfinished.

Badger marched up the steps. “Take him indoors,” he told his companions sternly. Then, while Toad was shoved through the doorway, kicking and protesting, Badger turned to face the _chauffeur_ who had been left in charge of the brand-new motor-car.

“I’m afraid we won’t need you today,” he said. “Mr. Toad has changed his mind. He won’t be needing the car. Please understand that this is final. There’s no need for you to wait.” Then he followed the others inside and shut the door.
“Now then!” he said to Toad, when the four of them were standing together in the Hall. “First of all, take off those ridiculous things!”
“Shan’t!” answered Toad, with great spirit. “What is the meaning of this disgraceful outrage? I demand an explanation at once.”
“Take them off him, then, you two,” Badger ordered curtly.

They had to lay Toad out flat on the floor, kicking and shouting all sorts of names at them, before they could get properly to work. Then Rat sat on him, and Mole pulled his motoring clothes off him piece by piece, and they stood him up on his own two legs again. A good deal of his bluster seemed to have drained away along with his fine outfit. Now that he was just Toad, and no longer the Terror of the Highway, he giggled weakly and looked pleadingly from one to the other, as though he understood the situation perfectly.
“You knew it was bound to come to this sooner or later, Toad,” Badger explained severely.

Every warning we’ve given you, you’ve brushed aside. You’ve gone right on throwing away the money your father left you, and with your wild driving, your wrecks, and your arguments with the police, you’re dragging the good name of us animals through the mud around here. Being independent is fine, but we animals don’t stand by while a friend makes a fool of himself past a certain limit, and you’ve hit that limit. Now, in plenty of ways you’re a decent fellow, and I’d rather not be too hard on you. So I’ll try one last time to knock some sense into you. You’re coming with me to the smoking room, where you’re going to hear a few truths about yourself, and then we’ll find out whether the Toad who walks out of there is the same Toad who walked in.”
He gripped Toad firmly by the arm, marched him into the smoking-room, and pulled the door shut behind the two of them.
“_That’s_ no use!” said Rat scornfully. “_Talking_ to Toad will never cure him. He’ll _say_ anything.”

They settled into armchairs and waited patiently. Through the closed door they could just make out the long, steady drone of Badger’s voice, rising and falling in waves of speechmaking. After a while they noticed that the sermon was being interrupted every so often by long, drawn-out sobs, plainly coming from Toad’s chest. Toad was a soft-hearted, affectionate fellow, and very easily converted to any point of view—for the time being.

After about three-quarters of an hour the door opened, and Badger came back out, solemnly leading by the paw a very limp and dejected Toad. His skin hung loosely on him, his legs wobbled, and his cheeks were streaked with the tears that Badger’s moving speech had brought out so abundantly.

“Take a seat there, Toad,” said Badger in a kind voice, pointing at a chair. “My friends,” he continued, “it gives me great pleasure to announce that Toad has finally realized how wrong he has been. He feels genuine regret for the foolish way he used to behave, and he has agreed to swear off motor-cars altogether, once and for all. He has given me his solemn word on it.”
“That is very good news,” said Mole gravely.
“Very good news indeed,” remarked Rat doubtfully, “if only—_if_ only——”
As he said this, he was staring hard at Toad, and he couldn’t shake the idea that he could make out something like the faint glint of a twinkle in the animal’s eye, sad as it still was.

“There’s just one more thing to be done,” continued Badger, well pleased. “Toad, I want you to repeat solemnly, in front of your friends here, what you freely admitted to me in the smoking-room just now. First, you are sorry for what you’ve done, and you see how foolish it all was?”
A long, long silence followed. Toad glanced desperately in every direction while the other animals waited, grim and quiet. Finally he answered.
“No!” he answered, rather sulkily but firmly. “I am _not_ sorry. And it wasn’t madness in the least! It was absolutely glorious!”
“What?” cried Badger, thoroughly appalled. “You backsliding wretch, didn’t you just say, in there——”

“Oh yes, yes, in _there_,” Toad broke in, impatient. “In _there_ I’d have said anything. You’re so eloquent, dear Badger, so touching, so persuasive, and you argue every point so awfully well—in _there_ you can twist me around your finger, and you know you can. But since then I’ve been thinking it over, turning it all around in my head, and the truth is that I’m not one bit sorry or repentant, so there’s no earthly use pretending I am. Well, is there?”
“Then you won’t promise,” said Badger, “never to touch a motor-car again?”
“Certainly not!” Toad declared. “Quite the opposite! I give you my faithful promise that the moment I lay eyes on a motor-car, poop-poop! away I go in it!”
“Told you so, didn’t I?” Rat remarked to Mole.

“All right, then,” said Badger firmly, getting to his feet. “You refuse to be talked around, so we’ll see what force can accomplish. I was afraid it would come to this from the start. You’re always inviting the three of us to stay in this grand house of yours, Toad, and now we’re taking you up on it. We’ll leave once we’ve brought you around to a sensible way of thinking, and not one minute sooner. You two, march him upstairs and lock him in his bedroom while the rest of us work out a plan.”

“It’s for your own good, Toady, really it is,” said Rat kindly, while Toad kicked and struggled all the way up the stairs in the grip of his two loyal friends. “Just think of the fun we’ll have together, the way we used to, once you’re completely over this—this wretched fit of yours!”
“We’ll take great care of everything for you until you’re well, Toad,” said Mole, “and we’ll make sure your money isn’t wasted the way it has been.”
“No more unfortunate scrapes with the police, Toad,” said Rat, as they pushed him into his bedroom.
“And no more weeks in the hospital, Toad, being bossed around by lady nurses,” Mole added, turning the key in the lock.
They went back down the stairs, with Toad shouting abuse at them through the keyhole, and then the three friends met to discuss the situation.

“It’s going to be a tiresome business,” said Badger with a sigh. “I’ve never seen Toad so determined. However, we will see it through. He must never be left unguarded for a single moment. We shall have to take turns being with him, until the poison has worked its way out of his system.”

They arranged shifts accordingly. Each animal took a turn sleeping in Toad’s room at night, and they split the day up among them. At first Toad was certainly very trying for his careful guardians. When his violent fits came over him, he would line up bedroom chairs in a rough imitation of a motor-car and crouch on the front one, bent forward and staring fixedly ahead, making strange and ghastly noises, until he reached the climax, when he would turn a complete somersault and lie flat amid the wreckage of the chairs, apparently quite satisfied for the moment. As time went on, however, these painful seizures grew gradually less frequent, and his friends tried to steer his mind into fresh channels. But his interest in other things didn’t seem to return, and he grew visibly listless and gloomy.

One fine morning it was Rat’s turn on guard, and he climbed the stairs to take over from Badger. He found Badger itching to get away and stretch his legs on a long tramp through his woods and along his own tunnels and burrows. “Toad’s still in bed,” Badger told him outside the door. “I can’t get anything out of him but, ‘Oh, leave me alone, I need nothing, maybe I’ll feel better soon, it may pass with time, please don’t worry,’ and so forth. Now mind yourself, Rat! When Toad is quiet and meek and acting like the hero of some Sunday-school storybook, that’s when he’s at his craftiest. He’s certainly up to something. I know him. Well, I really must go.”
“How are you today, old chap?” asked Rat cheerfully, as he came up to Toad’s bedside.

He had to wait several minutes before anything came back. Finally a weak voice answered, “Thank you ever so much, dear Ratty! How kind of you to ask! But first tell me how you are yourself, and how is the excellent Mole?”

“Oh, _we’ll_ be fine,” Rat answered. “Mole,” he added, without thinking, “is going for a jaunt with Badger. They won’t be back before lunch, so you and I can have a nice morning together, and I’ll do my best to entertain you. Come on now, up you get, there’s a good chap, and stop lying there sulking on such a lovely morning!”

“Dear, kind Rat,” Toad whispered, “you have no idea what state I’m in, or how far I am from ‘getting up’ at the moment—if I ever shall! But please don’t worry over me. I can’t bear being a burden to my friends, and I don’t expect to be one for much longer. In fact, I rather hope not.”

“Well, I hope not, too,” said Rat warmly. “You’ve caused us a dreadful amount of bother all this while, and I’m glad to hear that it’s going to end. And with weather like this, and the boating season only just starting! It’s really too bad of you, Toad! We don’t mind the trouble itself, but you’re making us miss so much.”

“I’m afraid it _is_ the bother that you mind, after all,” Toad replied in a feeble drawl. “I understand perfectly. It’s only natural. You’re worn out with fussing over me. I shouldn’t ask anything more of you. I know I’m a burden.”
“You certainly are,” said Rat. “But believe me, I’d put myself out for you in any way at all, if only you’d start behaving like a sensible animal.”

“If I could believe that, Ratty,” Toad whispered, weaker than ever, “then I would ask you—for the last time, very likely—to hurry round to the village as fast as you can—even now it may be too late—and bring the doctor. But never mind. It’s only a bother, and perhaps we should simply let things run their course.”
“Why on earth do you want a doctor?” asked Rat, stepping closer to look him over. Toad certainly lay very flat and still, and his voice was weaker, and he seemed a completely different animal.

“Surely you must have seen, lately——” Toad whispered. “But no—why should you? Noticing things is only a bother. Tomorrow, of course, you may find yourself thinking, ‘Oh, if only I had noticed sooner! If only I had done something!’ But no, it’s a bother. Never mind—forget I said anything.”

“Now look here, old man,” said Rat, starting to feel quite alarmed, “naturally I’ll bring you a doctor, if you truly believe you need one. But surely you can’t be as ill as all that yet. Let’s talk about something else.”

“I’m afraid, dear friend,” said Toad with a sorrowful smile, “that ‘talking’ will do very little in a case like this—and neither will doctors, for that matter. Still, a drowning animal clutches at any straw. And by the way—since you’re going anyway—I _hate_ to put you to more trouble, but I just remembered that you’ll walk right past the lawyer’s door—would you mind asking him to come up as well? It would be a comfort to me. There are times—perhaps I should say there is _a_ time—when a person must face unpleasant duties, no matter what it costs his worn-out constitution!”
“A lawyer! Oh, he must be truly ill!” the terrified Rat said to himself as he hurried out of the room, though he remembered to lock the door carefully behind him.
Out in the passage he stopped to think. The other two were miles away, and there was nobody he could ask.

“Better safe than sorry,” he decided after a moment. “I’ve seen Toad imagine himself dreadfully ill before, for no reason at all, but never once have I heard him ask for a lawyer! If nothing is really wrong, the doctor will tell him he’s a silly old fool and cheer him up, and that’s something gained. I’d best humor him and go. It won’t take long.” And off he ran to the village on his errand of mercy.

Toad had hopped lightly out of bed the moment he heard the key turn in the lock, and he watched Rat eagerly from the window until Rat disappeared down the carriage drive. Then, laughing heartily, he dressed as fast as he could in the smartest suit that came to hand, stuffed his pockets with money from a small drawer in the dressing table, and knotted the sheets from his bed into a makeshift rope. He tied one end around the middle post of the handsome Tudor window that was such a fine feature of his bedroom, scrambled out, slid easily to the ground, and set off in the opposite direction from Rat, marching along light-heartedly and whistling a cheerful tune.

It was a gloomy lunch for Rat when Badger and Mole finally came back, and he had to face them across the table with his pitiful, unconvincing story. You can imagine Badger’s sharp, even brutal, remarks, so we will skip them. But it hurt Rat that even Mole, though he took his friend’s side as far as he could, couldn’t help saying, “You’ve been a bit of a fool this time, Ratty! And Toad, of all animals!”
“He played his part awfully well,” said Rat, looking crushed.

“He played _you_ awfully well!” Badger shot back angrily. “Still, talking won’t fix anything. He’s gotten clean away for now, that much is certain. And the worst of it is, he’ll be so full of himself over what he thinks was his cleverness that he may do any sort of foolish thing. One comfort is that we’re free now, and don’t have to waste any more of our precious time standing guard. But we’d better keep sleeping at Toad Hall for a while longer. Toad may be brought back at any moment, on a stretcher or between two policemen.”

So Badger spoke, with no idea of what the future had in store, nor how much water, and how muddy and murky, would flow under the bridges before Toad would sit comfortably again in the Hall of his ancestors.

Meanwhile Toad, cheerful and carefree, was striding briskly along the high road, some miles from home. At first he had taken back paths, crossed many fields, and changed direction several times in case anyone was chasing him. But by now he felt safe from capture, the sun was smiling brightly down on him, and all of Nature seemed to join in a chorus of approval for the song of self-praise his own heart was singing, so he almost danced along the road in his satisfaction and conceit.

“That was a smart piece of work!” he said to himself, chuckling. “Brains against brute force, and brains came out on top, as they always do. Poor old Ratty! My, won’t he catch it when Badger gets back! A decent fellow, Ratty, with many good qualities, but very little intelligence and absolutely no education. I must take him in hand some day and see if I can make something of him.”

Stuffed full of conceited thoughts like these, he strode along with his head in the air until he reached a little town. There the sign of “The Red Lion,” swinging out over the road halfway down the main street, reminded him that he hadn’t had breakfast that day and was extremely hungry after his long walk. He marched into the inn, ordered the best lunch that could be got on such short notice, and sat down to eat it in the coffee room.

He was about halfway through his meal when a sound he knew only too well, coming down the street, made him jump and start trembling all over. The poop-poop! came closer and closer, the car could be heard turning into the inn yard and stopping, and Toad had to grab the leg of the table to hide his overwhelming emotion. Soon the party came into the coffee room, hungry, chatty and cheerful, going on and on about their morning’s adventures and the fine qualities of the machine that had carried them along so well. Toad listened eagerly, all ears, for a while, but at last he couldn’t bear it any longer. He slipped quietly out of the room, paid his bill at the bar, and as soon as he was outside strolled casually around to the inn yard. “There can’t be any harm,” he told himself, “in just _looking_ at it!”

The car stood in the middle of the yard with nobody watching it, since the stable hands and the other loungers were all at their dinner. Toad walked slowly around it, inspecting it, criticizing it, lost in deep thought.
“I wonder,” he said to himself after a while, “I wonder whether this kind of car _starts_ easily?”

The next moment, hardly knowing how it happened, he found he had hold of the crank handle and was turning it. As the familiar sound burst out, the old passion seized Toad and mastered him completely, body and soul. As if in a dream he found himself somehow sitting in the driver’s seat; as if in a dream he pulled the lever and swung the car around the yard and out through the archway; and, as if in a dream, every sense of right and wrong, every fear of the obvious consequences, seemed to be suspended for the time being. He picked up speed, and as the car gobbled up the street and leapt out onto the high road through the open countryside, he was aware of only one thing: that he was Toad once more, Toad at his best and highest, Toad the terror, the scatterer of traffic, the Lord of the lonely road, before whom everyone must give way or be struck into nothingness and everlasting night. He sang as he flew, and the car answered with a deep, humming drone; the miles were swallowed up beneath him as he raced he didn’t know where, following his instincts, living his hour, reckless of whatever might happen to him.

“It seems to me,” remarked the Chairman of the Bench of Magistrates cheerfully, “that the _only_ difficulty in this otherwise very clear case is how on earth we can make things hot enough for the incorrigible rogue and hardened ruffian we see cowering in the dock before us. Let me see: he has been found guilty, on the clearest evidence, first, of stealing a valuable motorcar; second, of driving in a way that endangered the public; and third, of gross impertinence to the country police. Mr. Clerk, would you please tell us the very stiffest penalty we can impose for each of these offenses? Without, of course, giving the prisoner the benefit of any doubt, because there isn’t any.”

The Clerk scratched his nose with his pen. “Some people would argue,” he remarked, “that stealing the motor-car was the gravest crime, and so it is. But insulting the police surely deserves the heaviest sentence, and so it should. Suppose you said twelve months for the theft, which is gentle; three years for the reckless driving, which is merciful; and fifteen years for the insolence, and from what we heard in the witness-box it was a rather nasty piece of insolence, even if you believe only a tenth of what was said, and I never believe more than that myself—then if I’ve added correctly, the total comes to nineteen years——”
“Excellent!” said the Chairman.
“—So you might as well round it up to a neat twenty years and be on the safe side,” the Clerk finished.

“A capital suggestion!” said the Chairman, nodding his approval. “Prisoner! Collect yourself and stand up straight. This time it will be twenty years. And take warning: if you ever come before us again, on any charge at all, we shall treat you very severely indeed!”

Then the brutal henchmen of the law fell upon the luckless Toad, loaded him with chains, and dragged him from the courthouse, shrieking, begging and protesting. They hauled him across the marketplace, where the playful crowd, always as hard on a caught criminal as they are sympathetic and helpful when someone is merely “wanted,” pelted him with jeers, carrots and popular catchphrases; past hooting schoolchildren, their innocent faces lit up with the delight they always take in the sight of a gentleman in trouble; across the hollow-sounding drawbridge, beneath the spiked portcullis, and under the frowning archway of the grim old castle, whose ancient towers soared high overhead; past guardrooms full of grinning off-duty soldiers, and past sentries who coughed in a horrid, sarcastic way, because that is as much as a sentry on duty dares to do to show his contempt and loathing of crime; up worn, winding stairs, past men-at-arms in steel helmets and breastplates, darting threatening looks through their visors; across courtyards where mastiffs strained at their leashes and pawed the air to get at him; past aged guards, their halberds propped against the wall, dozing over a meat pie and a flagon of brown ale; on and on, past the rack chamber and the thumbscrew room, past the turning that led to the private scaffold, until they reached the door of the grimmest dungeon, deep in the heart of the innermost keep. There at last they stopped, where an ancient jailer sat fingering a bunch of enormous keys.

“Zounds!” said the police sergeant, taking off his helmet and wiping his forehead. “Wake up, thou old fool, and take from us this vile Toad, a criminal of deepest guilt and matchless cunning and resourcefulness. Watch and guard him with all thy skill; and mark thee well, graybeard, should anything go amiss, thy old head shall answer for his—and a plague on the pair of them!”

The jailer gave a grim nod and rested his shriveled hand on the shoulder of the wretched Toad. The rusty key groaned in the lock and the huge door slammed shut behind them. And Toad was a helpless prisoner, shut away in the deepest dungeon of the most closely guarded tower of the sturdiest castle in the whole length and breadth of Merry England.

chapters.title: The Piper at the Gates of Dawn
paragraphs: The Willow-Wren was twittering his thin little song, tucked out of sight in the dark fringe of the river bank. It was past ten o’clock at night, yet the sky still held on to a few trailing scraps of light from the day that had gone, and the heavy, sulky heat of the scorching afternoon was breaking up and rolling away under the cool touch of the short midsummer night. Mole lay stretched out on the bank, still panting from the strain of a fierce day that had been cloudless from dawn until late sunset, and waited for his friend to come home. He had spent the day on the river with some other companions, which left the Water Rat free to keep a long-standing appointment with Otter. Then he had returned to find the house dark and empty, with no sign of Rat, who was surely staying out late with his old comrade. It was still far too hot to think of going indoors, so he lay on some cool dock leaves and went over the day and everything that had happened in it, and how very good it had all been.

Before long the Rat’s light footsteps could be heard coming over the dry, scorched grass. “Oh, the blessed coolness!” he said, and sat down, gazing thoughtfully into the river, quiet and lost in thought.
“You stayed for supper, of course?” Mole asked after a while.

“I simply had to,” said the Rat. “They wouldn’t hear of my leaving any earlier. You know how kind they always are. They did everything they could to make it cheerful for me, right up to the moment I left. But I felt like a brute the whole time, because I could see they were very unhappy, though they tried to hide it. Mole, I’m afraid they’re in trouble. Little Portly is missing again, and you know how much his father thinks of him, even though he never says much about it.”

“What, that youngster?” said Mole lightly. “Well, so he is. Why worry about it? He’s always wandering off and getting lost and then turning up again, he’s such an adventurous little fellow. But nothing bad ever happens to him. Everyone around here knows him and likes him, just as they like old Otter, and you can be sure some animal or other will come across him and bring him home safe and sound. Why, we’ve found him ourselves, miles from home, perfectly calm and cheerful!”

“Yes, but this time it’s more serious,” said the Rat gravely. “He’s been missing for several days now, and the Otters have searched everywhere, high and low, without finding the slightest trace. They’ve asked every animal for miles around, too, and nobody knows anything about him. Otter is plainly more worried than he’ll admit. I got it out of him that young Portly hasn’t learned to swim very well yet, and I could tell he’s thinking about the weir. There’s still a lot of water coming down, for this time of year, and the child has always been drawn to that place. And then there are—well, traps and such things—_you_ know. Otter is not the sort to fret about a son of his before there’s real cause. And now he _is_ fretting. When I left, he came out with me. He said he wanted some air and talked about stretching his legs. But I could see that wasn’t it, so I coaxed him along and quizzed him, and finally got the whole story out of him. He’s going to spend the night keeping watch at the ford. You know the spot where the old ford used to be, in the days gone by before they built the bridge?”
“I know it well,” said Mole. “But why would Otter choose to keep watch there?”

“Well, it seems that’s where he gave Portly his very first swimming lesson,” Rat went on. “Off that shallow, gravelly spit by the bank. It’s also where he taught him to fish, and where young Portly landed his first catch and was so tremendously proud of it. The little fellow adored the spot. Otter reckons that if the child comes wandering back from wherever he’s got to—if he _is_ anywhere by now, poor little chap—he might head for the ford he loved so much. Or if he stumbled onto it, he’d know it at once and linger there and play, maybe. So every night Otter goes and keeps watch—on the chance, you understand, only on the chance!”
For a while they were both silent, thinking of the same thing: the lonely, heartsick animal crouched by the ford, watching and waiting all through the long night—on the chance.
“Well, well,” said the Rat after a bit, “I suppose we ought to think about going to bed.” But he made no move to get up.

“Rat,” said Mole, “I simply can’t go home and settle in and fall asleep and _do_ nothing, even if there’s really nothing to be done. Let’s take out the boat and paddle upstream. The moon will rise in an hour or so, and then we’ll search as best we can. Anything is better than climbing into bed and doing _nothing_.”
“That’s just what I was thinking,” said the Rat. “It’s not a night for sleeping anyway, and daybreak isn’t so very far off. Then we may pick up some news of him from the early risers as we go along.”

They brought the boat out, and the Rat took the oars, paddling carefully. In midstream there was a clear, narrow path that faintly mirrored the sky, but wherever shadows from a bank, a bush or a tree fell across the water they looked as solid as the banks themselves, so Mole had to steer with care. Dark and deserted as it seemed, the night was full of small sounds, songs and chatter and rustling, which told of the busy little population who were up and about, going on with their trades and callings all night long, until the sunshine finally fell on them and sent them off to their well-earned rest. The water’s own noises were clearer than by day, too, its gurgles and “cloops” more startling and closer at hand, and again and again they jumped at what sounded like a sudden clear call from a real, speaking voice.

The line of the horizon stood clear and hard against the sky, and in one particular spot it showed black against a silvery glow that kept climbing and growing. At last the moon rose with slow majesty over the rim of the waiting earth, until it swung clear of the horizon and sailed off, free of its moorings. Once more they could see surfaces: wide meadows, quiet gardens, and the river itself from bank to bank, all softly revealed, all washed clean of mystery and terror, all shining again as they did by day, but with a difference that was enormous. Their old haunts greeted them again in different clothes, as if they had slipped away and put on this pure new outfit and come quietly back, smiling and shyly waiting to see whether they would still be recognized in it.

They tied their boat to a willow and stepped ashore into this silent, silver kingdom, where they patiently searched the hedges, the hollow trees, the little channels and their culverts, the ditches and the dry watercourses. Then they got into the boat again, crossed over, and worked their way up the stream in the same fashion. All the while the moon, calm and remote in a cloudless sky, did what she could to help them in their search, far away as she was, until her hour came and she sank reluctantly toward the earth and left them, and mystery once again held the fields and the river.

Then a change slowly began to show itself. The horizon grew clearer, and fields and trees came more into view, and somehow with a different look about them; the mystery began to fall away. A bird piped suddenly and then went quiet, and a light breeze sprang up and set the reeds and bulrushes rustling. Rat, who sat in the stern of the boat while Mole rowed, suddenly sat upright and listened with fierce attention. Mole, who was using gentle strokes just to keep the boat moving while he looked carefully along the banks, glanced at him with curiosity.

“It’s gone!” sighed Rat, sagging back onto his seat. “So lovely, and so strange, and so new. If it was going to end so soon, I almost wish I’d never heard it. It has stirred up a longing in me that hurts, and nothing seems worth doing except to hear that sound again and keep listening forever. No! There it is again!” he cried, suddenly alert.
