Then he fell silent for a long while, spellbound and entranced.

“Now it’s drifting away and I’m starting to lose it,” he said after a while. “Oh, Mole! The beauty of it! The merry bubbling and joy, the thin, clear, happy call of that faraway piping! I never dreamed of such music, and the call inside it is even stronger than the music is sweet! Row on, Mole, row! That music and that call must be meant for us.”
Mole, greatly puzzled, obeyed. “I don’t hear anything myself,” he said, “only the wind playing in the reeds and rushes and willow shoots.”

The Rat gave no answer, if he even heard. Rapt, carried away and trembling, he was possessed in every sense by this new, divine thing that had caught up his helpless soul and swung and dandled it, like a powerless but happy baby in a strong, steady grip.

Mole rowed steadily on in silence, and soon they came to a place where the river divided, with a long backwater branching off to one side. With a slight movement of his head, Rat, who had long since dropped the rudder lines, told the rower to take the backwater. The creeping tide of light kept gaining ground, and now they could see the colors of the flowers that studded the water’s edge.
“Clearer, and closer still,” cried the Rat happily. “Surely you can hear it now! Ah—at last—I can tell that you do!”

Breathless and spellbound, Mole stopped rowing as the flowing ripple of that glad piping broke over him like a wave, swept him up, and took complete hold of him. He saw the tears on his friend’s cheeks, and bowed his head, and understood. For a little while they hung there, brushed by the purple loosestrife that fringed the bank. Then the clear, commanding summons that went hand in hand with the intoxicating melody imposed its will on Mole, and mechanically he bent to his oars again. The light grew steadily stronger, yet no birds sang as they usually did at the approach of dawn, and except for the heavenly music everything was wonderfully still.

On either side of them as they glided on, the rich meadow grass seemed that morning fresher and greener than anything could be. Never had they noticed the roses so vivid, the willow-herb so riotous, the meadowsweet so fragrant and all-pervading. Then the murmur of the approaching weir began to fill the air, and they became aware that they were nearing the end, whatever it might be, that surely awaited their expedition.

The great weir was a wide half-circle of foam and glinting lights and shining shoulders of green water. It closed off the backwater from bank to bank, stirred the whole calm surface into twirling eddies and floating streaks of foam, and drowned out every other sound with its solemn, soothing rumble. In the very middle of the stream, held in the shimmering sweep of the weir’s outstretched arms, a small island lay anchored, edged thickly with willow and silver birch and alder. Reserved and shy, but full of meaning, it hid whatever it held behind a veil, keeping it until the hour should come, and with the hour, those who were called and chosen.

Slowly, but with no doubt or hesitation at all, and with a kind of solemn expectancy, the two animals passed through the broken, tumbling water and tied up their boat at the flowery edge of the island. In silence they stepped ashore and pushed through the blossoms and the scented plants and undergrowth that led up to level ground, until they stood on a little lawn of marvelous green, ringed round with Nature’s own orchard trees—crab apple, wild cherry and sloe.

“This is the spot from my song-dream, the very place the music was playing me toward,” the Rat whispered, as though in a trance. “If we’re going to find Him anywhere, surely it’s here, in this holy place!”

Then all at once Mole felt a great Awe come down over him, an awe that turned his muscles to water, bent his head low, and rooted his feet to the ground. It wasn’t panic or terror—in fact he felt wonderfully peaceful and happy—but the awe struck him and gripped him, and without seeing anything he knew it could only mean that some mighty Presence was very, very close. With an effort he turned to look for his friend, and saw him beside him, cowering, stricken, and shaking all over. And still the crowded, bird-filled branches around them were wholly silent, and still the light grew and grew.

Perhaps he would never have dared to lift his eyes, except that although the piping had now hushed, the call and the summons still seemed to rule him and command him. He could not refuse, even if Death himself were waiting to strike him down the instant he had looked with mortal eyes on things that are rightly kept hidden. Trembling, he obeyed, and raised his humble head. Then, in the perfect clearness of the coming dawn, while Nature, flushed with an amazing fullness of color, seemed to hold her breath for what would happen, he looked straight into the eyes of the Friend and Helper. He saw the backward sweep of the curved horns, gleaming in the growing daylight. He saw the stern, hooked nose between the kindly eyes that were looking down on them with good humor, while the bearded mouth broke into a half-smile at the corners. He saw the rippling muscles of the arm that lay across the broad chest, and the long, supple hand still holding the pan-pipes that had only just fallen away from the parted lips. He saw the splendid curves of the shaggy limbs, laid out in majestic ease on the grass. And last of all he saw, nestled between the very hooves, sleeping soundly in complete peace and contentment, the little, round, plump, childlike shape of the baby otter. All this he saw, for one moment, breathless and intense, vivid against the morning sky; and still, as he looked, he lived; and still, as he lived, he wondered.
“Rat!” he managed to whisper, shaking. “Are you afraid?”
“Afraid?” Rat murmured, his eyes shining with a love beyond words. “Afraid! Of _Him?_ Oh, never, never! And yet—and yet—oh, Mole, I am afraid!”
Then the two animals, crouching low to the ground, bowed their heads and worshiped.

Suddenly and magnificently, the sun’s broad golden disc showed itself over the horizon in front of them, and the first rays, shooting across the flat water-meadows, struck the animals full in the eyes and dazzled them. When they could look again, the Vision had vanished, and the air was full of the song of birds welcoming the dawn.

They stared blankly, in a dumb misery that deepened as they slowly understood all they had seen and all they had lost. Then a playful little breeze came dancing up from the surface of the water, tossed the aspens, shook the dewy roses, and blew lightly and lovingly in their faces; and with its soft touch came instant forgetting. For this is the last and best gift that the kindly demigod takes care to give to those whom he has shown himself to while helping them: the gift of forgetfulness. It is given so that the awful memory will not stay and grow, and overshadow fun and pleasure, and so that the great haunting memory will not spoil all the later lives of little animals who have been helped out of trouble, so that they may be happy and lighthearted as before.
Mole rubbed his eyes and stared at Rat, who was glancing around in a bewildered way. “Sorry, what was that, Rat?” he asked.

“I think all I said,” Rat answered slowly, “was that this looked like the right sort of place, and that if we were going to find him anywhere, it would be here. And look! Why, there he is, the little fellow!” And with a shout of delight he ran toward the sleeping Portly.

But Mole stood still for a moment, lost in thought. He was like someone suddenly woken from a beautiful dream, who struggles to remember it and can catch hold of nothing but a faint sense of how lovely it was—the loveliness of it!—until even that fades in its turn, and the dreamer bitterly accepts the hard, cold waking and everything that comes with it. So Mole, after wrestling with his memory for a short while, shook his head sadly and followed the Rat.

Portly woke with a joyful squeak and wriggled with delight at the sight of his father’s friends, who had played with him so often in days gone by. In a moment, though, his face went blank, and he started searching around in a circle, whining and pleading. He was like a child who has fallen happily asleep in its nurse’s arms and wakes to find itself alone, laid down in a strange place, and who looks in corners and cupboards and runs from room to room, with despair growing silently in its heart. Just so, Portly searched the island, and searched again, stubborn and tireless, until at last the black moment came when he had to give up, sit down, and cry bitterly.
Mole ran quickly to comfort the little animal, but Rat lingered behind, looking long and doubtfully at some hoof-marks pressed deep into the grass.
“Some—great—animal—has been here,” he murmured, slow and thoughtful, and he stood there pondering and pondering, his mind oddly stirred.
“Hurry up, Rat!” Mole called. “Remember poor Otter, waiting up there at the ford!”

Portly was soon comforted by the promise of a treat—a ride on the river in Mr. Rat’s real boat. The two animals led him down to the water’s edge, settled him safely between them in the bottom of the boat, and paddled off down the backwater. The sun was fully up by now and hot on them, the birds sang loudly and freely, and the flowers smiled and nodded from both banks. But somehow—or so the animals thought—the flowers had less richness and blaze of color than they seemed to remember seeing quite recently somewhere—they wondered where.

Once they were back on the main river, they turned the boat’s head upstream toward the spot where they knew their friend was keeping his lonely watch. As they drew near the familiar ford, Mole steered the boat in to the bank. They lifted Portly out and set him on his feet on the towpath, gave him his marching orders and a friendly farewell pat on the back, and pushed off into the middle of the stream. They watched the little animal waddle along the path, contented and full of importance. They watched him until they saw his muzzle suddenly lift and his waddle break into a clumsy trot as he hurried along, with shrill whines and wriggles of recognition. Looking up the river, they could see Otter spring up, tense and rigid, from the shallows where he had crouched in silent patience, and they could hear his astonished, joyful bark as he bounded up through the willow bushes onto the path. Then Mole, with a strong pull on one oar, swung the boat around and let the full stream carry them down again wherever it liked, their quest now happily ended.

“I’m oddly exhausted, Rat,” said Mole, drooping over his oars as the boat floated along. “You’ll say it’s from being up all night, but that’s nothing. This time of year we do the same on half the nights of the week. No, it feels as if I’d lived through something thrilling and rather frightening, and it had just finished, and still nothing in particular has taken place.”

“Or something very amazing and glorious and beautiful,” Rat murmured, leaning back and shutting his eyes. “I feel just the way you do, Mole, simply dead tired, though not in my body. How lucky that the current is carrying us home. Isn’t it lovely to feel the sun again, soaking right into your bones! And listen to the wind playing among the reeds!”
“It’s like music—far-off music,” said Mole, nodding drowsily.

“That’s what I was thinking,” murmured Rat, dreamy and languid. “Dance music—the lilting kind that runs on without a stop—but with words in it, too—it slips into words and out of them again—I catch them now and then—then it is dance music once more, and then nothing but the soft, thin whispering of the reeds.”
“You hear better than I do,” said Mole sadly. “I can’t catch the words.”

“Let me try to hand them over to you,” Rat said softly, eyes still closed. “Now it’s turning back into words—faint, but clear—_So awe will not stay—To spoil your play with fret—You’ll see me appear when help is near—But then you will forget!_ Now the reeds take up the tune—_forget, forget_, they sigh, and it dies off in a rustle and a whisper. Then the voice comes round again—

“_So limbs won’t be bloodied and torn—I spring the trap that is set—When I free the snare you may glimpse me there—For surely you will forget!_ Row in closer, Mole, closer to the reeds! It’s hard to catch, and with every minute it fades a bit more.

“_Helper and healer, I cheer—Small waifs in the woodland wet—Strays I find in it, wounds I bind in it—Bidding them all forget!_ Closer, Mole, closer! No, it’s no use; the song has faded into the talk of the reeds.”
“But what do the words mean?” asked Mole, wondering.

“That I don’t know,” Rat said simply. “I handed them on to you just as they came to me. Ah! Now they’re coming back, and this time full and clear! At last this time it’s the real thing, the unmistakable thing, simple—passionate—perfect——”
“Well, go on, then, let’s hear it,” said Mole, once he had waited patiently a few minutes, half dozing in the hot sun.

But there was no reply. Mole glanced over and understood why. A smile of great happiness rested on his face, with a trace of that listening look still hanging about it, and the tired Rat was sound asleep.

chapters.title: Toad’s Adventures
paragraphs: When Toad found himself shut up in a damp and stinking dungeon, with all the grim darkness of a medieval fortress between him and the sunny world of fine, well-paved roads where he had been so happy only a short while before, strutting about as if he had bought up every road in England, he threw himself flat on the floor, wept bitter tears, and gave himself up to black despair. “This is the end of everything” (he said), “or at least the end of the career of Toad, which is the same thing; the popular and handsome Toad, the rich and hospitable Toad, the Toad so free and careless and dashing! How can I hope ever to be set free again” (he said), “when I have been so justly locked up for stealing such a handsome motor-car in such a bold way, and for such outrageous and inventive cheek, handed out to so many fat, red-faced policemen!” (Here his sobs choked him.) “Stupid animal that I was” (he said), “now I must waste away in this dungeon, until the people who used to be proud to say they knew me have forgotten the very name of Toad! O wise old Badger!” (he said), “O clever, intelligent Rat and sensible Mole! What sound judgment, what a knowledge of people and affairs you have! O unhappy and abandoned Toad!” With lamentations like these he spent his days and nights for several weeks, refusing his meals and any snacks in between, though the grim old jailer, knowing that Toad’s pockets were well stuffed, kept pointing out that many comforts, and even luxuries, could be sent in from outside by arrangement—for a price.

Now the jailer had a daughter, a pleasant girl with a good heart, who helped her father with the lighter duties of his job. She was especially fond of animals, and besides her canary, whose cage hung on a nail in the massive wall of the keep during the day, to the great annoyance of prisoners who liked an after-dinner nap, and was covered with a lace cloth on the parlor table at night, she kept several spotted mice and a restless squirrel on a wheel. This kind-hearted girl, feeling sorry for Toad’s misery, said to her father one day, “Father! I can’t bear to see that poor creature so unhappy, and getting so thin! Let me take charge of him. You know how fond of animals I am. I’ll make him eat from my hand, and sit up, and do all sorts of things.”

Her father told her she could deal with the prisoner however she liked. He was fed up with Toad, with his sulks and his airs and his stinginess. So that very day she went off on her errand of mercy and tapped on the door of Toad’s cell.

“Come now, Toad, cheer up,” she said coaxingly as she came in. “Sit up and wipe your eyes and be a sensible animal. And please try to eat a little dinner. Look, I’ve brought you some of my own, fresh from the oven!”

It was bubble-and-squeak, laid between two plates, and its aroma filled the little cell. The sharp smell of cabbage drifted to the nose of Toad as he lay flat on the floor in his misery, and for a moment it made him suspect that life might not be quite the empty, hopeless business he had pictured. Still, he went on wailing and drumming his legs and would not be comforted. So the clever girl withdrew for the time being. But a good deal of the hot-cabbage smell stayed behind, as it always does, and between sobs Toad sniffed and mused, and little by little new and uplifting thoughts crept in: thoughts of chivalry and poetry and deeds still waiting to be done; of wide meadows with cattle grazing in them, swept by sun and wind; of kitchen gardens and tidy herb borders, and warm snapdragons crowded with bees; and of the cozy clink of dishes set on the table at Toad Hall, and the scrape of chair legs across the floor as everyone drew up close to the business of dinner. The air in the narrow cell took on a rosy glow. He began to think of his friends, and how they would surely find some way to help; of lawyers, and how much they would have enjoyed his case, and what a donkey he’d been not to hire a few; and finally of his own great cleverness and resourcefulness, and all he could accomplish if he only put his mighty mind to it. And the cure was nearly complete.

When the girl came back a few hours later she was carrying a tray with a cup of fragrant tea steaming on it, and a plate heaped with piping hot buttered toast, cut thick and browned on both sides, the butter running through the holes in great golden drops like honey from the comb. The smell of that buttered toast simply spoke to Toad, and in no uncertain terms. It spoke of warm kitchens, of breakfasts on bright frosty mornings, of snug parlor fires on winter evenings when the day’s ramble was done and slippered feet rested on the fender; of the purring of contented cats and the twittering of drowsy canaries. Toad sat bolt upright once more, wiped his eyes, sipped his tea and munched his toast, and before long he was chattering away about himself, and the house he lived in, and everything he got up to there, and how important he was, and how highly his friends thought of him.
The jailer’s daughter could see that talking about himself was doing Toad as much good as the tea, and so it was, and she urged him to keep going.
“Tell me about Toad Hall,” she said. “It sounds beautiful.”

“Toad Hall,” said Toad proudly, “is a desirable, self-contained gentleman’s residence, quite unique; dating in part from the fourteenth century, but fitted with every modern convenience. Up-to-date plumbing. Five minutes from church, post office, and golf links. Suitable for——”
“Goodness, you silly animal,” the girl said with a laugh, “I’m not looking to _rent_ the place. Tell me something _true_ about it. But first hold on while I go get you more tea and toast.”

She hurried off and was soon back with a second loaded tray. Toad dug into the toast with gusto, his mood fully restored to its usual cheerfulness, and told her all about Toad Hall: the boathouse, the fish pond and the old walled vegetable garden; then the pigsties, the stables, the dovecote and the chicken coop; then the dairy, the laundry house, the china cupboards and the linen closets (she was especially taken with those); and finally the banqueting hall, where the other animals would sit around the long table and Toad, at the top of his form, kept everyone entertained with songs and stories and general high jinks. After that she asked about his animal friends, and listened with real interest to how they lived and how they filled their days. She did not, naturally, mention that she liked animals as _pets_, since she was sensible enough to realize that Toad would take great offense. When she wished him good night, having topped up his water jug and fluffed his straw, Toad was once again the same sunny, pleased-with-himself creature he had always been. He sang a song or two of the kind he used to perform at his dinner parties, curled up in the straw, and enjoyed a splendid night’s sleep with the most delightful dreams.

Over the long, gloomy days that followed, the two of them had plenty of fascinating conversations. The jailer’s daughter came to feel quite sorry for Toad. It struck her as a real shame that a poor little animal should be shut up in a cell over what looked to her like a very minor misdeed. Toad, in his vanity, naturally took her concern for a sign of tender feelings growing in her heart, and he couldn’t help feeling a twinge of regret that the gap in their social standing was so enormous, for she was a handsome young woman, and she clearly thought the world of him.

One morning the girl seemed lost in thought, gave answers that had nothing to do with the question, and did not appear to Toad to be giving his witty sayings and sparkling remarks the attention they deserved.
“Toad,” she said at last, “please listen to me. I have an aunt who takes in washing.”
“Now, now,” said Toad with gracious good humor, “don’t you fret; put it out of your mind. Why, _I_ have several aunts who _should_ be washerwomen.”

“Please hush for a minute, Toad,” said the girl. “Talking too much is your biggest fault, and I’m trying to think, and you’re making my head ache. Like I told you, my aunt is a washerwoman; she washes for every prisoner in this castle—we like to keep that kind of paying work in the family, you see. She collects the laundry on Monday morning and delivers it again on Friday evening. Today is Thursday. Now here’s what I’ve been thinking: you’re very rich—or so you keep telling me—and she’s very poor. A few pounds would mean nothing to you, and a great deal to her. So I think that if she were approached in the proper way—squared, I believe is what you animals call it—the two of you could strike a bargain by which she lets you have her dress and bonnet and the rest, and you could walk out of the castle as the official washerwoman. You look a lot alike in many ways—especially around the middle.”
“We do _not_,” Toad said, offended. “My figure is a very elegant one—for an animal of my kind.”
“So is my aunt’s,” the girl shot back, “for a woman of _her_ kind. But suit yourself. What a horrid, proud, ungrateful animal you are, when I feel sorry for you and am trying to help!”

“Yes, yes, that’s all very well, and thank you kindly,” Toad said in a rush. “But really! Surely you can’t expect Mr. Toad of Toad Hall to go wandering around the countryside dressed up as a washerwoman!”
“Then you can stay right here as a toad,” the girl answered with spirit. “I suppose you’d rather leave in a carriage with four horses!”

Toad was an honest creature, and always the first to own up when he had been mistaken. “You are a good, kind, clever girl,” he said, “and I really am a proud and foolish toad. Please introduce me to your worthy aunt, and I’m sure that she and I can come to an agreement that pleases us both.”

The following evening the girl brought her aunt into the cell, with Toad’s week of laundry tied up in a towel. The old lady had been told what to expect. Toad had also been wise enough to set some gold sovereigns out on the table where she couldn’t miss them, and that very nearly closed the deal with nothing much left to discuss. In exchange for his money Toad got a cotton print dress, an apron, a shawl and a shabby black bonnet. The old woman asked for only one thing: that she be gagged, tied up and left in a heap in the corner. It was a rather flimsy trick, she admitted, but with a little colorful storytelling of her own to go with it, she hoped she could keep her position, however suspicious the whole business looked.

Toad loved the idea. Now he could walk out of the prison in style, his name as a fearsome and dangerous desperado still intact. He gladly pitched in to help the jailer’s daughter arrange her aunt so that she looked as much as possible like an innocent victim of events she could do nothing about.
“Now for you, Toad,” the girl said. “Off with that coat and vest of yours; you’re plump enough without them.”
Shaking with laughter, she fastened him into the cotton print gown with its “hooks and eyes,” draped the shawl in a practiced fold, and knotted the strings of the rusty bonnet beneath his chin.

“You’re the spitting image of her,” she giggled, “except that I’m sure you’ve never looked half this respectable in your whole life. Now, good-bye, Toad, and good luck. Walk straight out the way you came in; and if anybody speaks to you, which they probably will, since they’re only men, you may answer back a little, of course, but don’t forget that you’re a widow, all alone in the world, with a reputation to protect.”

With a quaking heart, but as firm a step as he could manage, Toad set out cautiously on what seemed a most harebrained and dangerous undertaking; but he was soon pleasantly surprised to find how easy everything was made for him, and a little humbled by the thought that both his popularity, and the sex that seemed to inspire it, really belonged to someone else. The washerwoman’s squat figure in its familiar cotton print seemed a passport through every barred door and grim gateway; even when he hesitated, unsure which turning to take, he found himself helped out of his trouble by the guard at the next gate, who was anxious to be off to his tea and told him to come along sharp and not keep him waiting there all night. The teasing and the jokes he had to put up with, and to which, of course, he had to give quick and effective replies, were in fact his chief danger; for Toad was an animal with a strong sense of his own dignity, and the teasing was mostly (he thought) poor and clumsy, and the jokes not funny at all. However, he kept his temper, though with great difficulty, matched his replies to his company and his supposed character, and did his best not to go beyond the bounds of good taste.

It felt like hours. He crossed the last courtyard, brushed off the insistent invitations in the last guardroom, and ducked away from the open arms of the last warder, who pleaded with feigned passion for just one farewell hug. At long last the small door set in the huge outer gate clicked shut behind him. The cool air of the free world touched his worried forehead, and he knew he was free!

Giddy at how easily his bold escape had worked, he set off briskly toward the town lights. He had no notion what to do next. He was sure of just one thing: he had to get far away, and fast, from a neighborhood where the lady he was obliged to impersonate was such a familiar and well-loved figure.

Walking along and turning things over in his mind, he noticed red and green lights some distance off at the edge of town, and heard engines huffing and snorting and freight cars clanking together as they were shunted about. “Aha!” he thought. “What luck! A railway station is exactly what I need more than anything in the world right now. Even better, I can reach it without passing through the town, so I won’t have to keep playing this humiliating part and trading quips that work wonderfully well but do nothing at all for a person’s dignity.”

He made his way to the station accordingly, looked at a timetable, and found that a train heading more or less toward his home was due to leave in half an hour. “More luck!” said Toad, his spirits rising fast, and went off to the ticket office to buy his ticket.

He named the station he knew to be closest to the village that Toad Hall dominated, and out of habit his fingers went hunting for money in the place where his waistcoat pocket ought to be. Here, though, the cotton dress, which had served him so loyally until then and which he had shamefully overlooked, got in his way and thwarted him. He wrestled with it as in a bad dream. This strange, eerie thing seemed to pin his hands down, turned every effort of his muscles to water, and mocked him the whole time. Behind him the other passengers lined up, tapping their feet, and called out advice and remarks of varying usefulness and bite. Finally—somehow, he never quite understood how—he broke through, got to the place where every waistcoat pocket has always been, and discovered not only that there was no money, but no pocket to keep it in, and no waistcoat to hold the pocket!

With horror he remembered that he had left his coat and waistcoat lying in his cell, and along with them his notebook, money, keys, watch, matches and pencil case: everything that makes life worth living, everything that raises the many-pocketed animal, the master of creation, above those lesser one-pocketed or pocketless beings who hop and trot about carelessly, with no equipment for the real fight.

In his misery he made one desperate try at bluffing his way through, and, falling back on his fine old manner—part country squire, part college professor—he said, “Look here! I find I’ve left my purse behind. Just hand me that ticket, will you, and I’ll send the money tomorrow? I’m well known in these parts.”

For a moment the clerk simply stared at him and at the rusty black bonnet, and then he burst out laughing. “I’d say you must be quite well known around here,” he said, “if you’ve pulled this stunt many times. Now step back from the window, madam, please; you’re holding up the other passengers!”

An old gentleman who had been poking him in the back for some moments now shoved him aside and, what was worse, called him his good woman, which made Toad angrier than anything else that had happened that evening.

Beaten and full of despair, he wandered blindly down the platform alongside the waiting train, with tears trickling down both sides of his nose. It was hard, he thought, to be within sight of safety and almost of home, and to be thwarted for lack of a few wretched shillings and by the petty, suspicious attitude of paid officials. Very soon his escape would be discovered, the hunt would be on, he would be caught, scorned, loaded with chains, and dragged back to prison and bread and water and straw; his guards and punishments would be doubled; and oh, what sarcastic remarks the girl would make! What was to be done? He was not quick on his feet; his figure was, unfortunately, easy to recognize. Could he not squeeze under the seat of a carriage? He had seen schoolboys do that when the travel money their thoughtful parents had given them had been spent on other and better things. As he pondered, he found himself opposite the engine, which was being oiled, wiped, and generally petted by its affectionate driver, a burly man with an oil can in one hand and a lump of cotton waste in the other.
“Hello, mother!” said the engine driver. “What’s the trouble? You don’t look very cheerful.”

“Oh, sir!” Toad wailed, bursting into fresh tears. “I’m a poor, unhappy washerwoman, and I’ve lost every penny, and I can’t pay for a ticket, and I _must_ get home tonight one way or another, and I haven’t the faintest idea what I’m going to do. Oh dear, oh dear!”
“That’s a nasty bit of luck, all right,” the engine driver said, thinking it over. “Lost your money, can’t get home—and I’ll bet you’ve got a few little ones waiting up for you, too?”
“Heaps of them,” sobbed Toad. “And they’ll be hungry—and playing with matches—and knocking over lamps, the little innocents!—and squabbling, and carrying on all over the place. Oh dear, oh dear!”

“Well, here’s what I’ll do,” said the kindly engine driver. “You say you’re a washerwoman by trade. Fine, that settles that. Now, I drive an engine, as you can plainly see, and it’s filthy work, no getting around it. I go through shirts like nobody’s business, and my wife’s honestly worn out from scrubbing them. So if you’ll do a few shirts for me once you’re home and send them over, I’ll let you ride on my engine. The Company doesn’t allow it, mind, but out here in the back of beyond nobody’s too fussy.”

Toad’s gloom changed to joy, and he hurried up into the engine’s cab. He had never washed a shirt in his entire life, and wouldn’t have known how if he tried, and in any case had no plans to start. But he told himself, “Once I’m safe at Toad Hall, with money in hand and pockets to keep it in, I’ll send the engine driver enough to cover a whole mountain of laundry. That will do just as well, or better.”

The guard waved his flag to say all was well, the driver answered with a merry toot of the whistle, and the train pulled away from the platform. Faster and faster it went. Real fields, trees, hedges, cows and horses went streaking past on either side, and Toad thought about how each passing minute brought him closer to Toad Hall, to friends who would sympathize, to coins jingling in his pocket, to a soft bed, a good dinner, and a hero’s welcome as he told the tale of his adventures and his astonishing cleverness. He started to hop about, shouting and singing scraps of songs. The engine driver stared. He had run into washerwomen now and again over the years, but never one remotely like this.

Many miles had gone by, and Toad was busy picking out his supper for when he reached home, when he noticed the driver looking puzzled. The man was leaning out beside the engine and straining to hear something. Then he watched him clamber up on the coal pile and peer over the roof of the train. He came back down and told Toad, “This is odd. Ours is the last train going this way tonight, but I could have sworn there was another one coming along behind us!”

Toad stopped his silly capering at once. He grew serious and gloomy, and a dull ache low down in his spine, spreading to his legs, made him want to sit down and try desperately not to think of all the things that might happen.
By this time the moon was shining brightly, and the engine driver, steadying himself on the coal, could see a long way down the track behind them.
A moment later he shouted, “Now I can see it plainly! It’s an engine, running on our track, coming up at a tremendous speed! It looks like somebody is after us!”
The miserable Toad, crouching in the coal dust, tried hard to think of something to do, without any success at all.

“They’re gaining on us fast!” cried the engine driver. And the engine is packed with the oddest crowd of people! Men dressed like old-time guards, waving halberds; policemen in their helmets, waving clubs; and shabbily dressed men in bowler hats, plainly and unmistakably plain-clothes detectives even at this distance, waving revolvers and walking sticks; all waving, and all shouting the same thing—‘Stop, stop, stop!’”

At that, Toad dropped to his knees in the coal, clasped his paws together and begged, “Save me, please just save me, dear good Mr. Engine Driver, and I’ll tell you everything! I’m not the plain washerwoman I appear to be! I have no children at home waiting for me, innocent or otherwise! I’m a toad—the famous and well-loved Mr. Toad, owner of a large estate. By my own great courage and brains I have just broken out of a foul dungeon where my enemies threw me, and if the men on that engine catch me again, it means chains, bread and water, a bed of straw and misery all over again for poor, unhappy, innocent Toad!”
The engine driver peered down at him, very severe, and said, “Now, no more fibbing. What did they put you in prison for?”

“It was nothing much,” said poor Toad, blushing deeply. “I only borrowed a motorcar while the owners were at lunch; they didn’t need it just then. I didn’t really mean to steal it; but people—especially magistrates—take such harsh views of thoughtless, high-spirited deeds.”

The engine driver looked very serious and said, “I’m afraid you have been a wicked toad indeed, and by rights I ought to hand you over to justice. But you are plainly in deep trouble and distress, so I won’t abandon you. For one thing, I don’t hold with motorcars; for another, I don’t hold with being ordered about by policemen when I’m on my own engine. And the sight of an animal in tears always makes me feel queer and soft-hearted. So cheer up, Toad! I’ll do my best, and we may beat them yet!”

They heaped on more coal and shoveled like mad. The fire roared, sparks streamed out, and the engine bucked and swayed, yet the chasers kept creeping closer. With a sigh the driver mopped his forehead with a wad of cotton waste and said, “It’s no use, Toad, I’m afraid. They’re traveling light, and their engine’s better than mine. We have only one thing left to try, and it’s your one chance, so pay close attention. Not far ahead there’s a long tunnel, and beyond it the track runs through a dense forest. I’ll give her everything I’ve got while we’re inside the tunnel, and the other crew will naturally ease off a little in case of a crash. Once we’re out, I’ll cut the steam and squeeze the brakes as hard as I can. The second it’s safe, you jump off and get into the trees before they come out of the tunnel and spot you. After that I’ll open her up again, and they can chase me as long and as far as they please. So get ready to leap when I give the word!”

More coal went on the fire, and the train plunged into the tunnel, where the engine rushed and roared and clattered, until at last they burst out the far end into fresh air and quiet moonlight, and saw the wood spreading dark and helpful on both sides of the track. The driver cut the steam and braked hard, Toad lowered himself onto the step, and as the train crawled along at barely a walking pace he heard the driver shout, “Now, jump!”
Toad leapt, tumbled down a short bank, got up without a scratch, and scrambled into the wood to hide.

Peering out, he watched his train gather speed again and race away out of sight. Then the pursuing engine came bursting from the tunnel, roaring and whistling, her ragged crew brandishing all their different weapons and yelling, “Stop! stop! stop!” Once they had thundered by, Toad laughed heartily—for the first time since he had been thrown into prison.

His laughter did not last. It dawned on him that it was very late, and dark, and cold, that he was in a wood he didn’t know, penniless, with no hope of supper and still a long way from home and friends. After the roar and clatter of the train, the total silence came as a shock. He didn’t dare step out from under the trees, so he plunged deeper into the wood, hoping to leave the railway as far behind as possible.

After weeks shut up behind walls, Toad found the wood strange and unwelcoming, and rather inclined, he felt, to poke fun at him. The mechanical churring of the nightjars made him imagine the whole place crawling with warders who were closing in. An owl came gliding at him without a sound and grazed his shoulder with a wing, and he leapt in the air, fully convinced it was a hand. Then it drifted away like a moth, chuckling its low ho! ho! ho!, which Toad considered very bad manners. At one point he came across a fox, who paused, looked him over from head to foot with a sneer and said, “Well, well, washerwoman! Half a pair of socks and a pillowcase short this week, and don’t let it happen again!” Then he swaggered away, sniggering. Toad searched around for a stone to hurl at him, and not finding one irritated him more than anything. Finally, cold and hungry and worn out, he found a hollow tree, piled branches and dead leaves into the best bed he could manage, and slept deeply until dawn.

chapters.title: Wayfarers All
paragraphs: The Water Rat was restless, and he couldn’t say exactly why. By every outward sign, summer was still in its full splendor. In the plowed fields the green had turned to gold, the rowan berries were reddening, and the woods were streaked here and there with a fierce tawny brown; yet light and warmth and color were all still there in full measure, with no chill hint of the year slipping away. But the steady chorus of the orchards and hedgerows had dwindled to a casual evening song from a few performers who had not yet tired. The robin was starting to make himself heard again, and there was a feeling in the air of change and leaving. The cuckoo, of course, had been silent for a long time; but many other feathered friends, who for months had belonged to the familiar landscape and its small society, were missing too, and it seemed that their ranks thinned a little more every day. Rat, who always noticed anything with wings, saw that their flight was turning southward day by day; and even as he lay in bed at night he thought he could make out, passing overhead in the dark, the beat and quiver of eager wings, obeying a stern summons.

Nature’s Grand Hotel has its Season, like all the others. The guests pack, pay, and leave one by one, and the seats at the _table-d’hôte_ sadly thin out at every meal; suites of rooms are closed, carpets are rolled up, and waiters are sent away. The boarders who are staying on, _en pension_, until the hotel opens fully again next year cannot help being affected by all this coming and going, all this eager talk of plans and routes and new quarters, this daily shrinking of the stream of company. You get unsettled and gloomy, and you start to grumble. Why this craving for change? Why not stay on quietly here, as we do, and enjoy yourselves? You don’t know this hotel out of season, or what fun we have among ourselves, those of us who remain to see the whole interesting year through. All very true, no doubt, the others always answer; we really envy you, and maybe some other year; but just now we have appointments, and the bus is waiting at the door, and our time is up! So they leave, with a smile and a nod, and we miss them, and feel resentful. The Rat was a self-sufficient sort of animal, rooted to the land, and whoever else went away, he stayed; still, he could not help noticing what was in the air, and feeling some of it in his bones.

It was hard to settle down to anything serious with all this coming and going. He left the water’s edge, where thick tall rushes stood in a stream that was growing slow and low, and wandered inland. He crossed a field or two of pasture that already looked dusty and dried out, and pushed into the great sea of wheat, yellow, rippling, and murmuring, full of quiet motion and small whispers. He often loved to wander here, through a forest of stiff, strong stalks that carried their own golden sky high above his head, a sky that was always dancing, shimmering, and talking softly, or swaying hard in the passing wind and righting itself with a toss and a merry laugh. He had many small friends here too, a whole society of their own, living full and busy lives but always with a spare moment to chat and swap news with a visitor. Today, though, polite as they were, the field-mice and harvest-mice seemed distracted. Many were busily digging and tunneling; others, gathered in little groups, were studying plans and drawings of small flats, described as desirable and compact and conveniently close to the Stores. Some were dragging out dusty trunks and dress-baskets, and others were already elbow-deep in packing their belongings; and everywhere piles and bundles of wheat, oats, barley, beech-mast, and nuts lay ready to be carried off.
“It’s old Ratty!” they shouted the moment they spotted him. “Come and give us a hand, Rat! Don’t just loaf around!”
“What are you all up to?” said the Water Rat sternly. “You know it’s nowhere near time to be thinking about winter quarters yet!”

“Oh, we know that,” explained one field-mouse, rather sheepishly; “but it’s always best to be in good time, isn’t it? We really _must_ get all the furniture and luggage and supplies moved out of here before those horrid machines start clattering around the fields; and then, you know, the best flats get snapped up so fast these days, and if you’re late you have to put up with _anything_; and they need so much fixing up, too, before you can move in. Of course we’re early, we know that; but we’re only just getting started.”
“Oh, bother _beginning_,” said the Rat. “It’s a gorgeous day. Come for a row, or take a walk along the hedgerows, or have a picnic in the woods, or something.”
“Well, I _don’t_ think I can _today_, thank you,” the field-mouse answered hastily. “Maybe some _other_ day, once we’re not so short of _time_——”
With a snort of scorn, the Rat spun around to leave, tripped over a hat-box, and fell, saying things that were not very dignified.

“If people were more careful,” said a field-mouse rather stiffly, “and watched where they were going, they wouldn’t hurt themselves, and lose their tempers. Mind that hold-all, Rat! You’d better sit down somewhere. In an hour or two we may have time to see to you.”
“From what I can see, you won’t be ‘free,’ as you put it, anytime before Christmas,” the Rat snapped sourly, picking his way out of the field.
He went back to his river feeling rather downhearted, his faithful, steady old river, which never packed up, moved out, or went off to winter quarters.

In the willows that fringed the bank he spotted a swallow perched. Soon another joined it, and then a third; and the birds, fidgeting restlessly on their branch, talked together in earnest, low voices.
“What, _already_?” said the Rat, wandering over. “Why the rush? It seems downright silly to me.”

“Oh, we’re not going yet, if that’s what you’re thinking,” the first swallow replied. “We’re only planning and getting organized. We’re talking it all through, you see: which way to fly this year, where to rest along the way, and so forth. That’s half the fun!”

“Fun?” said the Rat. “Now that’s exactly what I can’t make sense of. Suppose you _have_ to leave this lovely spot, and the friends who’ll miss you, and the cozy homes you’ve only just settled into. Fine. When the hour comes, I’m sure you’ll set off bravely, put up with all the hardship and discomfort and upheaval of something new, and pretend you’re not terribly unhappy. But to want to chatter about it, or even dwell on it, before you absolutely must——”

“No, naturally you don’t understand,” said the second swallow. “First we feel it stirring inside us, a sweet restlessness; then the memories come back one by one, like homing pigeons. They flutter through our dreams at night, and they fly with us as we wheel and circle by day. We long to ask each other questions, to compare notes and reassure ourselves that it was all really true, as the scents and sounds and names of long-forgotten places come back to us little by little and beckon.”

“Couldn’t you just stay on for this one year?” the Water Rat suggested, rather wistfully. “We’d all do our very best to make you feel at home. You can’t imagine the good times we have here while you’re off far away.”

“I tried ‘staying on’ once,” said the third swallow. “I’d grown so attached to the place that when the time came, I lagged behind and let the others fly on without me. For a few weeks that was fine. But then, oh, how wearily the nights dragged! The days were shivering and sunless, the air damp and bitter, and there wasn’t a single insect in a whole acre of it! No, it was hopeless. My nerve gave way, and one cold, stormy night I took off, keeping well inland because of the fierce easterly gales. Snow was falling heavily as I forced my way through the passes of the great mountains, and it was a hard struggle to get across. But I will never forget the blissful feeling of the hot sun on my back again as I swooped down toward the lakes lying so blue and calm below me, or the taste of my first fat insect! The past felt like a bad dream, and the future was one long happy holiday as I drifted south week after week, easy and lazy, lingering as long as I dared, yet always obeying the call! No, I’d had my warning. Never again did I think of disobeying.”

“Ah, yes, the call of the South, of the South!” twittered the other two dreamily. “Its songs, its colors, its shining air! Oh, do you remember——” and, forgetting the Rat, they slipped into passionate memories, while he listened, spellbound, and his heart burned inside him. He knew that something in him, too, was trembling at last, a chord that until now had lain dormant and unsuspected. The mere chatter of these south-bound birds, their pale secondhand reports, still had the power to awaken this wild new feeling and thrill him through and through; what would a single moment of the real thing do to him, one passionate touch of the true southern sun, one whiff of the genuine fragrance? With closed eyes he dared to dream for a moment, completely carried away, and when he looked again the river seemed steely and cold, and the green fields gray and lifeless. Then his loyal heart seemed to cry out against his weaker self for its betrayal.
“Why do you ever come back at all, then?” he demanded of the swallows, jealously. “What is there to attract you in this poor, drab little country?”

“And do you think,” said the first swallow, “that the other call isn’t for us too, in its proper season? The call of lush meadow grass, damp orchards, warm ponds humming with insects, of grazing cattle, of haymaking, and of all the farm buildings clustered around the House with the perfect Eaves?”
“Do you imagine,” asked the second one, that you’re the only living creature who aches with a hungry longing to hear the cuckoo’s call again?”

“All in good time,” said the third, “we’ll be homesick again for quiet water-lilies rocking on the surface of an English stream. Today, though, all that feels faded and thin and very far off. At this moment our blood is dancing to a different tune.”
Soon they were twittering to each other once more, and this time their heady chatter was all about violet seas, golden-brown sands, and walls where lizards lurk.

Restlessly the Rat wandered off again, climbed the slope that rose gently from the north bank of the river, and lay looking out toward the great ring of Downs that blocked his view farther south. They had always been his simple horizon, his Mountains of the Moon, the limit beyond which lay nothing he had cared to see or know. Today, as he gazed south with a new-born need stirring in his heart, the clear sky above their long, low outline seemed to throb with promise; today, the unseen was everything, and the unknown the only real fact of life. This side of the hills was now the true blank, and on the other side lay the crowded, colorful panorama that his inner eye saw so clearly. What seas lay beyond, green, leaping, and crested! What sunlit coasts, where white villas glittered against the olive woods! What quiet harbors, crowded with gallant ships bound for purple islands of wine and spice, islands set low in languid waters!

He got up and went down toward the river again; then changed his mind and went to the side of the dusty lane. There he lay half-buried in the thick, cool tangle under the hedge that bordered it, and could think about the hard road and all the wonderful world it led to; and about all the travelers who might have walked it, and the fortunes and adventures they had gone to look for, or had found without looking, out there, beyond, beyond!

Footsteps came to his ear, and the figure of someone walking rather wearily came into view; and he saw that it was a Rat, and a very dusty one. As he reached him, the traveler greeted him with a courteous gesture that had something foreign about it, hesitated a moment, and then, with a pleasant smile, left the track and sat down beside him in the cool grass. He seemed tired, and the Rat let him rest without questions, understanding something of what was in his mind, and knowing, too, how much all animals value, at times, plain silent company, when weary muscles loosen and the mind simply marks time.

The traveler was lean and sharp-featured, and a little bent at the shoulders; his paws were thin and long, his eyes much wrinkled at the corners, and he wore small gold earrings in his neat, well-shaped ears. His knitted jersey was a faded blue, his breeches, patched and stained, had begun life as blue, and the few belongings he carried were tied up in a blue cotton handkerchief.
When he had rested a while, the stranger sighed, sniffed the air, and looked around.

“That warm whiff on the breeze was clover,” he said. “And that sound behind us is cows, tearing at the grass and breathing softly between mouthfuls. Far off I can hear reapers at work, and over there a blue thread of smoke from a cottage climbs against the woods. The river must be close, because I hear a moorhen calling, and from your build I can tell you’re a sailor of fresh water. Everything seems asleep, and yet something is always going on. What a fine life you lead, my friend! Surely the best in the world, if only you’re strong enough to live it!”
“Yes, it’s _the_ life, the only life worth living,” answered the Water Rat dreamily, without his usual wholehearted conviction.

“I wouldn’t say precisely that,” the stranger answered carefully. “But I’m sure it’s the best. I’ve tried it, so I know. And because I’ve just tried it—six months of it—and know it’s the best, here I am, sore-footed and starving, trudging away from it, trudging south, following the old call, back to the old life, _the_ life that belongs to me and won’t let me go.”
“So here’s yet another one of them?” the Rat mused. “Where have you come from just now?” he asked. He hardly dared ask where the stranger was headed, since he seemed to know the answer all too well.

“A nice little farm,” the traveler said shortly. “Up that way”—he nodded toward the north. “Never mind about that. I had everything a creature could want—everything I had any right to expect from life, and more. And here I am anyway! Glad to be here, though, glad! Another stretch of road behind me, a few more hours closer to what my heart desires!”

His bright eyes stayed fixed on the horizon, and he seemed to be listening for a sound that was missing from the countryside behind him, even though it rang with the cheerful music of pastures and farmyards.
“You’re not one of _us_,” said the Water Rat, “nor a farmer either; nor even, I’d judge, from this country.”

“Right,” replied the stranger. “I’m a seafaring rat, I am, and the port I originally come from is Constantinople, though I’m a sort of foreigner there too, in a manner of speaking. You’ll have heard of Constantinople, friend? A beautiful city, old and glorious. And perhaps you’ve heard of Sigurd, King of Norway, who sailed there with sixty ships, and how he and his men rode in through streets that had been draped in purple and gold to honor them; and how the Emperor and Empress came down to dine with him aboard his own ship. When Sigurd sailed for home, a good many of his Northmen stayed on and joined the Emperor’s bodyguard, and my ancestor, born in Norway, stayed too, along with the ships Sigurd had given the Emperor. We’ve always been seafarers, and small wonder; as for me, the city where I was born is no more my home than any pleasant harbor between there and the London River. I know every one of them, and they know me. Put me down on any of their quays or beaches, and I’m home again.”

“I suppose you make great voyages,” said the Water Rat, growing more interested. “Months and months with no land in sight, supplies running low, water rationed, your mind in communion with the mighty ocean, and all that sort of thing?”

“Not at all,” said the Sea Rat frankly. “A life like the one you describe wouldn’t suit me in the least. I’m in the coasting trade, and I’m hardly ever out of sight of land. It’s the good times on shore that appeal to me, as much as any sailing. Oh, those southern seaports! The smell of them, the riding lights at night, the glamour!”

“Well, perhaps you’ve chosen the better way,” said the Water Rat, though rather doubtfully. “Then tell me about your coasting, if you feel like it, and what sort of harvest an animal of spirit might hope to bring home from it, to warm his later years with gallant memories by the fireside. Because, I’ll confess, my own life feels rather narrow and cramped to me today.”

“My last voyage,” began the Sea Rat, “the one that finally landed me in this country, headed for my farm inland with high hopes, will do as an example of any of them, and really as a summary of my colorful life. As usual, it began with family troubles. The storm warning went up at home, and I signed on to a small trading ship leaving Constantinople, sailing through those classic seas where every wave throbs with an undying memory, bound for the Greek islands and the Levant. Those were golden days and balmy nights! In and out of harbor all the time, old friends everywhere, sleeping in some cool temple or ruined cistern through the heat of the day, then feasting and singing after sundown under great stars set in a velvet sky! From there we turned and coasted up the Adriatic, its shores swimming in a haze of amber, rose, and aquamarine. We lay in wide, landlocked harbors, we roamed through ancient and noble cities, until at last one morning, as the sun rose royally behind us, we sailed into Venice down a path of gold. Oh, Venice is a fine city, where a rat can wander at his ease and enjoy himself! Or, when he’s tired of wandering, he can sit at the edge of the Grand Canal at night, feasting with his friends, while the air is full of music and the sky full of stars, and the lights flash and shimmer on the polished steel prows of the swaying gondolas, packed so tightly that you could walk across the canal on them from one side to the other! And then the food—do you like shellfish? Well, well, we won’t dwell on that now.”
He was silent for a while, and the Water Rat, silent too and spellbound, floated along dream canals and heard a phantom song ringing high between misty gray walls lapped by waves.

“At last we sailed south again,” the Sea Rat went on, “coasting down the Italian shore until we finally reached Palermo, and there I left the ship for a long, happy stretch on land. I never stay with one ship too long, because you get narrow-minded and prejudiced. Besides, Sicily is one of my favorite haunts. I know everybody there, and their ways suit me perfectly. I spent many pleasant weeks on the island, staying with friends in the hill country. When I grew restless again, I took a berth on a ship that traded with Sardinia and Corsica, and I was very glad to feel the fresh breeze and the sea spray on my face once more.”
“But isn’t it dreadfully hot and stuffy down in the—the hold, I think you call it?” the Water Rat asked.
The seafarer looked at him with the hint of a wink. “I’m an old hand,” he said, quite simply. “The captain’s cabin is good enough for me.”
“It’s a hard life, from all accounts,” murmured the Rat, lost in thought.
“Oh, for the crew it is,” the seafarer answered solemnly, again with a ghost of a wink.

“From Corsica,” he continued, “I got passage on a ship carrying wine to the mainland. We reached Alassio in the evening, stopped, hauled up our wine casks, and tossed them overboard, tied one to the next on a long line. Then the crew took to the boats and rowed toward shore, singing as they went, pulling behind them the long bobbing procession of casks, like a mile of porpoises. On the beach they had horses waiting, which dragged the casks up the steep street of the little town in a fine rush of clatter and scramble. When the last cask was in, we went off to eat and rest, and we sat up late into the night drinking with our friends. The next morning I headed for the great olive woods for a rest. I was done with islands for the time being, and there were plenty of ports and ships around, so I led a lazy life among the peasants, lying about watching them work, or stretched out high on the hillside with the blue Mediterranean far below me. And so, at last, by easy stages, partly on foot and partly by sea, I came to Marseilles, where I met old shipmates, visited great ocean-going vessels, and feasted once more. Talk about shellfish! Why, sometimes I dream about the shellfish of Marseilles, and wake up crying!”

“That reminds me,” said the polite Water Rat. “You mentioned that you were hungry, and I should have said something sooner. Of course you’ll stay and have your midday meal with me? My hole is close by, it’s well past noon, and you’re very welcome to whatever there is.”

“Now that’s kind and brotherly of you,” said the Sea Rat. “I really was hungry when I sat down, and ever since I carelessly mentioned shellfish, my pangs have been fierce. But couldn’t you bring it out here? I’m none too fond of going below deck unless I have to. Then, while we eat, I could tell you more about my voyages and the pleasant life I lead—at least, it’s very pleasant to me, and from your attention I judge it appeals to you too. Whereas if we go indoors, it’s a hundred to one that I’ll soon fall asleep.”

“That’s an excellent suggestion,” said the Water Rat, and hurried home. There he took out the lunch basket and packed a simple meal, in which, remembering the stranger’s origins and tastes, he made sure to include a yard of long French bread, a sausage with the garlic fairly singing out of it, some cheese that lay down and cried, and a long-necked, straw-covered flask in which lay bottled sunshine, shed and gathered on faraway southern slopes. Loaded down, he hurried back, and he blushed with pleasure at the old sailor’s praise of his taste and judgment as together they unpacked the basket and laid out the food on the grass by the roadside.

As soon as his hunger was somewhat eased, the Sea Rat went on with the story of his latest voyage. He led his simple listener from port to port in Spain, landed him at Lisbon, Oporto, and Bordeaux, introduced him to the pleasant harbors of Cornwall and Devon, and so up the Channel to that final quayside. There, coming ashore after long head winds, storm-driven and weather-beaten, he had caught the first magical hints and heralds of another Spring, and, fired by these, had hurried off on a long tramp inland, hungry to try life on some quiet farmstead, very far from the weary beating of any sea.

Spellbound and trembling with excitement, the Water Rat traveled with the Adventurer, mile after mile of sea. They crossed stormy bays, threaded busy anchorages, rode a racing tide over harbor bars, and sailed up winding rivers whose bustling little towns hid behind a sudden bend. Then, with a regretful sigh, he left the traveler standing on his dull inland farm, about which the Rat wanted to hear nothing.

By now the meal was finished. The Seafarer, rested and strengthened, his voice richer and his eyes lit with a brightness that seemed borrowed from some faraway lighthouse, filled his glass with the glowing red wine of the South. Leaning toward the Water Rat, he caught his gaze and held it, body and soul, as he talked. His eyes were the shifting, foam-streaked gray-green of leaping northern seas, and in the glass glowed a hot ruby that seemed the very heart of the South, throbbing for anyone brave enough to answer its pulse. Those twin lights, the changing gray and the steady red, overpowered the Water Rat and bound him fast, fascinated and helpless. The quiet world beyond their glow drifted far away and ceased to exist. And the talk, that wonderful talk, rolled on. Was it plain speech at all, or did it slip now and then into song? There was the sailors’ chanty as they hauled up the dripping anchor, the deep hum of the rigging in a howling northeast gale, the fisherman’s ballad as he hauled in his nets at sundown under an apricot sky, and guitar and mandolin chords drifting from a gondola or a caique. Did it turn into the cry of the wind, mournful at first, then shrill and angry as it picked up, rising to a tearing whistle and sinking to a musical trickle of air along the edge of a bellying sail? The spellbound listener seemed to hear all of these sounds, and with them the hungry complaints of gulls and sea-mews, the soft thunder of the breaking wave, and the protest of the shingle. Then it turned back into speech, and with a pounding heart he followed the adventures of a dozen seaports: the fights, the narrow escapes, the comebacks, the comradeship, the daring ventures. Or he hunted for treasure on islands, fished in still lagoons, and dozed all day on warm white sand. He heard tales of deep-sea fishing and the huge silver hauls of the mile-long net; of sudden dangers, such as the roar of breakers on a moonless night, or the tall bows of a great liner looming overhead out of the fog; of the joyful homecoming, the headland rounded, the harbor lights opening out; the groups dimly seen on the quay, the cheerful shout, the splash of the hawser; and the trudge up the steep little street toward the cozy glow of red-curtained windows.
At last, in his waking dream, it seemed the Adventurer had stood up, yet was still speaking, still keeping him pinned with those sea-gray eyes.

“And now,” he was saying softly, “I take to the road again, heading southwest for many a long and dusty day, until I reach the little gray sea town I know so well, which clings to one steep side of the harbor. There, through dark doorways, you look down flights of stone steps, overhung by great pink tufts of valerian and ending in a patch of sparkling blue water. The little boats tied to the rings and posts of the old sea wall are painted as gaily as the ones I climbed in and out of in my own childhood. The salmon leap on the flood tide, schools of mackerel flash and play past the quays and shores, and past the windows the great ships glide, night and day, up to their moorings or out to the open sea. There, sooner or later, the ships of all seafaring nations arrive, and there, at its appointed hour, the ship of my choice will drop its anchor. I’ll take my time, I’ll linger and wait, until at last the right one lies waiting for me, hauled out into midstream, loaded low, her bowsprit pointing down the harbor. I’ll slip aboard, by boat or along the rope. And then one morning I’ll wake to the song and tramp of the sailors, the clink of the capstan, and the rattle of the anchor chain coming merrily in. We’ll break out the jib and the foresail, the white houses along the harbor will glide slowly past us as she gathers enough speed to steer, and the voyage will have begun! As she pushes toward the headland she’ll dress herself in canvas, and then, once outside, comes the resounding slap of great green seas as she heels to the wind, pointing South!

“And you, you’ll come too, young brother. The days slip by and never come back, and the South is still waiting for you. Take the Adventure! Answer the call now, before the moment is gone for good! It’s only a door slammed behind you, one light-hearted step forward, and you’ve left the old life for the new! Then, some day, some day far off, wander home again if you like, when the cup is drained and the play is played, and settle down by your quiet river with a fine store of memories to keep you company. You’ll catch me up on the road easily enough, since you’re young and I’m getting old and go slowly. I’ll dawdle and look back, and in the end I’ll surely see you coming, eager and carefree, with all the South shining in your face!”

The voice faded and fell silent, the way an insect’s tiny trumpet quickly thins into nothing. And the Water Rat, frozen and staring, could finally make out only a distant speck on the white ribbon of the road.

Like a machine, he got up and began packing the lunch basket again, carefully and unhurriedly. Like a machine, he went home and gathered a few small necessities and some treasures he was fond of, and put them in a satchel. He moved slowly and deliberately about the room like a sleepwalker, always listening, lips parted. He slung the satchel over his shoulder and chose a sturdy stick for the road. With no hurry, but without the slightest hesitation, he stepped over the threshold at the very moment the Mole appeared in the doorway.
“Why, Ratty, where are you going?” the Mole asked, astonished, catching him by the arm.
“I’m going south with the rest of them,” the Rat murmured in a dreamy drone, never looking at him. “Down to the sea first, then aboard a ship, and on to the shores that are calling me!”

He pushed determinedly on, still unhurried but stubbornly set on his purpose. The Mole, now thoroughly alarmed, planted himself in front of him and looked into his eyes. They were glazed and fixed, and had turned a streaked, shifting gray—not his friend’s eyes at all, but the eyes of some other animal! Gripping him tightly, Mole dragged him indoors, threw him to the floor, and pinned him down.

For a few moments the Rat fought wildly, and then all at once his strength drained away. He lay still and worn out, eyes shut, trembling. After a while the Mole helped him up and settled him in a chair, where he sat slumped and shrunken into himself, his body wracked by violent shudders that gradually turned into a fit of dry, hysterical sobbing. Mole bolted the door, tossed the satchel into a drawer and locked it, then sat down quietly on the table beside his friend to wait for the strange attack to pass. Little by little the Rat sank into a restless doze, interrupted by jerks and jumbled mutterings about things strange, wild, and foreign, which the unenlightened Mole couldn’t make out. From that he drifted into deep sleep.

Very anxious, the Mole left him for a while and busied himself with household chores. It was getting dark when he came back to the parlor and found the Rat where he had left him, wide awake now, but listless, silent, and low in spirits. He took one quick look at his eyes and found them, to his great relief, clear and dark and brown again as before. Then he sat down and tried to cheer him up and help him tell what had happened to him.

Poor Ratty did his best, bit by bit, to explain what had happened. But how could he put into plain words what had mostly been a feeling, a hint? How could he recall, for someone else’s sake, the haunting sea voices that had sung to him, or retell secondhand the magic of the Seafarer’s hundred memories? Even to himself, now that the spell had lifted and the glamour was gone, it was hard to account for what had seemed, only hours before, the one and only thing to do. So it’s no wonder he failed to give the Mole any clear idea of what he’d been through that day.

One thing was clear to the Mole: the fit, or attack, had passed and left his friend in his right mind again, though shaken and low from the aftermath. But for the time being the Rat seemed to have lost all interest in the things that made up his everyday life, and in any cheerful thoughts of the different days and doings that the changing season was surely bringing.

So, casually, and as though he didn’t much care, the Mole began to talk about the harvest being brought in: the tall wagons and their straining teams, the haystacks growing higher, and the big moon rising over bare fields dotted with sheaves. He talked about the apples reddening all around, the nuts turning brown, the making of jams and preserves, and the distilling of cordials. Step by easy step he made his way to midwinter, with its hearty pleasures and its snug life at home, and by then he was simply poetic.
Little by little the Rat began to sit up and join in. His dull eyes brightened, and he lost some of his listening look.
After a while the tactful Mole slipped out and came back with a pencil and a few half-sheets of paper, which he set on the table by his friend’s elbow.

“It’s been a long time since you wrote any poetry,” he said. “You could try your hand at it this evening, instead of—well, brooding over things so much. I suspect you’ll feel a lot better once you’ve got something jotted down—even if it’s only the rhymes.”

The Rat pushed the paper away wearily, but the discreet Mole took the chance to leave the room. When he peeked in again some time later, the Rat was completely absorbed and deaf to the world, scribbling for a bit and then chewing the end of his pencil. It’s true that he chewed a good deal more than he scribbled, but it made the Mole happy to know that the cure had at least begun.

chapters.title: The Further Adventures of Toad
paragraphs: The front door of the hollow tree faced east, so Toad got his wake-up call early. It came partly from the bright sunlight pouring in on him, and partly from the terrible chill in his toes, which made him dream that he was at home in bed in his own fine room with the Tudor window, on a freezing winter night. In the dream his blankets had gotten up, grumbling and complaining that they couldn’t stand the cold one minute longer, and had run downstairs to warm themselves at the kitchen fire. He had followed them in his bare feet, along miles and miles of icy stone passages, arguing with them and begging them to be reasonable. He would probably have woken much sooner if he hadn’t spent weeks sleeping on straw over stone floors, and nearly forgotten how friendly thick blankets feel when they’re pulled up snugly under your chin.

He sat up and rubbed his eyes, then his complaining toes. For a moment he wondered where he was, and looked around for the familiar stone wall and the little barred window. Then, with a jump of his heart, he remembered everything: his escape, his flight, his pursuit. He remembered, first and best of all, that he was free!

Free! That one word and the thought behind it were worth fifty blankets. He felt warm from head to toe as he thought about the jolly world outside, which was surely waiting eagerly for his grand and triumphant entrance, ready to wait on him and cheer him on, anxious to help him and keep him company, just as it had always done in the old days before misfortune struck. He shook himself and combed the dry leaves out of his hair with his fingers. Then, his washing and dressing done, he marched out into the pleasant morning sun, cold but confident, hungry but hopeful, with all the nervous terrors of yesterday swept away by rest and sleep and honest, heartening sunshine.

He had the whole world to himself that early summer morning. The dewy woods, as he made his way through them, were empty and still. The green fields beyond the trees were his to do with as he liked. And the road itself, when he reached it, seemed in all that loneliness to be looking anxiously for company, like a stray dog. Toad, however, was looking for something that could talk and tell him plainly which way to go. It is all very well, when you have a light heart, a clear conscience and money in your pocket, and nobody combing the countryside to haul you back to prison, to follow wherever the road beckons and points, without caring where it leads. The practical Toad cared very much indeed, and he could have kicked the road for its helpless silence, when every minute counted.

Before long the shy, silent country road was joined by a bashful little brother in the form of a canal, which took its hand and wandered along beside it in perfect trust, though it had the same tongue-tied, close-mouthed manner toward strangers. “Bother them!” Toad said to himself. “But anyhow, one thing’s clear. They must both be coming _from_ somewhere, and going _to_ somewhere. You can’t argue with that. Toad, my boy!” So he marched patiently on along the water’s edge.

Around a bend in the canal came a lone horse, plodding along with his head bent as if lost in worried thought. A long line ran from the ropes on his collar, tight but sagging a little with each step, and the far end of it dripped pearly drops of water. Toad let the horse go by and stood waiting to see what the fates were sending him.

With a pleasant swirl of quiet water at its blunt bow, the barge slid up beside him. Its cheerfully painted side was level with the towpath, and its only occupant was a big, stout woman in a linen sun-bonnet, one brawny arm resting along the tiller.
“Lovely morning, ma’am!” she called to Toad as she came level with him.

“I dare say it is, ma’am!” Toad answered politely, walking along the towpath beside her. “I dare say it _is_ a lovely morning for those who aren’t in serious trouble, like I am. Here’s my married daughter, who sends for me in a great hurry to come to her right away. So off I go, not knowing what’s happening or about to happen, but fearing the worst, as you’ll understand, ma’am, if you’re a mother too. And I’ve left my business to look after itself—I’m in the washing and laundry line, you must know, ma’am—and I’ve left my little children to look after themselves, and a more mischievous and troublesome set of young imps never lived, ma’am! And I’ve lost all my money, and lost my way, and as for what may be happening to my married daughter, well, I can’t bear to think of it, ma’am!”
“And where does your married daughter live, ma’am?” asked the barge-woman.
“She lives near the river, ma’am,” said Toad. “Close to a fine house called Toad Hall, somewhere around here, in these parts. Perhaps you’ve heard of it.”

“Toad Hall? Why, I’m headed that way myself,” said the barge-woman. “This canal meets the river a few miles on, just above Toad Hall, and from there it’s an easy walk. Come along on the barge with me, and I’ll give you a ride.”

She steered the barge in close to the bank, and Toad, with many humble and grateful thanks, stepped lightly aboard and sat down, extremely pleased with himself. “Toad’s luck again!” he thought. “I always land on top!”
“So you’re in the washing business, ma’am?” the barge-woman said politely as they glided along. “And a very good business it is, I’m sure, if I’m not being too bold in saying so.”

“The finest business in the whole country,” Toad said breezily. “All the gentry come to me. They wouldn’t go to anyone else, not if you paid them, they know me so well. You see, I understand my trade inside out, and I look after everything myself. Washing, ironing, starching, fine shirts for gentlemen’s evening wear—all of it is done right under my own eye!”
“Surely you don’t do _all_ that work with your own two hands, ma’am?” the barge-woman asked, with respect in her voice.
“Oh, I have girls,” Toad said airily. “Twenty or so, always hard at work. But you know what _girls_ are like, ma’am! Nasty little hussies, that’s what _I_ call them!”
“So do I,” said the barge-woman heartily. “But I expect you keep yours in line, the lazy good-for-nothings! And are you _very_ fond of washing?”

“Love it?” said Toad. “I’m simply mad about it. Nothing makes me happier than standing with both arms plunged in the suds. But then, I have such a knack for it! There’s no effort in it whatsoever! Pure delight, ma’am, I promise you!”
“What a stroke of luck, running into you!” the barge-woman remarked thoughtfully. “A real bit of good fortune for the both of us!”
“Why, what do you mean?” asked Toad nervously.

“Well, look at me,” said the barge-woman. “_I_ like washing too, just as you do. And whether I like it or not, I have to do all my own, naturally, moving around the way I do. Now my husband is such a one for dodging his work and leaving the barge to me that I never get a moment to see to my own business. By rights he ought to be here now, either steering or looking after the horse, though luckily the horse has the sense to look after himself. Instead of which, he’s gone off with the dog to see if they can’t catch a rabbit for dinner somewhere. Says he’ll catch up with me at the next lock. Well, we’ll see about that. I don’t trust him once he’s off with that dog, who’s even worse than he is. But in the meantime, how am I supposed to get on with my washing?”
“Oh, never mind the washing,” said Toad, who didn’t like the subject. “Try to keep your mind on that rabbit. A nice fat young rabbit, I’ll bet. Have you got any onions?”
