“I can’t think about anything but my washing,” said the barge-woman, “and I’m amazed you can go on about rabbits with such a happy prospect ahead of you. I’ve got a whole heap of things stacked in a corner of the cabin. Just pick out one or two of the most necessary kind—I won’t embarrass a lady like you by describing them, but you’ll know them at a glance—and run them through the wash-tub as we go along. Why, it’ll be a pleasure for you, as you say yourself, and a real help to me. You’ll find a tub handy, plus soap, a kettle on the stove, and a bucket for hauling water up from the canal. Then I’ll know you’re enjoying yourself, rather than sitting around idle, gazing at the scenery and yawning your head off.”

“Here, let me do the steering!” said Toad, now thoroughly scared. “Then you can do your washing however you like. I might ruin your things, or not do them the way you want. I’m used to gentlemen’s clothes, really. That’s my specialty.”

“You, steer?” the barge-woman said with a laugh. “Steering a barge well takes a good deal of practice. And anyway, it’s boring work, and I’d like to see you enjoying yourself. No, you’ll get on with the washing you’re so crazy about, and I’ll keep to the tiller, which I know. Please don’t cheat me out of the joy of treating you!”

Toad was well and truly trapped. He looked this way and that for a way out, saw he was too far from the bank to jump, and sulkily gave in to his fate. “If it comes to that,” he thought desperately, “I suppose any fool can _wash!_”
He fetched a tub, soap and the other necessities from the cabin, picked out a few garments at random, tried to remember what he had seen in quick glances through laundry windows, and set to work.

Half an hour dragged by, and with each minute Toad grew more furious. Nothing he did to those wretched things seemed to please them or improve them in the slightest. He coaxed them, he slapped them, he pounded them with his fists; and all the while they grinned up at him from the tub, quite unreformed and perfectly happy in their original sin. Now and then he shot a nervous glance over his shoulder at the barge-woman, but she seemed to be staring off ahead, wholly taken up with her steering. His back hurt terribly, and to his horror he saw that his paws were starting to go all puckered. And Toad was extremely vain about his paws. Under his breath he mumbled words that no washerwoman and no Toad should ever let slip; and for the fiftieth time, the soap got away from him.
A sudden roar of laughter made him pull himself upright and spin around. There sat the barge-woman, thrown back in her seat, laughing helplessly, with tears streaming down her cheeks.

“I’ve been watching you the whole time,” she gasped. “I guessed you must be a fraud from the start, from the stuck-up way you talked. Some washerwoman you are! You never washed so much as a dishcloth in your life, I’ll bet!”
For quite a while Toad’s temper had been seething away nastily, and now it boiled right over. He lost all hold on himself.

“You common, vulgar, _fat_ barge-woman!” he bellowed. “How dare you speak to your betters in that tone! Washerwoman, indeed! Let me inform you that I am a Toad, a famous, respected, distinguished Toad! Things may look a little cloudy for me just now, but I refuse, absolutely _refuse_, to be laughed at by a barge-woman!”

The woman stepped closer and bent down to squint sharply under his bonnet. “Well, so you are!” she exclaimed. “I never did! A horrible, nasty, creeping Toad! And on my own clean barge, too! I won’t stand for _that_, and that’s flat.”

Letting go of the tiller for an instant, she flung out one huge, speckled arm and seized Toad by a front leg; her other hand clamped hard around a hind leg. Next, the whole world flipped upside down, the barge seemed to float lightly away across the sky, the wind shrieked past his ears, and Toad was sailing through the air, turning over and over as he flew.

The water, when he finally reached it with a loud splash, turned out to be quite cold enough for his taste, though its chill wasn’t enough to quench his proud spirit or cool the heat of his furious temper. He came up spluttering, and when he had wiped the duckweed out of his eyes, the first thing he saw was the fat barge-woman looking back at him over the stern of the departing barge and laughing. As he coughed and choked, he vowed to get even with her.

He struck out for the shore, but the cotton gown got badly in his way, and when he finally touched land he found it hard to climb the steep bank without help. He had to rest a minute or two to catch his breath. Then, gathering his wet skirts up over his arms, he started running after the barge as fast as his legs would carry him, wild with indignation and thirsting for revenge.

The barge-woman was still laughing as he came running up alongside. “Feed yourself through the mangle, washerwoman,” she called, “then iron your face flat and give it a crimp, and you’ll make a perfectly respectable-looking Toad!”

Toad didn’t bother to answer. What he craved was solid revenge, not cheap, breezy triumphs made of words, although he had one or two remarks tucked away that he would happily have delivered. Instead, he spotted just what he needed up ahead. He dashed forward and caught up with the horse, slipped the towrope loose and let it fall, sprang lightly onto the horse’s back, and drove it into a gallop with some hearty kicks in the ribs. Leaving the towpath behind, he turned his mount toward open country and down a bumpy lane. Once he glanced back: the barge had run aground against the opposite bank of the canal, and the barge-woman was flinging her arms about and yelling, “Stop, stop, stop!” “I’ve heard that tune before,” said Toad with a laugh, and he spurred his steed on through its headlong race.

The barge-horse wasn’t built for any very long effort, and its gallop soon slowed to a trot, and its trot to an easy walk. But Toad was perfectly content with this, knowing that he, at any rate, was moving, and the barge was not. He had quite recovered his temper now that he had done something he considered really clever. He was happy to jog along quietly in the sun, steering his horse along side roads and bridle-paths, and trying to forget how very long it had been since his last square meal, until the canal was left far behind him.

He had traveled some miles, his horse and he, and he was feeling drowsy in the hot sunshine, when the horse stopped, lowered his head and began to nibble the grass. Toad woke up and only just saved himself from tumbling off, with an effort. He looked around and found that he was on a wide common, dotted as far as he could see with patches of gorse and bramble. Near him stood a shabby gypsy caravan, and beside it a man sat on an upturned bucket, very busy smoking and staring out at the wide world. A fire of sticks was burning close by, and over the fire hung an iron pot, and out of that pot came bubblings and gurglings and a vague, suggestive steaminess. There were smells, too—warm, rich and varied smells—that twined and twisted and wreathed themselves at last into one complete, luscious, perfect smell, which seemed like the very soul of Nature taking shape and appearing to her children, a true Goddess, a mother of solace and comfort. Toad now knew very well that he had not really been hungry before. What he had felt earlier in the day had been a mere trifling pang. This was the real thing at last, no mistake about it, and it would have to be dealt with quickly, or there would be trouble for somebody or something. He looked the gypsy over carefully, wondering vaguely whether it would be easier to fight him or to sweet-talk him. So there he sat, sniffing and sniffing and looking at the gypsy, and the gypsy sat and smoked, and looked at him.
After a while the gypsy took the pipe out of his mouth and asked, as if it hardly mattered, “Want to sell that horse of yours?”

Toad was completely caught off guard. He had no idea that gypsies loved a bit of horse-trading and never passed up a chance at it, and it hadn’t crossed his mind that caravans were always traveling and needed a lot of pulling. He had never thought of turning the horse into cash, but the gypsy’s question seemed to open a path toward the two things he wanted so badly—ready money and a hearty breakfast.

“What?” he said. “Me, sell this beautiful young horse of mine? Oh, no; that’s out of the question. Who would take the laundry home to my customers every week? Besides, I’m far too fond of him, and he simply adores me.”
“Try loving a donkey instead,” suggested the gypsy. “Some folks do.”

“Apparently it escapes you,” Toad went on, “that this splendid horse of mine is far above your station. He’s partly a blood horse, you see; not the part that shows, naturally—some other part. And in his time he won prizes as a Hackney, too—that was before your day, mind you, but anybody who knows a thing about horses can still spot it right away. No, no, selling him is not to be thought of for a moment. Still, what would you care to offer me for this beautiful young horse of mine?”

The gypsy looked the horse over, then looked Toad over just as carefully, then looked at the horse again. “A shilling a leg,” he said shortly, and turned away, puffing on his pipe and staring down the whole wide world.
“A shilling a leg?” cried Toad. “Kindly give me a little time to figure that out and see exactly what it adds up to.”

He climbed down from his horse, left it to graze, sat down beside the gypsy, and counted on his fingers. At last he said, “A shilling a leg? Why, that comes to exactly four shillings, and not a penny more. Oh, no; I couldn’t dream of taking four shillings for this beautiful young horse of mine.”
“Well,” said the gypsy, “I’ll tell you what I’ll do. I’ll make it five shillings, and that’s three and sixpence more than the animal is worth. And that’s my final word.”

Then Toad sat and thought it over, long and hard. He was hungry and had no money at all, he was still some distance from home—he couldn’t tell how far—and his enemies might still be hunting for him. To someone in that position, five shillings can look like a great deal of money. On the other hand, it didn’t seem like much to get for a horse. But then again, the horse hadn’t cost him a thing, so whatever he got was pure profit. At last he said firmly, “Listen here, gypsy! I’ll tell you what we’ll do; and this is _my_ final word. You will hand over six shillings and sixpence, cash on the spot; and in addition to that, you will give me as much breakfast as I can possibly eat, at one sitting of course, out of that iron pot of yours that keeps sending out such delicious, exciting smells. In return, I will hand over my spirited young horse, with all the beautiful harness and trimmings on him thrown in for free. If that’s not good enough for you, say so, and I’ll be on my way. I know a man near here who’s wanted this horse of mine for years.”

The gypsy grumbled terribly and declared that a few more deals like this would ruin him. But in the end he dragged a grubby canvas bag from deep in his trouser pocket and counted six shillings and sixpence into Toad’s paw. Then he ducked into the caravan for a moment and came back with a big iron plate and a knife, fork, and spoon. He tipped up the pot, and a glorious stream of hot, rich stew gurgled onto the plate. It was truly the most beautiful stew in the world, made of partridges, and pheasants, and chickens, and hares, and rabbits, and peahens, and guinea fowl, and one or two other things. Toad held the plate on his lap, nearly in tears, and ate, and ate, and ate, and kept asking for more, and the gypsy never begrudged him any. He thought he had never had so good a breakfast in all his life.

Once Toad had loaded up on as much stew as he believed he could hold, he stood, told the gypsy good-bye, and bade the horse a tender farewell. The gypsy knew the riverside well and pointed out the way, and off Toad went on his travels again, in the highest of spirits. He was really a very different Toad from the creature he had been an hour earlier. The sun was shining brightly, his damp clothes had dried out completely, there was money in his pocket again, home and friends and safety were drawing near, and best of all, he had put away a hearty, hot, filling meal, which left him feeling large and strong and carefree and full of himself.

Strolling along merrily, he went over his adventures and narrow escapes in his mind, and how, just when the situation looked blackest, he had always found his way out; and his pride and vanity started swelling up inside him. “Ho, ho!” he told himself as he marched on, chin held high, “how clever I am! There can’t be another animal anywhere as brilliant as Toad! My enemies locked me in a prison, ringed round with sentries and watched all day and all night by jailers; yet I simply stroll out past every one of them, thanks to my talent and my courage. They hunt me down with engines, and policemen, and revolvers; I snap my fingers in their faces and disappear, laughing, into thin air. Then, sadly, a woman with a fat body and a wicked mind tosses me into a canal. So what? I swim to the bank, I grab her horse, I gallop away in triumph, and I sell that horse for a pocketful of money and a splendid breakfast! Ho, ho! I am The Toad, the handsome, the popular, the successful Toad!” He swelled up so much with conceit that, as he walked, he composed a song praising himself and bellowed it at the top of his lungs, even though nobody was there to listen but Toad. Quite possibly it was the most boastful song any animal has ever written.

“The world has known great Heroes,
As history books have showed;
But none whose name will rise to fame
As high as that of Toad!

“The clever men at Oxford
Know all that there is to be knowed.
But not one of them knows half as much
As brilliant Mr. Toad!

“The animals sat in the Ark and wept,
Their tears in rivers flowed.
Who called out, ‘There’s land ahead!’?
The cheering Mr. Toad!

“The soldiers saluted smartly
As they marched down the road.
Was it the King? Or Kitchener?
Oh no—it was Mr. Toad.

“The Queen and her ladies-in-waiting
Sat at the window and sewed.
She cried, ‘Look! Who’s that _handsome_ man?’
They answered, ‘Mr. Toad.’”
The song went on for a great many more verses just like these, but they were far too vain to set down on paper. What you have here are some of the gentler ones.
He sang as he walked, and walked as he sang, and grew more puffed up with every minute. But his pride was about to take a nasty fall.

Several miles of country lanes later, he came out onto the high road. As he turned along it and gazed down its pale length, he spotted something heading his way: first a speck, then a dot, then a blob, and then something that looked very familiar indeed; and a double blast of warning, all too well known to him, reached his delighted ears.

“Now this is more like it!” said the excited Toad. “This is real life again, this is the great world once more, the world I’ve been missing for so long! I’ll hail them, my brothers of the wheel, and spin them a yarn, the kind that’s worked so well so far; and of course they’ll give me a lift, and then I’ll talk to them some more; and perhaps, with luck, it may even end with my driving up to Toad Hall in a motor-car! That will be a slap in the face for Badger!”

He strode confidently out into the road to flag down the motor-car, which was rolling along at an easy pace and slowing as it came up to the lane; when all at once he went deathly pale, his heart melted into water, his knees shook and buckled under him, and he folded up and collapsed with a sickening pain in his stomach. And no wonder, the unhappy animal; for the car coming toward him was the very one he had stolen from the yard of the Red Lion Hotel on that fatal day when all his troubles began! And the people inside were the very same people he had sat watching at lunch in the coffee-room!

He sank into a shabby, wretched heap in the road, muttering in despair, “It’s all up! It’s all finished! Chains and policemen once more! Back to prison! Back to dry bread and water! Oh, what a fool I’ve been! Why did I have to go strutting around the countryside, singing conceited songs and flagging down strangers in broad daylight on the high road, when I could have hidden till dark and crept home quietly by the back ways! Oh, hapless Toad! Oh, ill-fated animal!”

The terrible motor-car crept nearer and nearer, until at last he heard it stop just short of him. Two gentlemen got out and walked around the trembling heap of crumpled misery lying in the road, and one of them said, “Oh dear! This is very sad! Here is a poor old soul—a washerwoman, it seems—who has fainted in the road! Perhaps the heat has overcome her, poor creature; or maybe she has had nothing to eat today. Let’s lift her into the car and take her to the nearest village, where no doubt she has friends.”
They gently lifted Toad into the motor-car, propped him up with soft cushions, and drove on.
When Toad heard them speaking so kindly and sympathetically, and realized that he hadn’t been recognized, his courage began to return, and he cautiously opened first one eye and then the other.
“Look,” said one of the gentlemen, “she’s already improving. It’s the fresh air that’s helping her. And how are you feeling now, ma’am?”
“Thank you so much, sir,” said Toad in a faint voice. “I feel ever so much better!” “Splendid,” said the gentleman. “Just lie perfectly still now, and most of all, don’t try to speak.”
“I won’t,” said Toad. “It’s only that I was thinking I’d be right as rain in no time if I could sit up front beside the driver, with the fresh air blowing straight into my face.”
“What a sensible woman!” said the gentleman. “Of course you may.” And so they carefully helped Toad up into the front seat next to the driver, and on they rolled.

Toad was almost himself again by now. He sat up and looked around, and tried to fight down the shivers, the yearnings, the old cravings that rose up and swarmed over him and took complete possession of him.
“Fate!” he told himself. “Why bother to strive? Why bother to struggle?” With that he turned to the driver beside him.

“Please, sir,” he said, “would you be so very kind as to let me have a go at driving the car for a bit? I’ve been watching you closely, and it seems so simple and so fascinating, and I would dearly love to tell my friends that I had once driven a motor-car!”

The driver found the request so funny that he roared with laughter, and the gentleman asked what was going on. When he was told, he said, to Toad’s great joy, “Bravo, ma’am! I admire your pluck. Give her a turn, and keep a close watch on her. She can’t do any harm.”

Toad eagerly scrambled into the seat the driver had left, took the steering wheel in his hands, listened with put-on humility to the instructions he was given, and set the car moving, but very slowly and carefully at first, for he was determined to be sensible.
The gentlemen in the back clapped their hands and cheered, and Toad heard them say, “How well she does it! Imagine a washerwoman driving as well as that, on her very first try!”
Toad went a little faster; then faster still, and faster.
The gentlemen shouted a warning from behind: “Careful there, washerwoman!” That irritated him, and he began to lose his head.

The driver made a move to take over, but Toad held him down in his seat with one elbow and opened the engine up all the way. The wind rushing at his face, the humming of the motor, and the light leaping of the car under him made his feeble brain reel as if he were drunk. “Washerwoman, indeed!” he cried wildly. “Ho! Ho! Behold the Toad, the motor-car snatcher, the jailbreaker, the Toad who always gets away! Sit tight and I’ll show you what driving truly is, because you’re being driven by the famous, the skillful, the absolutely fearless Toad!”

With a cry of horror, everyone in the car jumped up and hurled themselves at him. “Grab him!” they shouted. “Grab the Toad, the wicked animal who stole our motor-car! Tie him up, chain him, haul him to the nearest police station! Down with the desperate, dangerous Toad!”

Alas! They should have thought; they should have been more careful; they should have remembered to stop the motor-car somehow before trying any tricks like that. With a half-turn of the wheel, Toad sent the car crashing through the low hedge that ran along the roadside. One mighty leap, a violent jolt, and the wheels of the car were churning through the thick mud of a horse pond.

Suddenly Toad was soaring through the air, rising with the powerful lift and gentle arc of a swallow. He enjoyed it, and was just starting to wonder if he would keep on going until he sprouted wings and became a Toad-bird, when he came down flat on his back, with a thud, in the soft, lush grass of a meadow. He sat up. There, in the pond, was the motor-car, almost completely under water, and the gentlemen and the driver, hampered by their heavy long coats, were thrashing around in the water, quite unable to help themselves.

Quickly getting to his feet, he took off across the countryside at top speed, crashing through hedges, leaping ditches, and thundering over fields, until he ran out of breath, felt worn out, and had to slow to a comfortable walk. Once he had got his wind back and could think clearly, he began to giggle; the giggling turned to laughter, and he laughed so hard that he had to sit down beneath a hedge. “Ho, ho!” he exclaimed, delirious with admiration for himself. “Toad strikes again! Toad, as always, comes out ahead! Who talked them into giving him a ride? Who found a way to sit in front, for the fresh air? Who coaxed them into letting him try the driving? Who dumped the whole lot of them in a horse-pond? And who sailed off merrily and without a scratch through the air, leaving those narrow-minded, mean, timid sightseers lying in the mud, right where they belong? Why, Toad, naturally; clever Toad, marvelous Toad, _good_ Toad!”
Then he burst into song again, and chanted at the top of his voice—

“The motor-car went Poop-poop-poop,
As it raced along the road.
Who was it drove it into a pond?
Brilliant Mr. Toad!
Oh, how clever I am! How clever, how clever, how very clev——”
A faint noise far behind him made him turn his head and look. Oh horror! Oh misery! Oh despair!
Two fields away, a chauffeur in leather gaiters and two big country policemen were running toward him as fast as they could go!

Poor Toad jumped up and dashed off once more, with his heart in his throat. Oh dear!” he gasped between pants, “what an _ass_ I am! What a _vain_ and careless ass! Swaggering again! Bellowing and singing again! Sitting around and blabbing again! Oh dear! Oh dear! Oh dear!”

He glanced back and saw, to his horror, that they were catching up. He ran on desperately, but he kept looking behind him, and each time they had closed in a little more. He did his best, but he was a plump animal with short legs, and still they gained on him. Now he could hear them right at his heels. He stopped paying attention to where he was heading and stumbled on, blind and frantic, staring back over his shoulder at his triumphant enemies—when suddenly the ground vanished beneath his feet, he clutched at empty air, and, splash! he was in deep water over his head. It was fast water, water that swept him along with a force he could not fight; and he understood that in his blind panic he had run straight into the river!

He bobbed up to the surface and tried to catch hold of the reeds and rushes growing along the water’s edge beneath the bank, but the current was so strong that it ripped them out of his hands. “Oh my!” gasped poor Toad. “If I ever steal a motor-car again! If I ever sing another vain song”—and then down he went, and came up breathless and sputtering. Soon he saw that he was drifting toward a big dark hole in the bank, just above his head, and as the current carried him past it he reached up with one paw, caught the edge, and hung on. Then slowly and painfully he hauled himself up out of the water, until at last he could rest his elbows on the edge of the hole. He stayed there for some minutes, puffing and panting, for he was completely worn out.

As he sighed and blew and stared into the dark hole in front of him, something small and bright glinted and twinkled far inside, coming closer. As it drew near, a face slowly formed around it, and it was a familiar face!
Brown and small, with whiskers.
Serious and round, with neat ears and silky fur.
It was the Water Rat!

chapters.title: “Like Summer Tempests Came His Tears”
paragraphs: The Rat reached out one neat little brown paw, took a firm hold of Toad by the scruff of his neck, and heaved with all his might. Slowly but surely the dripping Toad came up over the edge of the hole, until at last he was standing safe and sound in the front hall. He was streaked with mud and pond weed, of course, and water poured off him in streams, but he was as happy and high-spirited as ever, now that he was in a friend’s house again, with no more dodging and ducking, and free to throw off a disguise that was beneath his dignity and took so much effort to keep up.

“Oh, Ratty!” he cried. “You can’t imagine the times I’ve had since I last saw you! Such trials, such sufferings, and all of them so nobly borne! And then such escapes, such disguises, such tricks, and all so cleverly planned and carried out! Thrown in prison—and escaped, naturally! Thrown into a canal—and swam to shore! Stole a horse—and sold him for a huge sum of money! Fooled everybody—made them all do exactly what I wanted! Oh, I _am_ a clever Toad, and no mistake! Guess what my latest exploit was! Just wait till I tell you——”

“Toad,” said the Water Rat, seriously and firmly, “you go upstairs right now, take off that old cotton rag that looks as though it once belonged to some washerwoman, scrub yourself thoroughly, put on some of my clothes, and try to come down looking like a gentleman, if you _can;_ because in my whole life I have never laid eyes on a shabbier, muddier, more disreputable-looking creature than you! Now stop showing off and arguing, and go! I’ll have something to say to you later!”

At first Toad was inclined to stay and talk back. He’d had quite enough of being ordered around in prison, and here it was starting all over again, it seemed, and from a Rat, too! But then he caught sight of himself in the mirror over the hat-stand, with the shabby black bonnet perched at a jaunty angle over one eye, and he changed his mind and went very quickly and meekly up to the Rat’s dressing-room. There he gave himself a thorough wash and brush-up and changed his clothes, and then stood for a long while in front of the mirror, admiring himself with pride and pleasure and thinking what complete fools everyone must have been to mistake him, even for a moment, for a washerwoman.

By the time he came downstairs again, lunch was on the table, and Toad was very glad to see it, for he had been through some difficult times and had done a great deal of hard exercise since the excellent breakfast the gypsy had given him. While they ate, Toad told the Rat all his adventures, dwelling mostly on his own cleverness, his presence of mind in emergencies, and his cunning in tight spots, and rather making it sound as though he’d had a merry and thrilling time of it. But the more he talked and boasted, the more serious and silent the Rat became.

When at last Toad had talked himself to a standstill, there was a silence for a while. Then the Rat said, “Now, Toady, I don’t want to hurt you, after everything you’ve already been through; but seriously, don’t you see what a perfect fool you’ve been making of yourself? By your own account you’ve been handcuffed, locked up, starved, chased, frightened out of your wits, insulted, laughed at, and thrown into the water in a most undignified way—by a woman, too! Where’s the amusement in that? Where’s the fun? And all because you just had to go and steal a motor-car. You know very well you’ve never had anything but trouble from motor-cars since the moment you first set eyes on one. But if you _will_ get mixed up with them—and you usually do, within five minutes of starting out—why _steal_ them? Be a cripple, if you find that exciting; go bankrupt, for a change, if you’ve set your heart on it; but why choose to be a convict? When are you going to be sensible, think of your friends, and try to be a credit to them? Do you imagine it’s any pleasure for me, for instance, to hear other animals saying, wherever I go, that I’m the fellow who keeps company with jailbirds?”

Now, here was one very reassuring thing about Toad: he was a truly kind-hearted creature, and he never held it against his real friends when they gave him a talking-to. Even when his heart was most firmly set on something, he could always see the matter from the other side. So even though, the whole time Rat was holding forth so earnestly, Toad kept muttering stubbornly to himself, “But it _was_ fun, all the same! Terrific fun!” and letting out peculiar, smothered noises from somewhere inside, k-i-ck-ck-ck, and poop-p-p, sounds a bit like choked snorts or soda-water bottles being uncorked, he nevertheless sighed deeply as soon as Rat was completely finished, and said, in a most polite and humble voice, “You’re quite right, Ratty! You are always so _wise_! Yes, I’ve been a vain old ass, I see that plainly; but from now on I mean to be a good Toad and give it all up. As for motor-cars, I haven’t cared half so much for them since I got dunked in that river of yours the other time. The truth is, as I clung to the rim of your hole, trying to catch my breath, a sudden thought struck me—a really dazzling thought—having to do with motor-boats—now, now! Don’t carry on so, old fellow, and stomp, and knock things over; it was only a thought, and we won’t say another word about it today. We’ll have our coffee, _and_ a smoke, and a peaceful chat, and then I’ll amble down to Toad Hall, change into my own clothes, and get everything running again as it always did. I’ve had my fill of adventures. From now on my life will be calm, steady, and respectable: I’ll putter around my estate, improve it, and do a little landscape gardening from time to time. There will always be some dinner waiting for my friends whenever they visit; and I’ll keep a pony-cart for jogging around the countryside, exactly as I did in the good old days, before I turned restless and started wanting to _do_ things.”
“Stroll quietly down to Toad Hall?” cried the Rat, in great excitement. “Whatever are you talking about? Are you telling me you really haven’t _heard?_”
“Heard what?” said Toad, going rather pale. “Out with it, Ratty! Quickly! Don’t hold anything back! What is it I haven’t heard?”
“Do you really mean,” shouted the Rat, thumping the table with his little fist, “that you’ve heard nothing at all about the Stoats and Weasels?”
What, the Wild Wooders?” cried Toad, shaking from head to foot. “No, not one word! What have they been doing?”
“—And how they’ve gone and taken over Toad Hall?” the Rat went on.
Toad propped his elbows on the table and rested his chin on his paws; a big tear gathered in each eye, spilled over, and dropped onto the table, plop! plop!
“Go on, Ratty,” he murmured after a moment. “Tell me everything. The worst is over. I’m an animal again. I can bear it.”

“When you—got—yourself into that—that—difficulty,” said the Rat, in a slow, weighty voice, “what I mean is, when you—vanished from society for a while, because of that misunderstanding over a—a machine, you know—”
Toad only nodded.

“Well, naturally it was talked about a good deal down here,” the Rat went on, “not only along the riverside but even in the Wild Wood. The animals took sides, as always happens. The River-bankers stood up for you and said you’d been shamefully treated and that there was no justice to be had in the country these days. But the Wild Wood animals said nasty things, and that it served you right, and that it was high time this sort of thing was stopped. And they got very cocky, and went around saying you were finished this time! You’d never come back, never, never!”
Toad nodded once more and said nothing.

“That’s the kind of nasty little animals they are,” the Rat said. “But Mole and Badger refused to give up, through every sort of trouble; they swore that you would be back before long, one way or another. How, they couldn’t say, but somehow!”
Toad began to sit up in his chair again and to smirk a little.

“They reasoned from history,” the Rat said. “Never once, they pointed out, had a criminal law managed to beat brazen cheek and glib talk like yours, backed by a heavy purse. So they made plans to bring their belongings over to Toad Hall, sleep there, air the place out, and have everything ready for the moment you showed up. Naturally they never imagined what would happen, though they did distrust the Wild Wood animals. And now I’ve reached the saddest and most tragic part of my tale. On one dark night—a _very_ dark night, with a howling wind and rain simply pouring down—a gang of weasels, armed to the teeth, tiptoed up the carriage-drive to the front entrance. At that same moment, a troop of desperate ferrets came across the kitchen-garden and took control of the backyard and the servants’ quarters; and a company of skirmishing stoats, who would stop at nothing, took over the conservatory and the billiard-room and guarded the French windows leading out to the lawn.

“The Mole and the Badger were sitting by the fire in the smoking-room, swapping stories and suspecting nothing, since it was no night for any creature to be outdoors, when those bloodthirsty villains smashed down the doors and burst in on them from all sides. They fought as well as they could, but what good was it? They had no weapons, they were caught off guard, and what can two animals do against hundreds? The villains grabbed them and beat them hard with sticks, those two poor faithful creatures, and threw them out into the cold and the wet, hurling insults and rude remarks after them!”
At this point the hard-hearted Toad let out a snicker, then recovered himself and did his best to put on a very solemn face.

“Ever since then,” the Rat went on, “the Wild Wooders have been living in Toad Hall and doing exactly as they please! They stay in bed till the afternoon, they eat breakfast whenever the mood strikes them, and the house is in such a state (so I hear) that you wouldn’t want anyone to see it! They’re getting through your food and your drink, cracking cheap jokes at your expense, and bellowing rude songs about—well, about prisons and judges and policemen. Nasty, personal songs, and not a bit funny. And they’ve been informing the shopkeepers and anyone else who’ll listen that they’re here to stay.”
“Oh, are they, now!” cried Toad, jumping up and grabbing a stick. “I’ll put a stop to that in no time!”
“There’s no point, Toad!” the Rat called after him. “Come back here and sit down; all you’ll do is land yourself in trouble.”

But Toad was gone, and there was no holding him. He marched quickly down the road with his stick over his shoulder, fuming and muttering to himself in his anger, until he came near his front gate, when suddenly a long yellow ferret with a gun popped up from behind the fence.
“Who goes there?” said the ferret sharply.
“Rubbish!” said Toad, furious. “How dare you speak to me that way? Get out of there this instant, or else I’ll——”
The ferret didn’t say a single word. He simply lifted his gun to his shoulder. Toad had the good sense to throw himself flat on the road, and—_Bang!_—a bullet whizzed past just above him.

Toad leaped up, badly shaken, and bolted down the road as fast as his legs could carry him. Behind him he could hear the ferret chuckling, and then other nasty, thin little giggles picking up the sound and passing it along.
He went back, thoroughly crestfallen, and told the Water Rat.
“What did I tell you?” said the Rat. “It’s no use. They’ve posted sentries, and they’re all armed. You’ll just have to wait.”
All the same, Toad wasn’t ready to give up so quickly. He fetched the boat and rowed up the river toward the spot where the garden side of Toad Hall ran down to the water’s edge.

Once his old home came into view, he stopped rowing and let the boat drift while he carefully studied the shore. Everything looked calm, empty and still. The whole front of Toad Hall lay before him, shining in the evening sun. Pigeons were settling along the straight edge of the roof in little groups of two and three, the garden was bursting with flowers, and there was the creek running up to the boat-house, with the small wooden bridge across it. It was all peaceful and deserted, and it seemed to be simply waiting for him to come back. He decided to check the boat-house first. Very cautiously he paddled to the mouth of the creek, and he was just gliding beneath the bridge when—_Crash!_

A huge stone came plummeting down and smashed right through the bottom of the boat. The boat flooded and went under, and Toad was left thrashing about in deep water. He glanced up and spotted two stoats hanging over the bridge railing, gleefully watching him. “Next time it’ll be your head, Toady!” they shouted down. Furious, Toad swam for the bank. The stoats laughed and laughed, holding each other up, and then laughed some more, until they very nearly had two fits—that is, one fit each, of course.
Toad trudged back wearily on foot and told the Water Rat about his disappointing experiences once again.

“Well, _what_ did I tell you?” said the Rat, very crossly. “And now, just look at this! See what you’ve gone and done! You’ve lost me the boat I was so fond of, that’s what! And completely ruined that nice suit I lent you! Honestly, Toad, of all the maddening animals alive—it’s a wonder you have any friends left at all!”

At that moment Toad saw clearly how foolish and mistaken his behavior had been. He owned up to his errors and his pigheadedness, and he apologized fully to Rat for losing his boat and ruining his clothes. Then he finished off with the honest surrender that always melted his friend’s objections and won him back: “Ratty! I can see now that I’ve been a stubborn, willful Toad! From this moment on, believe me, I’ll be humble and obedient, and I won’t do a single thing without your kind advice and your full approval!”

“If you truly mean that,” said the kindhearted Rat, whose anger had already faded, “then here is my advice. Since it’s so late, sit down to your supper, which will be on the table in a minute, and be patient. I’m quite certain there’s nothing we can do until we’ve seen Mole and Badger, heard what they have to report, and talked it over and taken their advice on this difficult business.”
“Oh, yes, of course, the Mole and the Badger,” said Toad, airily. “Whatever became of them, the dear fellows? I’d quite forgotten about them.”

“You may well ask!” said the Rat, with a note of reproach. “While you were tearing around the countryside in your pricey motor-cars, galloping proudly on thoroughbreds and dining on the best the land could offer, those two faithful, devoted creatures were camping out in the open in every kind of weather. They lived roughly all day and slept hard all night. They kept watch over your house, patrolled your grounds, never took their eyes off the stoats and weasels, and thought and planned and schemed about how to win your property back for you. Honestly, Toad, you don’t deserve friends so true and loyal. One of these days, when it’s too late, you’ll be sorry you didn’t appreciate them more while you had them!”

“I’m an ungrateful beast, I know,” sobbed Toad, weeping bitter tears. “Let me go out and look for them, out into the cold, dark night, to share their hardships and try to prove by——Wait a moment! Surely that was the clink of dishes on a tray! Supper’s finally here, hooray! Come on, Ratty!”

The Rat bore in mind that poor Toad had lived on prison food for a good long while, and that plenty of allowances had to be made. So he followed Toad to the table and kindly cheered on his brave attempts to make up for everything he’d missed.
They had only just finished eating and settled back into their armchairs when a loud, heavy knocking came at the door.
Toad was nervous, but the Rat gave him a mysterious nod, walked straight up to the door and opened it, and in came Mr. Badger.

He looked like someone who had been kept away from home and all its little comforts for several nights. His shoes were caked with mud, and he was rough and rumpled; but then, he had never been a very smart fellow, the Badger, even at his best. He walked solemnly up to Toad, shook him by the paw, and said, “Welcome home, Toad! Alas! What am I saying? Home, indeed! This is a sorry homecoming. Unhappy Toad!” Then he turned his back on him, sat down at the table, pulled his chair in, and helped himself to a big slice of cold pie.

Toad was quite alarmed by such a grave and ominous greeting; but the Rat whispered to him, “Never mind; take no notice, and don’t say anything to him just yet. He’s always rather gloomy and low when he’s waiting for his food. In half an hour he’ll be a completely different animal.”

So they waited in silence, and soon there came another, lighter knock. The Rat nodded to Toad, went to the door, and showed in the Mole, who looked very shabby and unwashed, with bits of hay and straw stuck in his fur.

“Hooray! Here’s old Toad!” cried the Mole, beaming all over. “Fancy having you back again!” And he began to dance around him. “We never dreamed you’d turn up so soon! Why, you must have escaped, you clever, resourceful, brilliant Toad!”
The Rat, alarmed, tugged at his elbow; but it was too late. Toad was already puffing himself up and swelling.

“Clever? Oh, no!” he said. “According to my friends, I’m not really clever at all. All I’ve done is break out of the toughest prison in England, that’s all! And seize a railway train and get away on it, that’s all! And disguise myself and wander the countryside fooling everybody, that’s all! Oh, no! I’m just a silly fool, I am! Let me tell you about a couple of my little adventures, Mole, and you can decide for yourself!”

“All right, all right,” said Mole, heading for the supper table. “Why don’t you talk while I eat? I haven’t had a bite since breakfast! Oh my! Oh my!” And he took a seat and piled his plate high with cold beef and pickles.

Toad planted his feet wide apart on the hearth-rug, shoved a paw into his trouser pocket, and drew out a fistful of silver coins. “Take a look at that!” he cried, holding it up. “Not bad for a few minutes’ work, eh? And how do you suppose I got it, Mole? Horse-dealing! That’s how I got it!”
“Go on, Toad,” said the Mole, enormously interested.

“Toad, do be quiet, please!” said the Rat. “And don’t you egg him on, Mole, when you know what he’s like. Please just tell us, as soon as you can, how things stand, and what’s best to be done now that Toad is finally back.”

“Things stand about as badly as they possibly could,” replied the Mole grumpily, “and as for what’s to be done, well, I’m blessed if I know! The Badger and I have circled the place again and again, by night and by day, and it’s always the same. Sentries posted everywhere, guns poked out at us, stones thrown at us; always an animal on the lookout, and when they see us, my! how they laugh! That’s what annoys me most!”
“This is a very tricky situation,” said the Rat, deep in thought. “But I believe I can now see, somewhere in the back of my mind, just what Toad ought to do. I’ll tell you. He ought to——”
“No, he oughtn’t!” the Mole shouted through a mouthful of food. “Not at all! You’ve got it wrong. What he ought to do is, he ought to——”

“Well, I won’t do it, whatever you say!” cried Toad, getting worked up. “I refuse to be bossed around by you fellows! We’re talking about my house, and I know exactly what to do, and I’ll tell you. I’m going to——”

Soon all three were talking at once, at the tops of their voices, and the racket was absolutely deafening, when a thin, dry voice cut through it, saying, “Be quiet at once, all of you!” and instantly everyone fell silent.

It was Badger. He had finished his pie, swung around in his chair, and was now giving them a stern look. Once he saw that he had their attention, and that everyone was plainly waiting for him to speak, he turned back to the table and reached for the cheese. Such was the respect that this admirable animal’s sterling qualities commanded that nobody uttered another word until he had completely finished eating and had brushed the crumbs off his knees. Toad squirmed and fidgeted quite a bit, but Rat kept him pinned firmly in his seat.
When the Badger was entirely done, he rose from his seat and stood in front of the fireplace, deep in thought. At last he spoke.

“Toad!” he said sternly. “You wicked, troublesome little creature! Aren’t you ashamed of yourself? What would your father, my dear old friend, have said if he’d been here tonight and known everything you’ve been up to?”
By now Toad was lying on the sofa with his feet up. He rolled over onto his face, shaking with sobs of remorse.

“There, there!” the Badger went on, more kindly. “Never mind. Stop crying. We’re going to let bygones be bygones and make a fresh start. But what the Mole says is quite true. The stoats are on guard at every point, and they make the best sentries in the world. It’s no use at all thinking of attacking the place. They’re too strong for us.”
“Then it’s hopeless,” Toad sobbed into the sofa cushions. “I’ll go and join the army as a soldier, and I’ll never set eyes on my beloved Toad Hall again!”
“Come now, cheer up, Toady!” said Badger. “Storming a place isn’t the only way to win it back. I haven’t had my final say yet. Now I’m going to let you in on a great secret.”

Toad slowly sat up and dried his eyes. Secrets held an enormous attraction for him, because he could never keep one, and he loved the wicked little thrill he felt whenever he went and told another animal, after faithfully promising not to.
“There—is—a—tunnel—underground,” Badger announced solemnly, “which runs from the riverbank, very close to where we sit, all the way to the heart of Toad Hall.”

“Oh, rubbish, Badger!” said Toad, rather breezily. “You’ve been listening to the tall tales people tell in the pubs around here. I know every inch of Toad Hall, inside and out. There’s nothing of the kind, I assure you!”

“Young friend,” said Badger, in a very stern tone, “your father was a decent animal—a good deal more decent than certain others I could name—and a close friend of mine. He told me plenty that he would never have dreamed of telling you. It was he who found that passage. He didn’t build it, of course, since it was dug hundreds of years before he moved in. But he repaired it and cleared it out, thinking it might come in handy someday if there was trouble or danger, and he showed it to me. ‘Don’t let my son hear about it,’ he said. ‘He’s a good lad, but he’s flighty and changeable, and he simply can’t keep a secret. If he ever lands in a truly tight spot where it could help him, then you may tell him about the secret passage—but not a moment sooner.’”
The other animals stared at Toad to see how he would take it. At first Toad was inclined to sulk; but he cheered up at once, like the good fellow he was.

“Well, well,” he said. “Perhaps I do talk rather a lot. When you’re as popular a fellow as I am—my friends crowd around me, we joke, we dazzle, we trade clever stories—and before I know it my tongue has run away with me. I have a gift for conversation, you see. People have told me I ought to run a _salon_, whatever that is. Never mind. Carry on, Badger. How is this tunnel of yours going to help us?”

“I’ve learned a thing or two lately,” Badger went on. “I had Otter dress up as a chimney sweep and turn up at the back door with brushes over his shoulder, asking for work. There’s a big banquet planned for tomorrow night. It’s someone’s birthday—the Chief Weasel’s, I believe—and every weasel will be crowded into the dining-hall, eating and drinking and laughing and making merry, with no suspicion at all. No guns, no swords, no sticks, no weapons of any kind!”
“But the sentries will be posted as usual,” remarked the Rat.

“Precisely,” said Badger. “That’s my point. The weasels will rely completely on their splendid sentries. And that’s where the tunnel comes in. That very handy passage runs straight up beneath the butler’s pantry, right beside the dining-hall!”
“Aha! That squeaky board in the butler’s pantry!” said Toad. “Now I understand!”
“We’ll creep quietly out into the butler’s pantry—” cried the Mole.
“—with our pistols and swords and sticks—” shouted the Rat.
“—and rush in on them,” said the Badger.
“—and thump them, and thump them, and thump them!” shouted Toad in a rapture, dashing around and around the room and leaping over the chairs.

“Very well, then,” said Badger, going back to his usual dry manner. “The plan is decided, so there’s nothing left for you to argue and bicker over. It’s getting very late, so every one of you off to bed this minute. We’ll make all the arrangements we need tomorrow morning.”

Naturally, Toad trooped off to bed along with the others, since he knew better than to refuse, even though he felt far too wound up to sleep. But it had been a long day packed with events, and clean sheets and blankets felt wonderfully welcoming after a thin layer of straw on the stone floor of a drafty cell. Before his head had been on the pillow for more than a few seconds, he was snoring contentedly. He dreamed a great deal, of course. There were roads that ran away from him just when he needed them, and canals that chased him down and caught him, and a barge that sailed into the banqueting-hall carrying his week’s laundry right in the middle of a dinner party he was hosting. Then he was by himself in the secret passage, pushing ahead, but it twisted and turned and gave itself a shake and sat up on end. Even so, in the end he somehow found himself back in Toad Hall, safe and victorious, with all his friends gathered around him, solemnly assuring him that he truly was a clever Toad.

He slept late the next morning, and when he finally came downstairs he found that the other animals had finished breakfast long before. Mole had slipped out alone and hadn’t told a soul where he was off to. Badger was sitting in the armchair with the newspaper, not troubling himself in the least over what would happen that very night. Rat, by contrast, was bustling around the room with his arms full of weapons of every sort, sorting them into four little piles on the floor. As he scurried about he kept muttering excitedly under his breath, “Here’s-a-sword-for-the-Rat, here’s-a-sword-for-the Mole, here’s-a-sword-for-the-Toad, here’s-a-sword-for-the-Badger! Here’s-a-pistol-for-the-Rat, here’s-a-pistol-for-the-Mole, here’s-a-pistol-for-the-Toad, here’s-a-pistol-for-the-Badger!” He went on like that in a steady, singsong way while the four little piles slowly grew taller and taller.

“That’s all well and good, Rat,” Badger said after a while, eyeing the busy little animal over the top of his newspaper. “I’m not criticizing you. But once we’ve gotten past the stoats and those hateful guns of theirs, I promise you we won’t need any swords or pistols. The four of us with our sticks, once we’re inside the dining-hall—well, we’ll sweep every last one of them off the floor in five minutes. I’d have handled the whole thing myself, only I didn’t want to rob you fellows of the fun!”
“It never hurts to play it safe,” said the Rat thoughtfully, rubbing a pistol barrel on his sleeve and peering down the length of it.
When he had finished breakfast, Toad snatched up a sturdy stick and swung it hard, thrashing imaginary animals. “I’ll learn ’em to steal my house!” he cried. “I’ll learn ’em, I’ll learn ’em!”
“Please don’t say ‘learn ’em,’ Toad,” said the Rat, deeply shocked. “That isn’t proper English.”

“Why do you keep nagging at Toad?” asked the Badger, rather irritably. “What’s wrong with his English? It’s just what I speak myself, and if it’s good enough for me, it ought to be good enough for you!”
“Forgive me,” the Rat said humbly. “It’s only that I _believe_ the proper phrase is ‘teach ’em,’ rather than ‘learn ’em.’”
“_Teaching_ ’em is not what we’re after,” snapped the Badger. “We mean to _learn_ ’em—yes, learn ’em, learn ’em! And mark my words, we’ll _manage_ it, too!”

“Oh, all right, whatever you say,” answered the Rat. He had gotten himself rather tangled up over the matter, so he crept off to a corner and mumbled away, “Learn ’em, teach ’em, teach ’em, learn ’em!” over and over, until Badger curtly ordered him to stop.
Soon the Mole came tumbling into the room, obviously very pleased with himself. “I’ve been having such fun!” he began at once. “I’ve been pulling the stoats’ legs!”
“I hope you’ve been very careful, Mole?” said the Rat anxiously.

“I should hope so,” said Mole confidently. “The idea came to me when I went into the kitchen to make sure Toad’s breakfast was being kept warm. There was that old washerwoman outfit he came home in yesterday, hanging over a clothes-horse by the fire. So I put it on, bonnet and shawl and all, and marched off to Toad Hall, bold as brass. The sentries were on watch, naturally, with their guns and their ‘Who goes there?’ and all that other nonsense. ‘Good morning, gentlemen!’ I said, very politely. ‘Any washing you’d like done today?’
“They looked down on me, all proud and stiff and haughty, and said, ‘Be off, washerwoman! We never wash anything while on duty.’ ‘Or at any other time?’ says I. Ho, ho, ho! Wasn’t I _funny_, Toad?”

“Poor, silly creature!” said Toad, in his loftiest manner. The truth was that he was terribly jealous of Mole for what he’d just done. It was precisely what he would have loved to do himself, if only he’d thought of it first and hadn’t gone and slept in.

“Some of the stoats turned quite pink,” the Mole continued, “and the Sergeant in charge said to me, very curtly, he said, ‘Now run away, my good woman, run away! Don’t keep my men idling and chatting at their posts.’ ‘Run away?’ says I. ‘It won’t be me that’s running away, a very short time from now!’”
“Oh, _Moly_, how could you?” said the Rat, dismayed.
The Badger put down his paper.
“I could see them perking up their ears and exchanging looks,” the Mole went on, “and the Sergeant told the others, ‘Pay no attention to _her;_ she hasn’t a notion what she’s talking about.’”

“‘Oh, don’t I?’” said I. “‘Well, let me tell you something. My daughter does the washing for Mr. Badger, so that ought to show you whether I know what I’m talking about; and _you’ll_ find out soon enough, too! A hundred bloodthirsty badgers, armed with rifles, are going to attack Toad Hall tonight, coming in across the paddock. Six boatloads of Rats, with pistols and cutlasses, will row up the river and land in the garden; while a hand-picked force of Toads, known as the Die-hards, or the Death-or-Glory Toads, will charge the orchard and sweep everything before them, yelling for revenge. There won’t be much of you left to wash by the time they’re through with you, unless you get out while you still can!’ Then I ran off, and once I was out of sight I hid; and after a while I came creeping back along the ditch and peeked at them through the hedge. They were all nervous and flustered, dashing off in every direction at once, tripping over each other, and everybody giving orders to everybody else and nobody listening; and the Sergeant kept sending groups of stoats off to far corners of the grounds, and then sending other fellows to fetch them back again; and I heard them grumbling to each other, ‘That’s just like the weasels; they get to stay nice and comfortable in the banqueting hall, with feasting and toasts and songs and all sorts of fun, while we have to stand guard out in the cold and the dark, and in the end get cut to pieces by bloodthirsty Badgers!’”
“Oh, you silly ass, Mole!” cried Toad. “You’ve gone and spoiled everything!”

“Mole,” the Badger said in his quiet, dry manner, “there’s more good sense in your little finger than certain other animals can boast of in their whole plump bodies. You’ve handled everything beautifully, and I’m starting to have great hopes for you. Good Mole! Clever Mole!”

Toad was simply wild with jealousy, especially since he couldn’t for the life of him work out what Mole had done that was so especially clever; but, luckily for him, before he could lose his temper or lay himself open to Badger’s sarcasm, the bell rang for lunch.

The meal was plain but sustaining: bacon, broad beans, and a macaroni pudding. When every plate was clean, the Badger sank into an armchair and announced, “Well, we’ve got our work cut out for us tonight, and it’ll likely be quite late before we’re through, so I’m going to catch forty winks while I can.” Then he drew a handkerchief over his face, and before long he was snoring.

The anxious, hard-working Rat went straight back to his preparations, running to and fro between his four little heaps and muttering, “Here’s-a-belt-for-the-Rat, here’s-a-belt-for-the-Mole, here’s-a-belt-for-the-Toad, here’s-a-belt-for-the-Badger!” and so on, with every new piece of equipment he dug out, of which there seemed to be no end; so Mole slipped his arm through Toad’s, led him out into the fresh air, plopped him into a wicker chair, and made him tell all his adventures from start to finish, which Toad was only too happy to do. Mole was a good listener, and Toad, with nobody to check his claims or criticize him unkindly, let himself go quite freely. In fact, much of what he told belonged more properly to the category of what-might-have-happened-if-I’d-only-thought-of-it-in-time-instead-of ten-minutes-afterwards. Those are always the best and the juiciest adventures; and why shouldn’t they be truly ours, just as much as the rather feeble things that actually happen?

chapters.title: The Return of Ulysses
paragraphs: As darkness fell, the Rat, looking excited and mysterious, called them back into the parlor, lined each of them up next to his own little pile, and began to outfit them for the coming expedition. He took it all very seriously and thoroughly, and the business ate up a good deal of time. First came a belt for each animal, then a sword to stick into each belt, then a cutlass on the other side to balance it. After that came a pair of pistols, a policeman’s truncheon, several pairs of handcuffs, some bandages and sticking plaster, and a flask and a sandwich case. The Badger laughed good-naturedly and said, “All right, Ratty! It keeps you happy and it doesn’t hurt me. I’m going to do everything I have to do with this stick right here.” But the Rat only said, “_Please_, Badger. I wouldn’t want you to blame me afterward and say I’d forgotten _something!_”

When everything was finally ready, the Badger picked up a dark lantern in one paw, gripped his big stick in the other, and said, “Right, follow me! Mole goes first, “cos I’m very pleased with him; Rat next; Toad last. And listen here, Toady! Don’t chatter the way you usually do, or you’ll be sent back, as sure as anything!”

Toad was so afraid of being left out that he accepted his lowly place without a murmur, and the animals set off. The Badger led them a short way along the river, then suddenly swung himself over the edge and into a hole in the riverbank, a little above the water. The Mole and the Rat followed in silence, swinging into the hole successfully, just as they had watched the Badger do. But when Toad’s turn came, of course he slipped and fell into the water with a loud splash and a squeal of alarm. His friends hauled him out, rubbed him down, wrung him out in a hurry, comforted him, and stood him back on his feet. But the Badger was truly angry, and told him that the very next time he made a fool of himself he would certainly be left behind.
And so at last they were inside the secret passage, and the expedition to take back the house had truly begun!

The tunnel was cold, dark, damp, low and narrow, and poor Toad started to shiver—partly out of dread at what might be waiting ahead, and partly because he was soaked to the skin. The lantern was a long way in front, and in the blackness he kept slipping a little behind. Then he heard Rat call back in warning, “_Come_ on, Toad!” and such terror seized him at the thought of being abandoned alone in the dark that he “came on” at a headlong rush, and crashed the Rat into the Mole and the Mole into the Badger, and for a moment nobody knew which way was up. The Badger took it for an attack from the rear, and since there was no space to swing a stick or a cutlass, he whipped out a pistol and was about to put a bullet in Toad. When he learned what had truly happened, he was furious, and said, “Well, this time that wretched Toad _shall_ be left behind!”

But Toad whimpered, and the other two promised to answer for his good behavior, and at last the Badger calmed down and the procession moved on. Only this time the Rat marched at the back, keeping a firm grip on Toad’s shoulder.
So they felt their way and shuffled along, ears pricked up and paws resting on their pistols, until at last the Badger said, “We should be just about underneath the Hall by now.”

Then suddenly they heard a confused rumble of sound, which seemed far away and yet also almost directly over their heads, as if people were shouting and cheering and stamping on the floor and banging on tables. Toad’s nervous terrors all came back, but the Badger just remarked calmly, “They _are_ carrying on, those Weasels!”

The tunnel started to climb. They groped forward a bit farther, and the racket broke out once more, plainly this time and right overhead. “Hoo-ray-hooray-hoo-ray-hooray!” they heard, with the drumming of little feet on the floor and the clink of glasses as small fists banged on a table. “_What_ a time they’re having!” said the Badger. “Come on!” They hurried until the passage ended abruptly, and they found themselves under the trapdoor leading up into the butler’s pantry.

Such a tremendous racket was going on in the banqueting hall that there was little risk of anyone overhearing them. The Badger said, “Now, boys, all together!” and the four of them set their shoulders against the trap door and heaved it back. Boosting one another up, they found themselves standing in the pantry, with only a door between them and the banqueting hall, where their unsuspecting enemies were carousing.

Coming out of the passage, they were met by a din that was positively deafening. At last, as the cheers and hammering gradually faded, one voice rose out of it: “Well, I don’t mean to keep you much longer”—(great applause)—“but before I take my seat”—(renewed cheering)—“I’d like to say a word about our generous host, Mr. Toad. We all know Toad!”—(great laughter)—“_Good_ Toad, _modest_ Toad, _honest_ Toad!” (shrieks of merriment).
“Just let me get my hands on him!” muttered Toad, grinding his teeth.
“Hold on a minute!” said the Badger, barely managing to hold him back. “Get ready, all of you!”
“—Let me sing you a little song,” the voice went on, “which I have composed about Toad”—(prolonged applause).
Then the Chief Weasel—for it was he—began in a high, squeaky voice—

“Toad he went out on a spree
Happily down the street—”
The Badger drew himself up, gripped his stick firmly in both paws, glanced around at his comrades, and cried—
“The hour has come! Follow me!”
And he threw the door wide open.
Goodness!
What a squealing and squeaking and screeching filled the air!

No wonder the terrified weasels dove under the tables and leaped wildly at the windows! No wonder the ferrets dashed madly for the fireplace and got hopelessly stuck in the chimney! No wonder tables and chairs were overturned, and glass and china went crashing to the floor, in the panic of that dreadful moment when the four Heroes strode angrily into the room! There was the mighty Badger, whiskers bristling, his great club whistling through the air; Mole, black and grim, waving his stick and shouting his awful war cry, “A Mole! A Mole!” Rat, desperate and determined, his belt bulging with weapons of every age and every kind; Toad, frantic with excitement and wounded pride, swollen to twice his usual size, leaping into the air and letting out Toad-whoops that chilled them to the bone! “Toad he went out on a spree!” he yelled. “_I’ll_ give them a spree!” and he went straight for the Chief Weasel. There were only four of them in all, but to the panic-stricken weasels the hall seemed full of monstrous animals, gray, black, brown and yellow, whooping and swinging enormous clubs. They broke and fled with squeals of terror and dismay, this way and that, out the windows, up the chimney, anywhere to get out of reach of those terrible sticks.

It was over quickly. The four Friends strode up and down the whole length of the hall, cracking their sticks down on every head that popped up, and within five minutes the room was empty of foes. From beyond the smashed windows came the faint shrieks of terrified weasels scurrying off across the lawn. Some dozen of the enemy lay sprawled on the floor, and the Mole was busy snapping handcuffs onto them. The Badger paused from his labors, leaned on his stick, and mopped his honest brow.

“Mole,” he said,” “you’re the best of fellows! Just slip outside and keep an eye on those stoat sentries of yours, and see what they’re up to. I have an idea that, thanks to you, we won’t have much trouble from _them_ tonight!”

The Mole promptly vanished through a window. The Badger ordered the other two to stand a table back on its legs, gather up the knives, forks, plates and glasses from the _wreckage_ on the floor, and hunt around for the makings of a supper. “I want some grub, I do,” he said, in the rather common way he had of speaking. “Get a move on, Toad, look lively! We’ve won your house back for you, and you haven’t offered us so much as a sandwich.” Toad was a bit hurt that the Badger had no kind words for him, the way he had for the Mole—no telling him what a fine fellow he was or how magnificently he’d fought. After all, he was especially pleased with himself, and with how he had charged the Chief Weasel and sent him flying over the table with a single blow of his stick. Still, he bustled about, and so did the Rat, and before long they turned up some guava jelly in a glass dish, a cold chicken, a hardly touched tongue, some trifle, and a good deal of lobster salad. In the pantry they also found a basket of French rolls and plenty of cheese, butter and celery. They were just about to sit down when the Mole came scrambling in through the window, chuckling, with an armful of rifles.

“It’s all over,” he reported. “As far as I can make out, the stoats were already very nervous and jumpy, and as soon as they heard the shrieks and yells and uproar inside the hall, some of them threw down their rifles and ran. The others stood their ground for a bit, but when the weasels came rushing out at them they thought they’d been betrayed. So the stoats grabbed the weasels, and the weasels struggled to get away, and they wrestled and wriggled and punched each other and rolled over and over, until most of ’em rolled into the river! They’ve all disappeared by now, one way or another, and I’ve got their rifles. So _that’s_ all taken care of!”

“Excellent, deserving animal!” said the Badger, his mouth stuffed with chicken and trifle. “Now, there’s one last thing I need from you, Mole, before you sit down to supper with the rest of us. I wouldn’t bother you with it, but I know you’re the one to trust to get a thing done, and I wish I could say that of everybody I know. I’d send Rat, if he weren’t a poet. Take those fellows lying on the floor up the stairs with you, and have some bedrooms swept out, tidied and made properly comfortable. Be sure they sweep _under_ the beds, put on fresh sheets and pillowcases, and fold one corner of the bedclothes back, just the way you know it should be done. Put a can of hot water, clean towels and new cakes of soap in every room. After that you may give each of them a good licking, if it would satisfy you, and send them off through the back door—we shan’t be seeing any more of _them_, I fancy. Then come back and have some of this cold tongue. It’s first-rate. I’m very pleased with you, Mole!”

The good-natured Mole took up a stick, lined his prisoners up in a row on the floor, barked “Quick march!” and marched his squad off upstairs. Some time later he came back, smiling, to report that every room was ready and as neat as a new pin. “And I didn’t have to lick them, either,” he added. “I figured they’d been licked enough for one night, on the whole, and when I put the point to the weasels they quite agreed, and said they wouldn’t dream of putting me to the trouble. They were very contrite and said they were terribly sorry for what they’d done, but it was all the fault of the Chief Weasel and the stoats, and if there was ever anything they could do for us to make amends, we had only to say so. So I handed each of them a roll and let them out the back, and off they bolted as fast as their legs would carry them!”

Then the Mole drew his chair up to the table and dug into the cold tongue, and Toad, gentleman that he was, set aside all his jealousy and said warmly, “Thank you kindly, dear Mole, for all your pains and trouble tonight, and above all for your cleverness this morning!” This pleased the Badger, who answered, “There spoke my brave Toad!” And so, in great joy and contentment, they finished supper and soon retired to bed between clean sheets, safe in Toad’s ancestral home, which they had won back by peerless valor, consummate strategy, and a proper way with sticks.

Toad, who as usual had slept far too long, came down to breakfast the next morning shamefully late. What he found on the table was a quantity of eggshells, a few crusts of cold, rubbery toast, a coffeepot three-quarters empty, and really not much else—which did little for his temper, since it was, after all, his own house. Out through the French windows of the breakfast room he could see the Mole and the Water Rat in wicker chairs on the lawn, evidently trading stories, roaring with laughter and kicking their short legs in the air. The Badger sat in an armchair, deep in the morning paper, and only glanced up and nodded as Toad came in. But Toad knew his man; he sat down, made the best breakfast he could, and merely told himself that he would get even with the others sooner or later. When he was nearly done, the Badger looked up and said rather shortly, “I’m sorry, Toad, but I’m afraid you’ve got a heavy morning’s work ahead. We really ought to hold a Banquet right away, you see, to celebrate this affair. It’s expected of you—in fact, it’s the rule.”

“Oh, very well!” Toad said at once. “Anything to oblige. Mind you, I can’t imagine why anybody would hold a Banquet in the morning. But you know I live for no one’s pleasure but my friends’—I simply find out what they want and then arrange it for ’em, you dear old Badger!”

“Don’t play stupider than you are,” the Badger replied crossly, “and stop chuckling and spluttering into your coffee while you talk; it’s bad manners. What I mean is that the Banquet will be at night, naturally, but the invitations must be written and sent off right away, and you’re the one to write them. Now sit down at that table—you’ll find stacks of letter paper there, with ‘Toad Hall’ across the top in blue and gold—and write invitations to all our friends. If you stick to it, we’ll have them out before lunch. And _I’ll_ pitch in too, and take my share of the load. _I’ll_ order the Banquet.”

“What!” Toad cried, aghast. “Me, cooped up inside scratching out a pile of rotten letters on a glorious morning like this, when what I want is to tour my estate, put every creature and every corner right, and strut and enjoy myself! Certainly not! I’ll be—I’ll see you——Wait just a moment, though! Why, of course, dear Badger! What are my pleasure and comfort beside those of other people! You want it done, and done it shall be. Off you go, Badger, order the Banquet, order anything you please; then run along and join our young friends outdoors in their innocent fun, and never mind poor me with my cares and toils. I give up this lovely morning on the altar of duty and friendship!”

The Badger eyed him with deep suspicion, but Toad’s frank, open face made it hard to accuse him of any bad motive behind this change of heart. So he left the room and headed for the kitchen, and the moment the door shut behind him, Toad rushed to the writing desk. A wonderful idea had struck him while he was talking. He _would_ write the invitations! He would make sure to mention the leading part he had played in the fight, and how he had knocked the Chief Weasel flat; he would hint at his adventures and the whole triumphant career he had to tell about; and on the back he would set out a sort of program of entertainment for the evening—something like this, as he sketched it in his head:—
SPEECH. . . . BY TOAD. (TOAD will deliver further speeches in the course of the evening.)
ADDRESS. . . BY TOAD SYNOPSIS—Our Prison System—the Waterways of Old England—Horse-dealing, and How to Deal—Property, Its Rights and Its Duties—Back to the Land—A Typical English Squire.
SONG. . . . BY TOAD. (Written by himself.)
OTHER COMPOSITIONS. BY TOAD will be sung in the course of the evening by the. . . COMPOSER.

The idea delighted him enormously, and he worked so hard that all the letters were finished by noon. Just then he was told that a small, rather bedraggled weasel was at the door, timidly asking whether he could be of any help to the gentlemen. Toad strutted out and found one of the prisoners from the night before, very respectful and eager to please. He patted him on the head, pushed the bundle of invitations into his paw, and told him to run along quickly and deliver them as fast as he could; and if he cared to come back in the evening, there might be a shilling for him, or then again there might not. The poor weasel seemed truly grateful, and hurried off eagerly to do his errand.

When the other animals came back for lunch, noisy and windblown after a morning on the river, Mole, whose conscience had been nagging him, looked uneasily at Toad, expecting to find him sulking or low. Instead Toad was so cocky and puffed up that Mole began to suspect something, while Rat and Badger traded meaningful looks.

The moment the meal ended, Toad pushed his paws deep into his trouser pockets, tossed out a careless “Well, look after yourselves, you fellows! Ask for anything you want!” and began to swagger off toward the garden, meaning to think up an idea or two for his coming speeches, when the Rat grabbed him by the arm.

Toad had a fair idea what Rat was after and did his best to slip away, but when Badger firmly took his other arm, he saw that the game was up. The two of them marched him into the small smoking room off the entrance hall, shut the door, and sat him down in a chair. Then they both stood in front of him, while Toad sat silent, looking at them with great suspicion and bad temper.

“Now, look here, Toad,” said the Rat. “This is about the Banquet, and I’m very sorry to have to speak to you this way. But we need you to understand, plainly and once and for all, that there will be no speeches and no songs. Get it into your head that this time we aren’t arguing with you—we’re just telling you.”
Toad realized he was caught in a trap. The others knew him too well; they had seen through him and beaten him to it. All his lovely daydreams lay in ruins.
“Can’t I sing them just one _little_ song?” he begged pitifully.

“No, not _one_ little song,” the Rat answered firmly, though his heart ached at the sight of poor disappointed Toad’s trembling lip. “It’s no good, Toady. You know very well that your songs are nothing but conceit and boasting and vanity, and your speeches are nothing but self-praise and—and—well, shameless exaggeration and—and——”
“And hot air,” put in Badger, in his blunt way.

“It’s for your own good, Toady,” the Rat went on. “You know you _must_ turn over a new leaf sooner or later, and this looks like a splendid moment to start—a kind of turning point in your career. And please don’t think that saying all this doesn’t hurt me more than it hurts you.”

Toad sat sunk in thought for a long while. At last he raised his head, and strong emotion showed plainly on his face. “You have won, my friends,” he said in a broken voice. “It was only a small thing I asked—merely permission to blossom and expand for one more evening, to let myself go and hear the thunderous applause that always seems to me—somehow—to bring out my best qualities. But you are right, I know, and I am wrong. From now on I will be a very different Toad. My friends, you will never have cause to blush for me again. But oh dear, oh dear, this is a hard world!”
And pressing his handkerchief to his face, he left the room with faltering steps.
“Badger,” said the Rat, “_I_ feel like a brute. I wonder how _you_ feel?”

“Oh, I know, I know,” the Badger said gloomily. “But it had to be done. This good fellow has to live here, stand on his own feet, and command respect. Would you want him to be a common laughingstock, mocked and jeered at by stoats and weasels?”

“Of course not,” said the Rat. “And since we’re on the subject of weasels, it’s lucky we ran into that little fellow just as he set off with Toad’s invitations. Something you’d told me made me suspicious, so I peeked at a couple of them, and they were downright shameful. I confiscated the lot, and our good Mole is now installed in the blue boudoir, writing out plain, simple invitation cards instead.”

At last the hour of the banquet drew near, and Toad, who had gone up to his bedroom after leaving the others, was still sitting there, gloomy and thoughtful. With his brow resting on his paw, he pondered long and deeply. Gradually his face cleared, and he began to smile long, slow smiles. Then he started giggling in a shy, self-conscious way. At last he got up, locked the door, drew the curtains across the windows, gathered all the chairs in the room and set them in a semicircle, and took his place in front of them, visibly swelling. Then he bowed, coughed twice, and, letting himself go, sang at the top of his voice to the enraptured audience that his imagination saw so clearly.
TOAD’S LAST LITTLE SONG!

The Toad—came—home!
Panic ran through the parlors and howls rang through the halls,
There was weeping in the cowsheds and screaming in the stalls,
When the Toad—came—home!

When the Toad—came—home!
There was smashing of the windows and crashing of the doors,
There was chasing after weasels who fainted on the floors,
When the Toad—came—home!

Boom! go the drums!
The trumpeters are tooting, the soldiers are saluting,
The cannons are all shooting and the motorcars are hooting,
As the—Hero—comes!

Shout—Hooray!
And let everyone in the crowd try to shout it very loud,
In honor of an animal of whom you’re rightly proud,
For it’s Toad’s—great—day!
He sang it at the top of his voice, with tremendous feeling and flourish, and when he was finished he started right in and sang it all over again.
Then he heaved a deep sigh, a long, long, long sigh.
